an-01.text: Listen to an announcement in a chemistry class.

Before we start today's lab, a quick safety reminder. Starting this week, the department is requiring splash goggles, not regular safety glasses, whenever acids are on the bench. If you don't have a pair, the stockroom will lend you one, but you'll need to leave your student ID there until you return it. Also, please tie back long hair and keep your bags in the cubbies by the door, not under the benches.

an-02.text: Listen to an announcement in a geology class.

Okay, about Saturday's field trip to Miller Canyon. The bus will now leave at seven thirty instead of eight, because the park asked us to finish before the afternoon heat. Meet in the parking lot behind the science building, not out front. Bring water, a hat, and sturdy shoes; sandals won't be allowed on the trail. And don't forget your field notebook, because you'll be sketching rock layers for your next assignment.

an-03.text: Listen to an announcement in a history class.

I have an update about the midterm. Because so many of you asked for more time, the exam will now take place during our two-hour Thursday session instead of Tuesday. The format is also changing slightly: there will be three short-answer questions instead of five, plus one essay. I'll post a list of possible essay topics online by Friday, so you can prepare in advance. Your study guides from last week are still useful.

an-04.text: Listen to an announcement in a business class.

Hi everyone, I'm going over the rules for the group project. Teams should have four members, no more and no fewer. You can choose your own teammates, but please send me your team list by next Wednesday. If you haven't joined a team by then, I'll assign you to one. At the end of the project, each person will rate their teammates' contributions, and those ratings will count for ten percent of your grade.

an-05.text: Listen to an announcement in a biology class.

Next Monday we'll have a guest speaker, Dr. Ellen Park, a wildlife veterinarian who works at a rehabilitation center for injured birds. She'll talk about how the center treats birds and prepares them to return to the wild. Since she's coming in person, please read the short article I posted before class, and come with at least one question for her. The talk will start right at ten, so don't be late.

an-06.text: Listen to an announcement in an art history class.

For your next paper, you'll need to visit the university art museum and choose one painting from the landscape gallery on the second floor. The museum is free for students, but it's closed on Mondays, so plan accordingly. Photography is allowed, but no flash. Take careful notes on color, composition, and the painting's label. Your paper will compare that painting with one of the works we've discussed in class.

an-07.text: Listen to an announcement in a statistics class.

Quick announcement for the statistics section. My office hours are moving from Tuesday afternoons to Wednesday mornings, nine to eleven, in room two-fourteen of the math building. The reason is that the tutoring center is now open Tuesday afternoons, and a lot of you were going there anyway. If neither time works for you, send me an email and we can set up a short video call instead.

an-08.text: Listen to an announcement at the campus library.

Attention, library visitors. Starting Monday and continuing through the end of final exams, the main library will stay open twenty-four hours a day. After midnight, you'll need to show your student ID at the front entrance to come in. The café on the ground floor will also stay open until two a.m. Please remember that the third floor is a silent study area at all hours, so take phone calls and group discussions to the first floor.

an-09.text: Listen to an announcement on the campus radio station.

Good morning. This is a message from Campus Transportation. Because of road construction on College Avenue, the blue shuttle line will follow a detour for the next three weeks. Buses will not stop at the Student Union. Instead, please use the temporary stop on Elm Street, about a block away. Expect delays of five to ten minutes during busy hours. Updated maps are available on the transportation website.

an-10.text: Listen to an announcement at a new student orientation.

Welcome, everyone! I'm one of your orientation leaders. Here's the plan for the rest of today. At one o'clock, we'll split into small groups for a campus tour, so check your name tag for your group color. At three, you'll meet with an academic advisor to choose your first-semester classes. Then at six, there's a free dinner on the main lawn. If it rains, dinner moves to the gym.

an-11.text: Listen to an announcement at the campus recreation center.

Hello, swimmers. The recreation center pool will be closed from November third through the tenth while we replace the filtration system. During that week, students can use the pool at Riverside Community Center for free; just show your student ID at the front desk there. Lap swim classes are canceled for the week, but the instructors will hold dry-land training sessions in Studio B at the usual times.

an-12.text: Listen to an announcement at a campus basketball game.

Good evening, fans, and thanks for coming out to tonight's game! A few quick notes. At halftime, we'll hold a free-throw contest, and three students chosen from the crowd will compete for a semester parking pass. Also, the first five hundred students through the gates received a free team T-shirt. If you got one, wear it to Saturday's home game, when we're trying to fill the arena with our school color.

an-13.text: Listen to an announcement at a campus awards ceremony.

Good afternoon, everyone. It's my pleasure to announce the winners of this year's student poetry contest. We received over two hundred entries, the most in the contest's history. First place goes to Daniel Reyes, a sophomore in biology, for his poem about his grandmother's garden. Daniel will receive a five-hundred-dollar prize, and his poem will be printed in the spring issue of the campus literary magazine.

an-14.text: Listen to an announcement in a physics class.

Before you leave, there's been a change to the final exam that'll affect how you study. Originally, I said the final would only cover material since the midterm. However, after reviewing your midterm results, I've decided to make it cumulative, since several early concepts, especially conservation of momentum, clearly need reinforcement. To balance that out, you'll be allowed to bring one page of handwritten formulas. Printed or photocopied sheets won't be accepted, so start compiling yours now.

an-15.text: Listen to an announcement in an anthropology class.

A reminder about your fieldwork projects. Anyone planning to interview people, even friends or family, must collect a signed consent form from each participant before the interview takes place, not afterward. Forms collected after the fact won't count, and I won't be able to accept data gathered without them. Also, remove names and any identifying details from your transcripts. If your project only involves observing public spaces, you don't need consent forms, but please describe your observation site in your proposal.

an-16.text: Listen to an announcement in a microbiology lab.

Everyone, please listen carefully before handling today's cultures. Although the bacteria we're using aren't considered dangerous, we treat every sample as potentially infectious. That means gloves and lab coats stay on until you've disinfected your bench. Broken glass that has touched a culture doesn't go in the regular glass box; it goes in the red sharps container by the sink. And if you spill anything, don't wipe it up immediately. Cover it with paper towels, soak it with disinfectant, and wait ten minutes.

an-17.text: Listen to an announcement in an environmental science class.

About next Friday's trip to the Pine Hollow wetlands: you'll need to submit the signed liability waiver by Wednesday, or you won't be able to board the van. Bring waterproof boots. The boardwalk is partly flooded this season, and we'll be wading in to collect water samples. If heavy rain is forecast, we'll postpone to the following Friday rather than cancel, so keep that date open. Anyone who can't attend either day should see me about an alternative assignment.

an-18.text: Listen to an announcement in an architecture class.

I'm delighted to confirm that Maria Lindqvist, the structural engineer behind the new pedestrian bridge downtown, will join us on Thursday. Since her talk focuses on the bridge's cable design, I'd strongly suggest reviewing chapter seven on tension structures beforehand; otherwise, much of it may be hard to follow. Because she's speaking during our regular session, attendance counts as usual. Afterward, she's agreed to stay for informal questions, so if you're considering a career in engineering, that's a rare opportunity.

an-19.text: Listen to an announcement in a linguistics class.

Let me clarify the policy on term paper drafts, since there's been some confusion. Submitting a draft is optional, but if you turn one in by November fifteenth, I'll give you written feedback, and you'll be allowed to revise the final version after it's graded. Students who skip the draft won't have that revision option. As for late final papers, they'll lose five percent per day, with no exceptions except documented emergencies.

an-20.text: Listen to an announcement on the campus radio station.

As many of you know, renovation of the library's east wing begins next month. During construction, the print journals and newspapers housed there will be moved temporarily to the Science Annex. Most current journals will remain available, but older volumes will be placed in off-site storage. You can still request them online, and they'll be delivered to the main circulation desk within two business days. We expect the east wing to reopen by the start of fall semester.

an-21.text: Listen to an announcement at a student government meeting.

Good afternoon. Beginning in January, the university will launch a bike-share program with stations at ten locations across campus. Students can ride free for the first thirty minutes of each trip. At the same time, the price of daytime parking permits will rise by fifteen percent. The additional revenue won't go into the general budget; instead, it will fund the bike-share system and expanded shuttle service. Our goal is to give commuters practical alternatives, not just higher fees.

an-22.text: Listen to an announcement at a graduate research symposium.

Thank you all for attending this year's symposium. Before we close, I'm pleased to announce the winner of the Graduate Research Prize. This year's committee faced a particularly difficult choice, but it ultimately selected Kwame Asante, a doctoral student in civil engineering, for his work on low-cost sensors that detect cracks in aging bridges. The judges noted that his project stood out not only for its technical quality but also for its potential to help cities with limited maintenance budgets.

an-23.text: Listen to an announcement from the campus facilities office.

This is an important notice from Facilities Management. Hartwell Hall will be closed this coming Saturday and Sunday while crews replace the building's main electrical panel. Power will be off throughout the building, so anyone with experiments running in Hartwell labs must shut them down safely by Friday at five p.m. Refrigerated samples can be stored temporarily in the cold room at the Life Sciences Building, but space is limited, so reserve a shelf through our website as soon as possible.

an-24.text: Listen to an announcement at a campus sporting event.

Good morning, and welcome to the Fall River Regatta, hosted by our rowing team for the first time in twelve years. Spectators can watch from the north bank, where bleachers have been set up near the finish line. Please don't stand on the footbridge; it needs to stay clear for emergency crews. Free shuttles to the river leave from the stadium every fifteen minutes, and since parking near the boathouse is reserved for team trailers, we strongly encourage you to use them.

an-25.text: Listen to an announcement at a residence hall meeting.

Thanks for having me. I'm here to remind everyone that the fall career fair is next Thursday in the Student Union ballroom. This year, over eighty employers are registered, which is a record. To make better use of your time, we're asking students to preregister online; that way, employers can review your resume before you arrive. Students who preregister by Monday will also get early access from eleven to noon, an hour before the doors open to everyone else.

an-26.text: Listen to an announcement on the campus radio station.

Hi, this is the outreach coordinator for the campus observatory. On Friday night, we're hosting a public viewing session to observe Jupiter, which is especially bright this month. Telescopes on the roof will be available from eight until eleven. Admission is free, but since the roof holds only forty people at a time, visitors will be admitted in groups every half hour. If it's cloudy, we'll move indoors for a planetarium show instead.

an2-01.text: Listen to an announcement in a psychology class.

Okay, before you go, a reminder about research participation. Everyone in this course needs to take part in three hours of psychology studies by the end of the semester. You can sign up for studies through the department website, and each one lists how long it takes. If you'd rather not participate, you can write a short summary of a published study instead. Just keep in mind that the sign-up system closes two weeks before finals.

an2-02.text: Listen to an announcement in an economics class.

Hi, everyone. Starting with problem set four, we're no longer collecting paper copies in class. Instead, please upload your work as a single PDF through the course website by Friday at midnight. If you work by hand, that's fine; just scan your pages with your phone and combine them into one file. Files that are hard to read won't be graded, so please check your scan carefully before you submit it.

an2-03.text: Listen to an announcement in a music appreciation class.

For this unit, each of you needs to attend one live concert and write a two-page response. The music department has several free student recitals over the next month, and any of those will count. If you'd like to go to a concert off campus, that's fine too, but keep your ticket or the printed program, since you'll have to attach it to your paper. Responses are due the Monday after the break.

an2-04.text: Listen to an announcement in a computer science class.

Before next Tuesday's lab, please install the programming environment we'll be using for the rest of the term. The instructions are posted on the course page, and the whole process takes about twenty minutes. If you run into problems, don't wait until the lab starts. Come to the help session on Monday evening in the computer science lounge, and bring your laptop. We won't have time to fix installations during the lab itself.

an2-05.text: Listen to an announcement in a sociology class.

Next week we're doing peer review for your essay drafts. Bring two printed copies of your draft to class on Wednesday. I'll put you in pairs, and you'll each read your partner's essay and fill out a short feedback form, which I'll hand out. The form asks you to identify the main argument and suggest one area for improvement. Peer review counts toward your participation grade, so please don't skip it.

an2-06.text: Listen to an announcement in a marine biology class.

Our trip to the tide pools at Rocky Point is set for Saturday morning. Low tide is at seven forty-five, so we need to leave campus by six thirty to get there in time. Wear shoes with good grip, because the rocks can be very slippery. You're welcome to look at and photograph the animals, but please don't remove anything from the pools. We should be back on campus by eleven.

an2-07.text: Listen to an announcement in a philosophy class.

A quick change to the reading schedule. Instead of starting the chapter on free will on Thursday, we're going to spend one more class on the ethics readings, since our discussion today ran out of time. So for Thursday, please reread the second ethics article and come with one question you'd like the class to discuss. The free will chapter moves to next Tuesday, and everything after that shifts back by one class.

an2-08.text: Listen to an announcement in a nursing class.

Starting next week, you'll begin practicing in the simulation lab with our patient mannequins. Please wear your clinical uniform and closed-toe shoes, just as you would in a hospital. Food and drinks aren't allowed anywhere in the lab, since the mannequins contain sensitive electronics. Each session is only ninety minutes long, so arrive ten minutes early to check in and put your belongings in the lockers.

an2-09.text: Listen to an announcement in a Spanish class.

Okay, about the oral exams next week. Instead of taking them during class, you'll each have a ten-minute appointment in my office. A sign-up sheet is posted on my door, and the time slots run from Monday through Wednesday. You'll have a short conversation with me about your daily routine and your plans for the summer. Since we won't meet as a class next week, use that time to practice speaking with a partner.

an2-10.text: Listen to an announcement in an accounting class.

One thing about Friday's exam: you may use a calculator, but only a basic or financial model. Graphing calculators and phones won't be permitted, because they can store notes. If you're not sure whether your calculator is allowed, bring it to my office hours before Friday and I'll check it for you. I'll also have a few spare basic calculators at the front of the room on exam day for anyone who forgets.

an2-11.text: Listen to an announcement in a film studies class.

Hi, everyone. Just a reminder that this week's film will be shown on Wednesday at seven p.m. in the media center auditorium, not in our usual classroom. The film is about two and a half hours long, so plan to stay until nearly ten. If you can't make the screening, a copy is available in the library's media room, but it can't be checked out or taken home, so you'll need to watch it there.

an2-12.text: Listen to an announcement in a mechanical engineering class.

Before anyone can use the machine shop for your design project, you need to complete a safety training session. Sessions are held every Tuesday and Thursday at four in the basement of the engineering building, and each one lasts about an hour. After you finish, you'll get a sticker on your student ID, and the shop staff will check for it at the door. Without it, you won't be allowed to use any of the equipment.

an2-13.text: Listen to an announcement in a political science class.

Next Thursday we'll hold in-class debates on the topics from unit three. I've posted the teams online; there are four teams of five, and each team has already been assigned a side. You'll have fifteen minutes to present your arguments and five minutes to respond to the other team. Please meet with your team at least once before Thursday to decide who will speak and in what order.

an2-14.text: Listen to an announcement in a nutrition class.

For the next assignment, you'll keep a food diary for five days, including at least one weekend day. Write down everything you eat and drink, along with rough portion sizes. You don't need to change your diet at all; the goal is simply to record it honestly. Afterward, you'll enter your diary into the free nutrition app we demonstrated last week and write a one-page reflection on what you notice.

an2-15.text: Listen to an announcement in a creative writing class.

I've posted the workshop schedule for the rest of the term. Each of you will have one story discussed, and you'll find your date on the course page. Please send your story to the whole class by email at least three days before your workshop, so everyone has time to read it carefully. If you need to switch dates, you can trade with a classmate, but please let me know about the change.

an2-16.text: Listen to an announcement in a botany class.

This Thursday, instead of meeting in our usual lecture hall, we'll meet at the university greenhouse behind the agriculture building. We'll be looking at the tropical plant collection, which ties in with this week's chapter on leaf adaptations. It gets very warm and humid inside, so dress in light layers. Also, bring a pencil and a notebook rather than a pen, since ink tends to smear in that humidity.

an2-17.text: Listen to an announcement in a calculus class.

Hey, everyone. I'm holding an extra review session for the second exam this Sunday from two to four in room one-oh-eight of the math building. I'll go over the practice problems that gave people the most trouble, especially the ones on related rates. It's completely optional, and I won't be introducing anything new. If you have specific questions, email them to me by Saturday so I can include them.

an2-18.text: Listen to an announcement in an organic chemistry lab.

I want to clarify the make-up policy for missed labs, since a few of you have asked. Each student can make up one lab during the semester, and it must be done during make-up week at the end of November. A second missed lab will receive a zero, unless you have a documented emergency. Also, keep in mind that make-up week only offers experiments from the second half of the term, not the first.

an2-19.text: Listen to an announcement in a neuroscience class.

Sign-ups for the journal article presentations open tonight at eight on the course website. Each article can be chosen by only one person, and it's first come, first served. If you don't sign up by Sunday, I'll assign you whatever's left, which tend to be the longer, more technical papers. One more thing: presentations in the first two weeks will be graded a little more generously, since those presenters have less time to prepare.

an2-20.text: Listen to an announcement in an urban planning class.

For the final project, you'll work in groups, each studying one neighborhood in the city. I'm letting you choose your neighborhood, but there's a condition: at least one person in each group must have a car or be willing to take the bus there several times, because you'll need to observe the area in person on different days. Groups that pick a neighborhood without a plan for getting there will be reassigned to the one closest to campus.

an2-21.text: Listen to an announcement in a journalism class.

For your profile stories, I want to be clear about sources. You need at least three people you interviewed yourself, and no more than one of them can be a relative or a roommate. Quotes taken from social media or other news stories don't count toward those three, although you can still use them for background. And if a source asks not to be named, check with me first, because anonymous sources need my approval.

an2-22.text: Listen to an announcement in a finance class.

Let me explain how the weekly quizzes work, because they're different from last semester. There will be ten quizzes, and I'll drop your two lowest scores. Because of that, there are no make-up quizzes, even if you're sick, so missing one just means it becomes one of your dropped scores. However, if you take all ten and score above eighty on each, you won't have to take the cumulative section of the final exam.

an2-23.text: Listen to an announcement in a data science class.

Everyone should have received an email with your cloud computing credits for the semester. Each of you gets fifty dollars' worth, which is plenty for the assignments if you shut down your virtual machines when you're done. Machines left running overnight keep using credits, and once your credits are gone, we can't give you more. So please turn on the automatic shutdown option described in the setup guide before you start assignment two.

an2-24.text: Listen to an announcement in an archaeology class.

Starting today, you'll be cataloging the pottery fragments from last summer's excavation. Please handle each piece with both hands and over the padded trays, never over the bare table. You may wash fragments labeled with a green tag, but those with a red tag still have residue we plan to analyze, so they must stay exactly as they are. If a fragment has no tag at all, set it aside and ask me before doing anything.

an2-25.text: Listen to an announcement in a theater class.

Rehearsals for the spring production start next Monday. Cast members are expected at every rehearsal listed on their call sheet, which I'll post each Friday. If you know you'll miss one, tell the stage manager at least forty-eight hours ahead. After two unexcused absences, your role may be given to your understudy. Crew members don't attend regular rehearsals, but everyone must be present for technical week, which starts April third.

an2-26.text: Listen to an announcement in a genetics class.

Some news about Thursday. Our guest speaker, a genetic counselor from the regional hospital, has had to reschedule, so she'll speak to us the following Thursday instead. That means we'll swap topics: this Thursday we'll cover gene regulation, which I'd planned for next week. So read chapter twelve, not chapter eleven, before Thursday. The reflection paper on her talk will still be due one week after she speaks.

an2-27.text: Listen to an announcement in an ecology class.

For the stream survey, each group will need a water quality kit, which you can check out from the biology stockroom. Kits are loaned for forty-eight hours only, and there are just six of them for eleven groups, so coordinate with other groups and don't keep a kit longer than you need. Also, the meters inside must be calibrated on the day you use them; readings from an uncalibrated meter won't be accepted.

an2-28.text: Listen to an announcement in a Latin class.

For the translation exam, you may bring a printed Latin dictionary, but not one with notes or highlighting, and no electronic dictionaries of any kind. The passage will be one you haven't seen before, about two hundred words long. Since you'll have only ninety minutes, I'd suggest relying on the dictionary for rare words only. Students who look up every word usually don't finish in time.

an2-29.text: Listen to an announcement in an electrical engineering lab.

Your circuit kits are available at the front of the room. Each kit requires a twenty-dollar deposit, which you'll get back at the end of the semester if every part is returned. If you lose a small part, like a resistor, you can replace it yourself from the electronics shop, and you'll still get your full deposit. But if the breadboard or the power supply is missing or damaged, the deposit won't be refunded.

an2-30.text: Listen to an announcement in a public health class.

For the community survey project, your questionnaire needs my approval before you give it to anyone. Submit it by October twentieth. I'll return it within a week, either approved or with requested changes. If changes are needed, you'll have to resubmit, which could take another week, so don't wait until the deadline if you can help it. Remember, you need at least thirty completed surveys for your final report, which is due December first.

an2-31.text: Listen to an announcement in a graphic design class.

The portfolio review is two weeks from today, and you'll need printed copies of all five pieces. The design lab printer is free, but it's only available during staffed hours, ten to six on weekdays, and the line gets very long the week before reviews. The copy center downtown is open later, but it charges per page. Either way, pieces printed on regular office paper won't be accepted; use the heavy matte paper from the lab.

an2-32.text: Listen to an announcement in an education class.

A reminder that you need twenty hours of classroom observation at a local school before the end of the term. The school district now requires a background check for all observers, and it can take up to three weeks to process. You can't begin observing until it's cleared. So if you haven't started the check yet, do it this week. Hours completed at a summer camp or tutoring center won't count.

an2-33.text: Listen to an announcement in a geography class.

About the mapping software for this course. The university license lets you use it only on lab computers or while connected to the campus network. If you want to work from home, you'll need to connect through the university's remote access service first; otherwise, the program won't open. Also, the license server goes down for maintenance every Sunday night from ten to midnight. Remember, assignments are due Monday at nine a.m.

an2-34.text: Listen to an announcement in a literature class.

I've learned that the campus bookstore ran short of copies of the second novel, and the new shipment won't arrive until the end of the month. So we'll read the third novel next instead and return to the second one afterward. The third novel is shorter, so the reading pace won't change much. If you already bought the second novel and started it, keep going; just be aware that we won't discuss it for a few weeks.

an2-35.text: Listen to an announcement in a campus dining hall.

Good evening, everyone. Starting next Monday, Harbor Dining Hall will stay open until midnight from Sunday through Thursday. After nine p.m., we'll serve a lighter menu with sandwiches, salads, and hot soup, but the grill will be closed. Late-night meals will count as a regular meal swipe. On Fridays and Saturdays, closing time will stay at nine, just as it is now.

an2-36.text: Listen to an announcement at the campus library.

Hello, everyone. The library now lends laptops to students at the circulation desk on the first floor. You can borrow one for up to four hours at a time, and you'll need your student ID. Laptops have to stay inside the library, and an alarm will sound if one passes through the exit. If your own computer breaks down, you can also request a laptop for a full week by filling out a form at the technology desk.

an2-37.text: Listen to an announcement at a residence hall meeting.

Hi, everyone. Quick update from the housing office. If you want to change rooms this semester, the request window opens next Monday and closes Friday at five. Requests are made online through the housing website, not at the front desk. Moves will happen the following weekend, and you'll need to clean your old room before you get the key to your new one. Please note that room changes aren't guaranteed, since space is limited.

an2-38.text: Listen to an announcement on the campus radio station.

Good evening. This is a reminder from Campus Safety about our evening escort van. Every night from eight p.m. to two a.m., the van will take students anywhere on campus or to housing within one mile. To request a ride, call the number on the back of your student ID or use the campus safety app. Rides are always free, but during busy hours you may need to wait up to twenty minutes, so plan ahead.

an2-39.text: Listen to an announcement at the campus recreation center.

Hey, everybody. Good news: the climbing wall reopens this Saturday now that its new holds are installed. Before you climb, everyone, including returning climbers, has to complete a thirty-minute orientation, since the routes and safety equipment have changed. Orientations will run every hour on Saturday and Sunday from ten to four. Climbing shoes are available to borrow at the front desk, but you'll need to bring your own chalk.

an2-40.text: Listen to an announcement from the student health center.

Hello, this is the student health center. Our free flu shot clinic will be held next Tuesday and Wednesday from ten a.m. to three p.m. in the lobby of the student union. No appointment is needed, but please bring your student ID and, if possible, wear a short-sleeved shirt, which makes things faster. If you can't come on those days, you can get a shot at the health center itself on any weekday, also free of charge.

an2-41.text: Listen to an announcement at a student government meeting.

Good afternoon. A reminder that student government elections are next week, and for the first time, all voting will be done online. You'll get an email with a personal voting link on Monday morning, and the polls will stay open until Wednesday at eight p.m. If you don't receive the email, check your spam folder first, and then contact the elections committee. Candidate statements are already posted on our website.

an2-42.text: Listen to an announcement on the campus radio station.

Hi, everyone! The fall club fair is happening this Thursday from eleven to three on the main quad. More than one hundred student clubs will be there, from hiking and chess to robotics and film. Walk around, talk to members, and sign up for any club's email list. If it rains, the fair will move to the gym in the recreation center. And the first two hundred visitors will get a free water bottle.

an2-43.text: Listen to an announcement from the campus athletics department.

Heading to Saturday's football game? The athletics department has a new bag policy. Only clear plastic bags or small purses no bigger than your hand will be allowed into the stadium. Backpacks won't be permitted, and there's no place to store them at the gates. Free clear bags will be handed out at the student union on Friday afternoon while supplies last. Gates open ninety minutes before kickoff.

an2-44.text: Listen to an announcement from the campus sustainability office.

Hi, everyone. As move-out week approaches, please don't throw away things you no longer need. We're collecting clothing, small appliances, unopened food, and school supplies in donation bins in every residence hall lobby. Everything we collect will go to local charities. We can't accept mattresses or anything that's broken, though. The bins will be available from May first through the last day of move-out.

an2-45.text: Listen to an announcement from the campus information technology office.

Attention, students and staff. The university email system will be unavailable this Saturday from midnight until six a.m. for scheduled maintenance. During that time, you won't be able to send or receive messages, but any email sent to you will be delivered once the system is back up. The online course system won't be affected. If you have trouble with your email after six a.m., please contact the IT help desk.

an2-46.text: Listen to an announcement from the campus facilities office.

at1-01.text: Listen to a talk in a marine biology class.

Okay, so today I want to talk about a clever trick some ocean animals use to hide. Picture yourself as a predator swimming near the seafloor at night, looking up. What do you see? Moonlight filtering down from the surface. Now, anything swimming above you shows up as a dark silhouette against that light. That's a real problem for prey. So how do you hide when there's nowhere to hide? Well, some animals produce their own light on their undersides. It's called counterillumination. The idea is to match the brightness of the light coming from above, so the silhouette basically disappears. A great example is the Hawaiian bobtail squid. Here's the interesting part: the squid doesn't make the light itself. It has a special organ on its underside that houses glowing bacteria. The squid gives the bacteria food and shelter, and the bacteria provide the glow. And the squid can actually adjust the light, using a kind of shutter made of ink, so the brightness matches the moonlight. Then every morning, it pushes most of the bacteria out into the water, and the population grows back by nightfall. So it's a partnership, and a pretty efficient one.

at1-02.text: Listen to a talk in an astronomy class.

Alright, let's start with a quick question. Which planet is the hottest in our solar system? Most people guess Mercury, and that makes sense, right? It's the closest planet to the Sun. But actually, the answer is Venus. Its surface temperature is around four hundred sixty degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead, and that's hotter than anywhere on Mercury. So what's going on? The key is the atmosphere. Mercury has almost no atmosphere at all, so the heat it gets from the Sun escapes back into space pretty easily. Its night side actually gets extremely cold. Venus is the opposite. It has a very thick atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide. Sunlight passes through and warms the surface, and the surface then gives off heat as infrared radiation. But carbon dioxide absorbs that infrared energy, so the heat can't get out. It's trapped. Now, this happens on Earth too, in a much milder way. It's the greenhouse effect. On Venus, though, the effect is so extreme that the temperature is about the same everywhere, day side or night side, poles or equator. So distance from the Sun isn't the whole story. What surrounds a planet matters just as much.

at1-03.text: Listen to a talk in a geology class.

So, today we're talking about caves, specifically limestone caves, which are the most common kind. You might think caves are carved out by rushing underground rivers, but most of the work is actually done by something much quieter: chemistry. Here's how it works. When rain falls, it picks up a little carbon dioxide from the air, and even more from the soil as it soaks into the ground. That carbon dioxide combines with the water to form a weak acid called carbonic acid. Now, on its own, carbonic acid isn't very strong. You drink it every time you have a fizzy drink. But limestone is made of calcium carbonate, and calcium carbonate dissolves in acid. So as this slightly acidic water seeps through cracks in the rock, it slowly dissolves the limestone and widens those cracks. Over hundreds of thousands of years, the cracks become passages, and the passages become huge chambers. And the process can also run in reverse. When water drips from a cave ceiling, it releases some carbon dioxide into the cave air, and the dissolved minerals come back out of the water. That's how stalactites form, one tiny layer at a time. So the same chemistry that hollows out a cave also decorates it.

at1-04.text: Listen to a talk in a botany class.

Okay, if you've ever kept a plant on a windowsill, you've probably noticed that after a week or so, it starts leaning toward the window. This is called phototropism, growth in response to light. But how does a plant, which has no eyes and no muscles, manage to bend? Well, the answer involves a plant hormone called auxin. Auxin is produced near the tip of the stem, and one of its jobs is to make cells grow longer. Now, here's the thing. When light hits the stem from one side, auxin moves away from the light, toward the shaded side. So the cells on the shaded side get more auxin, and they stretch more than the cells on the sunny side. And when one side of a stem grows longer than the other, what happens? The stem curves toward the shorter side, which is the side facing the light. Charles Darwin and his son actually did early experiments on this. They covered the tips of grass seedlings with little caps, and the seedlings stopped bending toward the light. That told them the tip was detecting the light, even though the bending happened lower down. So the plant isn't really moving toward light. It's growing unevenly, on purpose.

at1-05.text: Listen to a talk in an environmental science class.

Let's turn to something many of you have probably felt without knowing the name for it. Have you ever noticed that a city feels hotter than the countryside around it, especially at night? That's called the urban heat island effect, and on some evenings a city can be several degrees warmer than nearby farmland. So why does this happen? There are a few reasons. First, think about the materials. Asphalt, concrete, and dark rooftops absorb a lot of sunlight during the day and store it as heat. Then, after sunset, they slowly release that heat back into the air, which is why the difference is often biggest at night. Second, cities have fewer trees and less exposed soil. In the countryside, plants release water vapor through their leaves, and that process cools the air, a bit like sweating cools your skin. Third, there's heat from cars, air conditioners, and factories. Now, the good news is that cities can fight back. Some are planting more street trees. Others are painting rooftops white or light gray so they reflect sunlight instead of absorbing it. Some cities have even tested lighter-colored pavement on a few streets, and surface temperatures there dropped noticeably. So small design choices can add up.

at1-06.text: Listen to a talk in a biology class.

So, honeybees have a problem. A single forager might find a great patch of flowers a kilometer or more from the hive. How does she tell her sisters where it is? She can't exactly draw a map. Well, she dances. Specifically, she does what's called the waggle dance. Back inside the dark hive, she runs in a straight line across the honeycomb, shaking her body from side to side, then circles back and repeats it, again and again. The other bees crowd around and follow her movements. Now, here's the clever part. The direction of that straight run tells the others which way to fly. If she runs straight up the comb, that means fly directly toward the sun. If she runs at an angle, say, forty degrees to the right of straight up, the food is forty degrees to the right of the sun. And the length of the waggle run tells them distance. A longer waggle means the flowers are farther away. What's remarkable is that bees adjust the angle as the sun moves across the sky during the day. So the dance isn't fixed. It's updated. Researchers figured much of this out by moving feeding stations around and watching how the dances changed.

at1-07.text: Listen to a talk in a chemistry class.

Now, I want to look at something so ordinary we almost never question it: ice floats. For almost any other substance, the solid form is denser than the liquid, so the solid sinks. Solid wax sinks in melted wax, for instance. Water breaks that pattern, and the reason comes down to hydrogen bonding. A water molecule is bent, with the oxygen carrying a slight negative charge and the hydrogens a slight positive charge. So neighboring molecules attract each other. In liquid water, those hydrogen bonds are constantly breaking and re-forming, which lets molecules crowd fairly close together. But when water freezes, each molecule locks into bonds with four neighbors in a rigid, open, hexagonal arrangement. That structure has a lot of empty space in it, so ice ends up roughly nine percent less dense than liquid water. Here's why that matters beyond the chemistry lab. When a lake freezes in winter, the ice forms on top and acts as an insulating layer. The water underneath stays liquid, and fish and other organisms survive. Now, imagine the reverse. If ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up, layer after layer, and many might freeze solid. So this one odd property of a small molecule has enormous consequences for life on Earth.

at1-08.text: Listen to a talk in an ecology class.

Today I want to introduce the idea of a keystone species. The term comes from architecture. In a stone arch, the keystone is the wedge-shaped piece at the very top, and if you pull it out, the whole arch collapses. Ecologists borrowed that image for species whose effect on an ecosystem is far larger than their numbers would suggest. The classic example is the sea otter along the Pacific coast of North America. Sea otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins eat kelp, the giant seaweed that forms underwater forests. Now, during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, otters were hunted almost to extinction for their fur. And what happened? With their main predator gone, urchin populations exploded, and they grazed the kelp down to bare rock. Researchers have a name for these places: urchin barrens. When otters were protected and returned to some areas, urchin numbers dropped and kelp forests came back, along with the fish, crabs, and other animals that depend on them. So notice what's going on here. Otters don't eat kelp at all, yet they determine whether kelp forests exist. That's an indirect effect passing down through a food chain, and ecologists call it a trophic cascade. It's also a reminder that removing one species can reshape an entire community in ways nobody predicted.

at1-09.text: Listen to a talk in a physics class.

So here's a question children ask all the time, and plenty of adults can't answer: why is the sky blue? Sunlight looks white, but it's really a mixture of all the colors, each with a different wavelength. Red light has the longest wavelengths we can see, and violet and blue have the shortest. Now, when sunlight enters the atmosphere, it runs into gas molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, which are far smaller than the wavelength of the light. Those tiny molecules scatter light in all directions, but not equally. Shorter wavelengths are scattered much more strongly than longer ones. Blue light, for instance, is scattered several times more than red light. This is called Rayleigh scattering. So wherever you look in the sky, you're seeing blue light that's been bounced toward you from all over. Okay, but if violet is scattered even more, why isn't the sky violet? Partly because sunlight contains less violet to begin with, and partly because our eyes are much less sensitive to it. Now, the same physics explains sunsets. When the sun is low, its light travels through far more atmosphere to reach you. By then, most of the blue has been scattered away from your line of sight, leaving mostly the reds and oranges.

at1-10.text: Listen to a talk in an earth science class.

Let's talk about one of the most valuable archives in climate science, and it isn't stored in a library. It's stored in ice. In places like Antarctica and Greenland, snow falls and never fully melts. Each year's snow gets buried by the next, and gradually the weight compresses it into solid ice. So if you drill straight down, you pull up a cylinder, an ice core, that's essentially a timeline, with older ice the deeper you go. Some Antarctic cores reach back around eight hundred thousand years. Now, what can we actually learn from them? Two things in particular. First, as snow turns to ice, it traps tiny bubbles of air. Those bubbles are samples of the ancient atmosphere, so we can measure how much carbon dioxide was in the air at different times. Second, the ice itself records temperature. Water molecules come in slightly heavier and lighter forms, called isotopes, and the ratio between them in snow depends on how cold it was when the snow formed. Put those two records side by side, and you find that carbon dioxide levels and temperature rose and fell together across many glacial cycles. Of course, there are complications. Near the bottom, ice can flow and fold, scrambling the layers. So researchers have to choose drilling sites very carefully.

at1-11.text: Listen to a talk in a plant biology class.

Okay, so when you walk through a forest, you see individual trees, each one apparently standing on its own. But underground, a lot of those trees are connected. The connection comes from fungi. Most plants form partnerships with fungi called mycorrhizae. The fungus wraps around or even grows into the plant's roots, and then sends out incredibly fine threads, called hyphae, far into the soil. Those threads are much thinner than roots, so they can reach water and nutrients, especially phosphorus, that roots can't get to. The fungus passes those nutrients to the plant, and in return, the plant supplies the fungus with sugars it makes through photosynthesis. Now, here's where it gets interesting. A single fungus can link to several trees at once, sometimes trees of different species. Experiments using carbon labeled so it can be traced have shown that carbon can move from one tree to another through these fungal links. Some researchers have argued that large, older trees support shaded seedlings this way. I'd be careful with that interpretation, though. How much carbon actually moves in a natural forest, and whether it really helps the receiving tree, is still debated. What's well established is the basic trade: nutrients for sugar. The bigger network story is promising, but it's not settled.

at1-12.text: Listen to a talk in an astronomy class.

Have you ever noticed that we always see the same face of the Moon? The craters and dark patches are always in the same places. Now, that might make you think the Moon doesn't rotate at all. But it does. It rotates exactly once for every orbit around Earth, about twenty-seven days, so the same side always faces us. This is called tidal locking, and it isn't a coincidence. Here's how it happens. Earth's gravity pulls more strongly on the near side of the Moon than on the far side, and that stretches the Moon slightly, creating two bulges. Early in its history, the Moon spun faster than it does now. As it rotated, those bulges kept getting carried slightly ahead of the line between Earth and the Moon, and Earth's gravity kept tugging them back. That tug acted like a brake. Over millions of years, the Moon's spin slowed until it matched its orbit, and at that point, the bulges stayed lined up and the braking stopped. And the Moon isn't the only body affected. The same process is slowly acting on Earth, too. Our days are getting longer by a tiny fraction of a second each century. In fact, many moons in the solar system are tidally locked to their planets. So what we see in our own sky is actually a very common outcome.

at2-01.text: Listen to a talk in a psychology class.

Okay, let's get started. Today I want to talk about something called the mere exposure effect. So, here's the basic idea: the more often we're exposed to something, the more we tend to like it, even if nothing about it changes. Sounds a little strange, right? Why would just seeing something again make us like it more? Well, think about a song you didn't care for the first time you heard it. Then it keeps playing in the café where you study, and a few weeks later, you catch yourself humming it. You didn't decide to like it. It just grew on you. Researchers have tested this with all kinds of things—unfamiliar words, faces, even simple shapes. In one classic type of study, people were shown shapes so quickly they couldn't say whether they'd seen them before. And yet, when asked which shapes they preferred, they still picked the ones they'd been shown more often. Now, one explanation is that familiar things are easier for the brain to process, and we tend to mistake that ease for liking. But here's the thing: the effect has limits. If the exposure goes on too long, people get bored, and liking actually starts to drop. So repetition helps, but only up to a point.

at2-02.text: Listen to a talk in an economics class.

So last time we defined costs in terms of what you give up going forward. Today I want to look at a way people routinely violate that logic, which economists call the sunk cost fallacy. A sunk cost is money, time, or effort that's already been spent and can't be recovered. Now, in standard economic theory, sunk costs should be irrelevant. Your decision should depend only on future costs and future benefits. Whatever you've already spent is gone no matter what you choose next. But that's not how people actually behave, is it? Imagine you've paid for a nonrefundable concert ticket, and on the night of the show you feel sick and there's a snowstorm. A lot of people will go anyway, saying, "Well, I already paid for it." But the payment is gone either way. The real question is simply whether the evening will be better at the concert or at home. And this isn't just about individuals. Organizations do it too—they'll keep pouring money into a failing project because they've invested so much already. Psychologists suggest a couple of reasons. One is that people hate to admit a loss. Another is that abandoning a project can look wasteful, even when continuing is the more wasteful option. So, the lesson here: when you're deciding, look forward, not back.

at2-03.text: Listen to a talk in a sociology class.

All right, today we're looking at social networks—not the apps on your phone, but the actual web of people you're connected to. And I want to start with a question. If you were looking for a job, who do you think would be more helpful: your closest friends, or people you barely know? Most people say close friends. They care about you, right? But sociologists studying how people actually found jobs discovered something surprising. Many people heard about their jobs through acquaintances—a former classmate, someone they'd met at a conference, a neighbor they chatted with now and then. Researchers call these connections "weak ties." So why would weak ties be so useful? Here's the thing. Your close friends tend to know the same people you know, go to the same places, and hear the same news. Their information overlaps a lot with yours. Acquaintances, on the other hand, move in different circles. They're like bridges to groups you'd never reach on your own, so they're more likely to tell you something you haven't already heard. Now, that doesn't mean strong ties aren't important. When you need emotional support or a big favor, close friends are usually the ones who show up. Weak ties are just better at carrying new information.

at2-04.text: Listen to a talk in a linguistics class.

Today we're turning to what happens when languages come into contact under very particular conditions. Picture a situation—historically, often a trading port or a plantation—where groups of people with no shared language suddenly need to communicate every day. What do they do? Often, what emerges is a pidgin. Now, a pidgin isn't anyone's native language. It's a contact language, and it's typically quite reduced. The vocabulary usually comes mostly from one dominant language, the grammar is simplified—you might see little or no verb inflection, for instance—and it's used for a limited range of purposes, like trade or giving instructions at work. But here's where it gets really interesting. When children grow up in a community where a pidgin is widely used, they acquire it as their first language. And in the process, the language changes dramatically. Within a generation or two, it develops consistent ways to mark tense, more complex sentence structures, and an expanded vocabulary for every area of life. At that point, linguists call it a creole. So why does this matter? Well, for one thing, creoles were long dismissed as broken versions of other languages. That view is simply wrong. A creole is a full, rule-governed language. And the speed at which children build that grammar tells us something important about the human capacity for language itself.

at2-05.text: Listen to a talk in an education class.

So, let me ask you something. When you study for an exam, what do you usually do? I'm guessing a lot of you reread your notes or highlight the textbook. Am I right? Yeah, I see some nods. Well, today we're talking about a finding that might change your habits. It's called the testing effect, or sometimes retrieval practice. The idea is that trying to pull information out of your memory—actually testing yourself—helps you remember it much better than simply reviewing it again. Here's a typical experiment. Students read a short passage. Then one group rereads it a few times, while another group reads it once and then practices writing down everything they can recall. A few minutes later, the rereading group often does just as well, or even better. But a week later? The group that practiced recalling remembers significantly more. Now, why don't more students do this? Part of the problem is that rereading feels productive. The material looks familiar, so you think you know it. Testing yourself, on the other hand, feels harder because you notice the gaps. But that effort is exactly what strengthens memory. So, for teachers, this suggests that frequent low-stakes quizzes aren't just a way to check learning. They're actually a way to create it.

at2-06.text: Listen to a talk in a marketing class.

So, we've been talking about how consumers compare options. Today I want to show you how a company can influence that comparison by adding an option that almost nobody is expected to buy. This is known as the decoy effect. Let's use a movie theater. Say the theater sells a small popcorn for three dollars and a large for seven. A lot of people look at that and think, "Seven dollars? That's a big jump," and they buy the small. Now the theater adds a medium popcorn for six fifty. Suddenly, the large looks like a bargain—only fifty cents more than the medium for a lot more popcorn. And in studies of this kind of setup, sales of the large option tend to go up. The medium isn't really there to be sold. It's a decoy. It's designed to be clearly worse than the large but close to it in price, so it makes the large look attractive by comparison. Now, why does this work? Traditional economic models assume that adding an option nobody wants shouldn't change how people choose between the others. But people rarely judge value in absolute terms. We judge it relative to whatever's in front of us. So, when you're reading a menu or a price list, it's worth asking: which of these options is here just to make another one look good?

at2-07.text: Listen to a talk in an anthropology class.

Okay, last week we talked about markets. Today we're looking at exchange that isn't really about buying and selling at all. And one of the most famous examples comes from the Trobriand Islands, off the coast of New Guinea. It's called the kula ring. So, here's how it works. People on a ring of islands travel long distances by canoe to exchange two kinds of valuable objects: necklaces made of red shell, and armbands made of white shell. And these move in opposite directions. The necklaces travel around the ring clockwise, and the armbands travel counterclockwise. Now, you might be wondering, what are these objects used for? Can you trade them for food or tools? Not really. That's what puzzled early anthropologists. The objects aren't kept permanently, either. You hold one for a while, and then you pass it on to a partner on the next island. So what's the point? Well, the value lies in the relationships. Each exchange creates a lasting partnership, often between people who live far apart. And having famous objects pass through your hands brings prestige. Alongside the kula, ordinary trade often takes place too, so these partnerships help keep a whole network of islands connected. The lesson here is that exchange can be about building social bonds, not just getting things.

at2-08.text: Listen to a talk in a communication class.

Let's pick up where we left off with early theories of mass media. You'll remember that some early thinkers imagined media as a kind of direct injection: a message goes out, and audiences simply absorb it. Today I want to look at research that complicated that picture considerably. In the 1940s and 1950s, researchers began interviewing people about how they made everyday decisions—what products to buy, which movies to see, what fashions to follow. And what they found was that media messages often didn't reach people directly. Instead, they seemed to flow in two steps. First, information from newspapers and radio reached a group of people the researchers called opinion leaders. These were folks who paid close attention to the media in a particular area. Then, in the second step, those opinion leaders passed ideas along—through ordinary conversation—to friends, family, and coworkers who paid less attention. Now, here's what surprised the researchers. Opinion leaders weren't necessarily wealthy or powerful. They were spread throughout every social group, and someone might be an opinion leader about fashion but not about movies. So, what's the takeaway? Personal influence matters, and it often filters what media can accomplish. Later research found the process is more complex than just two steps, but the core insight—that people shape how media messages travel—has held up remarkably well.

at2-09.text: Listen to part of a podcast about the power of default options.

Welcome back to the show. Today I want to talk about one of the simplest but most powerful ideas in behavioral economics: the default option. So, what's a default? It's simply what happens if you don't make a choice. Think about when you install a new app. There's a box that's already checked, maybe for receiving notifications. Most people just leave it that way. They don't really decide; they go with whatever was set for them. Now, here's why this matters. Let's take retirement savings. For a long time, many companies required employees to sign up if they wanted to join a savings plan. Lots of people meant to do it but never got around to it. Then some companies flipped the default. New employees were enrolled automatically, and they could leave the plan anytime they wanted. And participation jumped dramatically—even though the choices available were exactly the same. So why do defaults have such a strong pull? There are a few reasons. Making a decision takes effort, and people often put it off. Some people also see the default as a kind of recommendation—like, "This must be the sensible option." And, honestly, sticking with the default just feels safer. So, next time you fill out a form, take a second to look at what's already been chosen for you.

at2-10.text: Listen to part of a podcast about unusual forms of money.

Hi, everyone, and welcome to another episode. Today's story is about some of the strangest money ever used, and what it reveals about what money really is. On the island of Yap, in the western Pacific, people traditionally used large stone discs as a form of currency. Some were small enough to carry, but others were taller than a person and weighed several tons. And here's the remarkable part: the stone wasn't found on Yap. It was quarried on islands hundreds of kilometers away and brought back by canoe, at enormous risk. So, how do you spend a stone that weighs as much as a car? Well, you don't move it. When ownership changed hands, the stone usually stayed exactly where it was. Everyone in the community simply knew, and remembered, who owned it. There's even a well-known account of a huge stone that sank to the bottom of the sea during transport. Did that make it worthless? Not at all. The community agreed it existed, so its owner's family was still considered wealthy—even though no one had seen the stone in generations. Now, you might think that's odd, but is it really so different from today? Most of our money is just numbers in a record. What gives it value is that everyone agrees on who owns what.

at2-11.text: Listen to a talk in an organizational psychology class.

Today I want to talk about one of the most cited, and most debated, findings in the history of workplace research: the Hawthorne effect. The name comes from a series of studies done in the 1920s and 1930s at a large factory near Chicago. The original question was practical: does better lighting make workers more productive? So the researchers increased the lighting for one group of workers, and productivity went up. Fine, that makes sense. But then they dimmed the lights—and productivity went up again. In some cases, it kept rising until the workers could barely see. So what was going on? The interpretation that became famous was that the workers weren't responding to the lighting at all. They were responding to being studied. Knowing that researchers were paying attention to them changed how they behaved. And that's what we now call the Hawthorne effect: people change their behavior because they know they're being observed. Now, here's the complication. When later scholars went back and reanalyzed the original data, many found it far less clear-cut than the textbooks suggest. Changes in productivity could also be explained by things like feedback, practice, or changes in how workers were paid. So, does that mean the effect isn't real? Not exactly. But it does mean we should treat a famous story with some caution.

at2-12.text: Listen to a talk in a developmental psychology class.

Okay, so today we're going to look at a kind of mistake that young children make when they're learning to talk—and why that mistake is actually a good sign. If you've spent time around a three- or four-year-old, you've probably heard something like, "I goed to the park," or "I saw two mouses." Now, adults almost never say "goed" or "mouses." So where do children get these words? They can't be copying them. Here's what's happening. The child has figured out a general rule of English: to talk about the past, you add "-ed," and to make a plural, you add "-s." And then they apply that rule to everything—even to irregular words that don't follow it. Linguists call this overregularization. And what's really interesting is the pattern over time. Very young children often say "went" correctly at first, probably because they've memorized it as a single word. Then, as they learn the rule, they switch to "goed." And later, they go back to "went" again, once they've learned which words are exceptions. So their accuracy actually gets worse before it gets better. So, why does this matter? Because it shows that children aren't just imitating what they hear. They're actively working out the system behind the language. The errors are evidence of learning, not a lack of it.

at3-01.text: Listen to a talk in a history class.

Okay, so last time we talked about how slowly news traveled in eighteenth-century Europe. Today I want to look at a system that changed that, and it's one most people have never heard of: the optical telegraph. In the 1790s, a French engineer named Claude Chappe built a chain of towers across the countryside, each one within sight of the next. On top of every tower sat a wooden beam with two movable arms. By setting the arms at different angles, an operator could form dozens of distinct shapes, and each shape stood for a letter, a number, or even a whole phrase from a codebook. Now, here's how it worked in practice. An operator would watch the neighboring tower through a telescope, copy the shape he saw, and then the next tower down the line would copy him. A short message could cross hundreds of kilometers in under an hour. Compare that with a rider on horseback, who might need several days. So why don't we remember it? Well, the system had a serious weakness. It only worked in daylight and clear weather. Fog, rain, or nightfall shut the whole line down. And within about fifty years, the electric telegraph arrived and did the same job in any conditions.

at3-02.text: Listen to a talk in an art history class.

Alright, let's get into technique, because technique explains a lot about why some wall paintings survive and others don't. When we say fresco, we usually mean true fresco, or buon fresco. The painter spreads a fresh layer of wet lime plaster on the wall and then brushes on pigments mixed only with water. As the plaster dries, a chemical reaction takes place: the lime absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and forms a thin crystalline skin that locks the pigment in place. The color doesn't sit on the wall; it becomes part of the wall. Now, the catch is time. The plaster stays workable for about a day, so painters divided a composition into sections called giornate, which means a day's work. If you look closely at some Renaissance ceilings, you can actually spot the seams between those patches. The alternative was fresco secco, painting onto plaster that had already dried, using a binder like egg or glue. That's far more forgiving, and certain blues and greens that react badly with lime could only be applied this way. But here's the problem. Secco paint is just a surface layer, so over the centuries it tends to flake off. So when you see a famous mural where a figure's robe has faded to bare plaster, what do you think probably happened there?

at3-03.text: Listen to a talk in an archaeology class.

So, how do archaeologists put a date on a wooden beam from a house that was abandoned eight hundred years ago? One of the most precise tools we have is dendrochronology, which is just a fancy name for tree-ring dating. Here's the basic idea. Every year, a tree in a temperate climate adds a new ring of wood. In a good year, with plenty of rain, the ring is wide. In a dry year, it's narrow. Now, every tree in the same region experiences the same weather, so they all record the same pattern of wide and narrow rings, kind of like a barcode. Researchers start with living trees, where they know exactly which year each ring belongs to. Then they find older timbers whose inner rings overlap with the outer rings of the younger samples, and they match the patterns. By chaining samples together like this, some regions now have master sequences going back thousands of years. So when we find a beam at a site, we compare its rings to the master sequence and see where it fits. If the outermost ring under the bark is still there, we can sometimes say not just the year the tree was cut, but even the season. Pretty remarkable for something you can see with a magnifying glass.

at3-04.text: Listen to a talk in a music class.

Today's topic sounds technical, but stick with me, because it shapes almost every piece of Western music you've ever heard. It's the question of tuning. Here's the problem. If you tune strings using pure mathematical ratios, the intervals sound beautifully smooth. A perfect fifth, for example, is a ratio of three to two. But if you keep stacking those pure fifths, twelve of them, you'd expect to land back on the note you started from, just several octaves higher. You don't. You overshoot by a small amount, called the Pythagorean comma. So something has to give. For centuries, keyboard tuners dealt with this by making most intervals pure and pushing all the error into one or two rarely used keys. That worked as long as composers stayed in comfortable keys. Play in the wrong key, though, and you got a sour, howling interval that musicians nicknamed the wolf. Equal temperament solves this differently. Instead of hiding the error in one place, it spreads it evenly across all twelve notes of the octave. Every fifth is just slightly narrow, so slightly that most listeners never notice. The result? Every key sounds equally in tune, or, if you like, equally a little out of tune. And that freedom let composers move through any key they wanted.

at3-05.text: Listen to a talk in an architecture class.

Okay, before air conditioning, how did people in very hot, dry places keep buildings cool? Today I want to look at one clever answer: the wind catcher. You find these towers across parts of the Middle East and North Africa, rising above the rooftops, with openings near the top. So, how do they work? First, the tower is tall because wind blows faster and cleaner higher above the ground, away from the dust. The opening facing the breeze catches that moving air and channels it down a shaft into the rooms below. Meanwhile, warm air inside the house rises and escapes through openings on the opposite side of the tower. So you get a steady flow of air without using any energy at all. Now, some designers went a step further. They directed the incoming air over a pool of water or through an underground channel before it entered the living space. As the water evaporates, it absorbs heat, so the air arrives noticeably cooler. And here's the interesting part for us as future architects. Engineers today are studying these old towers and adapting the same principles for modern buildings, because they cut energy use. Sometimes the best new idea is a very old one.

at3-06.text: Listen to a talk in a film studies class.

Let's start today with an experiment that's become almost legendary in film theory. In the early 1920s, the Russian filmmaker Lev Kuleshov took a single close-up of an actor's face, a fairly neutral, expressionless face. He then edited it together with three different shots. In one version, the face was followed by a bowl of soup. In another, by a small child playing with a toy. In the third, by a woman resting on a sofa. According to Kuleshov's account, audiences praised the actor's subtle performance. They saw hunger in his face after the soup, tenderness after the child, longing after the woman. But of course, it was the same shot every time. So what's going on? The point is that viewers don't read a shot in isolation. They read it in relation to what comes before and after, and they actively build meaning by linking the two. Kuleshov concluded that editing, not the individual image, was the essential creative act of cinema. Now, I should add a word of caution. The original footage has been lost, and some later attempts to repeat the experiment found weaker effects than the legend suggests. Still, modern studies do show that context shifts how we interpret facial expressions. So the principle holds, even if the story's been polished a bit in the retelling.

at3-07.text: Listen to a talk in a literature class.

Today we're starting a new unit on the epistolary novel. That's a novel told entirely through documents the characters write, usually letters, but sometimes diary entries too. The form was hugely popular in eighteenth-century Europe. So, why would an author choose to tell a story this way? Let's think about what letters give us. First, immediacy. A character writes about something that happened that very morning, often without knowing how things will turn out. So we, as readers, experience the suspense right along with them. Second, letters let us hear several voices. If three characters write about the same event, we get three different versions, and we have to decide whom to trust. That puts a lot of the interpretive work on the reader. Now, the form has drawbacks too. Authors had to come up with reasons for characters to write constantly, and sometimes it gets a little silly. You'll find a heroine describing a dramatic scene in a long letter at a moment when, realistically, she wouldn't have had time to pick up a pen. Writers of the period were teased about this. Still, the influence lasted. Think about novels today that are told through text messages or emails. Same basic idea, new technology.

at3-08.text: Listen to a talk in a computer science class.

Okay, so far we've stored data in lists, and you've probably noticed the problem. To find one item in a list of a million entries, you might have to check every single one. Today's structure, the hash table, avoids that. Here's the idea. Instead of searching, we compute where an item should live. A hash function takes a key, say a student's name, and turns it into a number. We use that number as an index into an array, and we store the record right there. Later, when we want that record back, we just run the same function on the name and jump straight to the slot. No searching required. Now, there's a catch, and it's an unavoidable one. Because there are far more possible names than there are slots in the array, two different keys will sometimes produce the same index. We call that a collision. One common fix is chaining: each slot holds a small list, and colliding items simply share it. As long as the hash function spreads keys evenly, those lists stay short, and lookups remain very fast on average. But what happens if the function is poorly designed and sends most keys to the same few slots? Then you're right back where you started, searching through long lists one item at a time.

at3-09.text: Listen to a talk in a civil engineering class.

So, last week we looked at how tall buildings resist wind. Today I want to show you one of the more surprising solutions engineers use: the tuned mass damper. Picture a skyscraper on a windy day. Every structure has a natural frequency, a rhythm at which it tends to sway. If the wind pushes at the right rhythm, the swaying builds up, and people on the upper floors may actually feel a bit seasick. The building is perfectly safe, but it's uncomfortable. So here's the clever part. Engineers mount a very heavy mass near the top of the building, sometimes hundreds of tons of steel or concrete, and they tune it to the same frequency as the building. When the building leans one way, the mass lags behind and moves the opposite way, pulling against the motion. Energy is transferred from the building into the mass, and dampers attached to it turn that energy into heat. The result is that swaying can be cut dramatically. Some towers even put their damper on display, painted in bright colors, so visitors can watch it work. Now, why not just make the building stiffer instead? Well, you can, but adding stiffness to a very tall tower is often far more expensive than adding one well-placed mass.

at3-10.text: Listen to a talk in a philosophy class.

Let's begin with a puzzle that philosophers have argued about for over two thousand years. Imagine a wooden ship kept in a harbor as a monument. Over the years, as planks rot, they're replaced one at a time with new ones, until eventually not a single original plank remains. Is it still the same ship? Most people's instinct is yes. The change happened gradually, and the ship kept its shape, its name, and its function the whole time. Now, here's where it gets tricky. Suppose someone collected all the discarded old planks and reassembled them, exactly as before. Now we have two ships. Which one is the original? The one made of the original material, or the one that was continuously maintained in the harbor? Philosophers have offered different answers. Some say identity depends on continuity, on an unbroken history. Others say it depends on material composition. And some argue that the question doesn't have a deep answer at all, that same ship is just a label we apply for practical purposes, and the puzzle shows us where that label stops being useful. Why should we care? Because the same question applies to us. The cells in your body are constantly being replaced. So what exactly makes you the same person you were ten years ago?

at3-11.text: Listen to a talk in a medieval history class.

Today we're turning to the craft guilds of medieval European towns. If you were a baker, a weaver, or a shoemaker in, say, the thirteenth century, chances are you belonged to one. So what exactly was a guild? Basically, it was an association of people practicing the same trade in the same town. And it controlled a lot. Guilds set standards for quality, fixed prices, and decided who was allowed to work in the trade at all. Here's how someone got in. A boy, and occasionally a girl, would start as an apprentice, living with a master and learning the craft for several years, often without pay. Next came the journeyman stage. The word comes from the French journée, meaning a day, because journeymen were paid by the day. Finally, to become a master, a journeyman might have to produce a masterpiece, an example of his work judged by the guild. That's where our modern word comes from.
