Now, were guilds good or bad for the economy? Historians disagree. On one hand, they protected buyers from poor-quality goods and supported members who fell ill. On the other, they limited competition and sometimes kept talented outsiders from working at all. We'll read two articles that take opposite sides.

at3-12.text: Listen to a talk in a materials engineering class.

Here's a question that puzzled engineers in the nineteenth century. Railway axles that were strong enough to carry far more than their usual load would suddenly crack after years of perfectly normal service. Nothing had overloaded them. So what was going on? The answer is something we now call metal fatigue. When a metal part is loaded and unloaded over and over, like an axle that bends slightly with every turn of the wheel, tiny cracks can form, usually at a point where stress is concentrated, such as a sharp corner, a scratch, or a hole. Each cycle opens the crack a little further. Individually, the growth is microscopic. But after millions of cycles, the remaining metal becomes too thin to hold the load, and the part fails suddenly, even though no single load ever exceeded its strength. A German engineer, August Wöhler, ran careful tests in the 1860s and found that for many steels, there's a stress level below which a part can survive an essentially unlimited number of cycles. That insight has shaped design ever since. So what do engineers do about fatigue? They round off sharp corners, polish surfaces, and inspect critical parts regularly to catch cracks while they're still small. Notice that none of these steps make the metal any stronger. They just give cracks fewer places to start.

at4-01.text: Listen to a talk in a zoology class.

Okay, so let's think about a problem. A small bat hunting at night has to find a moth the size of your fingernail, in total darkness, while flying. How does it do it? It listens. Most bats use echolocation, which means producing sounds and interpreting the echoes that bounce back. Now, these calls are usually ultrasonic, too high-pitched for humans to hear, and they're incredibly loud, some about as loud as a smoke alarm right next to your ear. So why doesn't the bat deafen itself? Well, just before each call, tiny muscles in its middle ear contract and briefly dampen its hearing, then relax in time to catch the echo. Here's another clever part. When a bat is searching, it calls maybe ten times a second. But as it closes in on an insect, the calls speed up dramatically, to nearly two hundred per second. Researchers call this the feeding buzz. More calls mean more updates on exactly where the moth is moving. Think of it like a camera switching from occasional snapshots to rapid-fire video at the crucial moment. And the moths aren't helpless. Some species can hear bat calls and react by diving toward the ground, and a few tiger moths even produce clicks of their own that seem to jam the bat's signal.

at4-02.text: Listen to a talk in an entomology class.

So, when you think of an insect growing up, you probably picture a caterpillar turning into a butterfly. But that's only one of the two main strategies. Let's define them. In incomplete metamorphosis, the young insect, called a nymph, looks like a smaller version of the adult, just without working wings. Grasshoppers are a good example. A nymph grows by molting, shedding its hard outer skeleton several times, and its wing buds get bigger with each molt until the final one produces a winged adult. Complete metamorphosis is different. There are four stages: egg, larva, pupa, and adult. The larva, like a caterpillar or a maggot, looks nothing like the adult. And inside the pupa, much of the larval body is broken down, and adult structures are built from small clusters of cells that were set aside earlier. Now, why would that second strategy be so successful? Beetles, flies, butterflies, bees, and wasps all use it, and together they make up the large majority of insect species. One popular explanation is that larvae and adults don't compete. A caterpillar chews leaves; a butterfly sips nectar. It's like a company with two separate divisions, one devoted entirely to eating and growing, the other to dispersing and reproducing. Each can specialize without getting in the other's way.

at4-03.text: Listen to a talk in an ornithology class.

Today we're going to look at one of the hardest questions in ornithology: how do migratory birds sense Earth's magnetic field? We know they do. In classic experiments, caged songbirds in the migration season hop in a consistent direction, and when researchers rotate the magnetic field around the cage using electric coils, the birds turn to follow it. So the compass is real. But where is it? There are two main explanations. The first proposes tiny particles of magnetite, an iron-rich mineral that behaves like a microscopic compass needle. The idea was that cells containing magnetite, perhaps in the upper beak, would detect the field directly. Now, that idea has run into trouble. Some of the iron-rich cells researchers found in pigeon beaks turned out to be immune cells, not sensory cells. The second explanation is stranger. It involves a protein in the bird's eye called a cryptochrome. When light strikes it, it creates pairs of molecules with unpaired electrons, and the way those pairs behave depends slightly on the angle of the magnetic field. So the bird might literally see the field, perhaps as a pattern laid over its vision. Here's a clue supporting this: in experiments, the birds' compass worked only under certain colors of light, which is what you'd predict if a light-triggered reaction were involved. Still, the full mechanism hasn't been confirmed.

at4-04.text: Listen to a talk in an oceanography class.

Now, when we talk about ocean currents, most people think of wind-driven surface currents. But there's a slower, deeper circulation that's driven by something else: differences in density. We call it thermohaline circulation, from the Greek words for heat and salt, because those are the two things that control seawater density. Cold water is denser than warm water, and salty water is denser than fresh water. So, where does the deep circulation begin? In just a few places, mainly the far North Atlantic and around Antarctica. In the North Atlantic, warm, salty water carried north by surface currents gives up its heat to the frigid air. And when sea ice forms nearby, the ice leaves most of its salt behind in the water around it. So the water becomes both colder and saltier, dense enough to sink thousands of meters. That sinking water then spreads slowly along the ocean floor and eventually rises again elsewhere, a journey that can take around a thousand years. It's sometimes called the global conveyor belt. Here's the concern. If large amounts of fresh water from melting ice sheets pour into the North Atlantic, the surface water there could become less salty, and therefore less dense. It might not sink as readily. The circulation could weaken, though how much and how quickly remain open questions.

at4-05.text: Listen to a talk in a meteorology class.

So, here's something that surprises people. Hail falls most often in the warm months, not in winter. How can ice fall out of the sky on a hot afternoon? The answer is the thunderstorm. Hail forms inside tall storm clouds called cumulonimbus clouds, which have very strong updrafts, currents of air rushing upward. Now, high in these clouds, temperatures are well below freezing, but a lot of the water there is still liquid. It's what we call supercooled water, liquid below zero degrees Celsius, because it hasn't found anything to freeze onto. So when a small ice particle, called an embryo, is carried up through that region, the supercooled droplets freeze onto it on contact, and the hailstone grows. The updraft keeps it suspended. Some stones get swept up and down through different parts of the cloud, and if you cut one in half, you'll often see layers, a bit like the rings of an onion. Clear layers form where water spread over the stone and froze slowly, letting air escape. Cloudy layers form where droplets froze instantly and trapped tiny air bubbles. Eventually the stone gets too heavy for the updraft to support, and it falls. And the stronger the updraft, the larger the hail it can hold up. That's why the most violent storms produce the biggest stones.

at4-06.text: Listen to a talk in a climatology class.

Today I want to tackle a question that puzzled scientists for over a century: what sets the rhythm of the ice ages? Over the last million years or so, great ice sheets have advanced and retreated again and again. One explanation, developed in the early twentieth century by a Serbian engineer named Milutin Milankovitch, points to changes in Earth's orbit. There are three main cycles. First, the shape of the orbit stretches from nearly circular to slightly oval and back over roughly a hundred thousand years. Second, the tilt of Earth's axis varies between about twenty-two and twenty-four and a half degrees over about forty-one thousand years. Third, the axis slowly wobbles, like a spinning top, over about twenty-six thousand years. Now, these cycles barely change the total sunlight Earth receives. What they change is where and when it arrives, especially how much sunlight reaches the far north in summer. And that's the key. Ice sheets grow when northern summers are too cool to melt the previous winter's snow. The theory was elegant, and in the nineteen seventies, ocean sediment records confirmed these rhythms. But there's a puzzle. For the last million years, the ice ages have followed the hundred-thousand-year cycle, even though that cycle has the weakest direct effect on sunlight. So something on Earth itself, perhaps carbon dioxide or the ice sheets, must be amplifying it.

at4-07.text: Listen to a talk in a volcanology class.

So why do some volcanoes ooze lava gently while others blow themselves apart? Think about Hawaii, where lava often flows out in glowing rivers that people can watch from a safe distance, versus an eruption that blasts ash kilometers into the sky. The difference mostly comes down to two things: how sticky the magma is, and how much gas it holds. Geologists call that stickiness viscosity, a liquid's resistance to flow. Honey has a high viscosity; water has a low one. Now, magma viscosity depends largely on silica. Silica-rich magma forms long chains of linked molecules, which make it thick and sluggish. Basalt, the magma in Hawaii, is relatively low in silica, so it's runny. Here's where gas comes in. Magma contains dissolved water vapor and carbon dioxide, kept in solution by pressure, sort of like the gas in a sealed bottle of soda. As magma rises and the pressure drops, that gas forms bubbles. In runny basalt, the bubbles escape easily, and the eruption stays fairly calm. But in thick, silica-rich magma, the bubbles are trapped. Pressure builds until the magma shatters into fragments, which we call ash, and the result is an explosive eruption. Of course, it's not perfectly simple. Even a basalt eruption can turn explosive if the rising magma meets groundwater.

at4-08.text: Listen to a talk in a paleontology class.

So last week we established that birds are living dinosaurs. Today's question follows from that: why did feathers evolve in the first place? The obvious answer is flight. But the fossil record makes that hard to accept. Since the nineteen nineties, many feathered dinosaurs have been found, especially in northeastern China, and a lot of them clearly couldn't fly. Some had only simple, hairlike filaments, nothing like the stiff, asymmetrical flight feathers of a modern bird. So feathers seem to have appeared long before flight. Now, if not flight, then what? One explanation is insulation. Simple filaments would trap air close to the body, like the down on a duckling, which would help an active, warm-blooded animal hold its heat. A second explanation is display. Some fossil feathers preserve tiny structures called melanosomes, the packets that hold pigment, and their shapes let researchers estimate the original colors. Several small dinosaurs appear to have had banded tails or reddish crests, the kind of patterns animals today use to attract mates or signal rivals. So which is right? Well, these aren't mutually exclusive. A structure can evolve for one job and later be taken over for another. Biologists call that exaptation. Feathers may have started as insulation, been elaborated for display, and only much later been used to fly.

at4-09.text: Listen to a talk in a genetics class.

Okay, here's a puzzle to start with. Almost every calico cat, the ones with patches of orange and black fur, is female. Why would coat color depend on sex? Well, in cats, one of the main genes for fur color sits on the X chromosome. One version of the gene gives orange fur; the other gives black. Now, females have two X chromosomes, while males have one X and one Y. So a female can carry both the orange version and the black version. A male normally carries only one, so he's either orange or black, not both. But wait. If a female has both versions, why isn't she a blend, some kind of brownish orange? This is where X inactivation comes in. Early in development, in each cell of a female embryo, one of the two X chromosomes is randomly shut down, packed up so tightly that its genes are mostly silent. And every cell descended from that one keeps the same choice. So as those groups of cells spread out and form the skin, you get patches, some where the orange X is active and some where the black X is active. The white patches, by the way, come from a different gene altogether. And male calicos do occasionally exist, usually because they have an extra X chromosome, but they're quite rare.

at4-10.text: Listen to a talk in a microbiology class.

Now, we usually think of genes as being passed down from parent to offspring. That's called vertical transfer. But bacteria do something that complicates the picture enormously. They can pass genes sideways, to cells that aren't their descendants, even to different species. We call that horizontal gene transfer, and it happens in three main ways. First, transformation. When a bacterium dies and breaks open, fragments of its DNA float free, and some bacteria can pick up that DNA from their surroundings and incorporate it. Second, transduction. Here, a virus that infects bacteria accidentally packages a bit of its host's DNA and then injects it into the next cell it infects. So the virus acts like a courier. Third, conjugation, where two bacteria make direct contact, and one passes a copy of a small ring of DNA, called a plasmid, to the other. Plasmids often carry genes for antibiotic resistance. So why does this matter so much? Think about how a useful trait usually spreads in animals: a helpful mutation arises and has to spread over many generations. In bacteria, a resistance gene that evolved in one harmless species in your gut can jump into a dangerous one in a single step. It also creates a headache for biologists who try to draw family trees of bacteria, because the branches keep crossing.

at4-11.text: Listen to a talk in a neuroscience class.

Today's question is one of the oldest in neuroscience: what physically changes in the brain when you learn something? Back in the nineteen forties, a psychologist named Donald Hebb proposed an answer that's often summarized as, cells that fire together wire together. His idea was that if one neuron repeatedly helps to activate another, the connection between them, the synapse, gets stronger. Then, in the early nineteen seventies, researchers working with rabbits stimulated a pathway into the hippocampus, a brain region essential for forming new memories, with a rapid burst of electrical pulses. Afterward, a single ordinary pulse produced a much larger response, and that boost lasted hours, sometimes days. They called it long-term potentiation, a lasting increase in the strength of a synapse following intense activity. Now, how does it work? A key player is a receptor called the NMDA receptor. It acts like a lock that needs two keys at once: it opens only when the receiving neuron is already active and is also getting a chemical signal from the sending neuron. That's essentially Hebb's rule built into a molecule. When it opens, calcium flows in and triggers changes that strengthen the synapse. But here's the caveat. Showing that long-term potentiation exists isn't the same as proving it's how memories are stored. That link is strongly supported, but it's still being tested.

at4-12.text: Listen to a talk in a physiology class.

So, picture a duck standing on ice. Its feet are bare, no feathers, pressed against a frozen surface. Why doesn't it lose huge amounts of body heat through them? The answer is an arrangement called countercurrent heat exchange. Here's the setup. In a duck's legs, the arteries carrying warm blood down to the feet run right alongside the veins carrying cold blood back up to the body. And the blood in them flows in opposite directions, which is where the word countercurrent comes from. So as warm blood travels down, it passes its heat to the cold blood coming up. By the time arterial blood reaches the feet, it's already cool, so there's little heat left to lose to the ice. Meanwhile, the returning blood has been warmed before it reenters the body. Now, why does the opposite direction matter? If the two streams flowed the same way, they'd quickly reach the same middle temperature, and heat exchange would stop. Flowing in opposite directions, the blood going down always stays a little warmer than the blood beside it, so heat keeps moving across. Engineers use the same principle in industrial heat exchangers. And you find it in nature again and again, in the flippers of dolphins and the tails of beavers, for instance. Some fish, like tuna, even use it to keep their swimming muscles warmer than the surrounding water.

at4-13.text: Listen to a talk in an astronomy class.

How do you measure the distance to a star that's far too remote for any ruler? For nearby stars, astronomers can use parallax, the small shift in a star's apparent position as Earth moves around the Sun. But beyond a few thousand light-years, that shift is too tiny to measure. So we need another method, and one of the most important came from a discovery made in the early nineteen hundreds by Henrietta Leavitt. She was studying a type of star called a Cepheid variable, which brightens and dims in a regular cycle because the star itself is swelling and shrinking. Now, Leavitt looked at Cepheids in a nearby galaxy called the Small Magellanic Cloud. Since those stars are all roughly the same distance from us, differences in how bright they looked had to reflect real differences in how bright they were. And she found a clear pattern: the longer a Cepheid's cycle, the more luminous the star. That turns Cepheids into what astronomers call standard candles. Measure the period, and you know the star's true brightness. Compare that with how bright it appears, and you can work out its distance, the same way you could judge the distance to a light bulb of known wattage. Of course, the method first had to be calibrated with nearby Cepheids measured by parallax.

at4-14.text: Listen to a talk in a planetary science class.

So, the evidence that Mars once had liquid water on its surface is overwhelming: dried river valleys, ancient deltas, minerals that form only in water. But liquid water today would quickly freeze or evaporate, because the Martian atmosphere is less than one percent as thick as Earth's. So where did the rest of the air go? There are two broad explanations, and they probably both played a part. The first is about size. Mars has only about a tenth of Earth's mass, so its interior cooled faster. Earth's magnetic field is generated by molten iron churning in its core, and Mars seems to have lost that kind of global magnetic field early on. Why does that matter? Without a magnetic field, the solar wind, the stream of charged particles from the Sun, strikes the upper atmosphere directly and gradually strips gas away into space. Spacecraft orbiting Mars have measured this loss happening today. The second explanation is that some of the atmosphere never left the planet. Carbon dioxide could have reacted with rocks and water to form carbonate minerals, locking the gas into the crust. Here's the catch. Orbiters have found carbonates, but far too few to account for a thick early atmosphere. So most scientists now think escape to space was the bigger factor, though the exact balance is still debated.

at4-15.text: Listen to a talk in a physics class.

So, imagine dropping a bowling ball and a feather from a tall building. Which lands first? The bowling ball, obviously. But in a vacuum, they'd land at the same moment, because gravity accelerates all objects at the same rate. Astronauts actually demonstrated this on the Moon with a hammer and a feather. So the difference on Earth comes from air resistance, or drag. Now, drag isn't constant. It grows as an object moves faster. So picture a skydiver jumping from a plane. At first she's moving slowly, drag is small, and gravity pulls her faster and faster. But as her speed increases, drag increases too, until eventually the upward drag equals her weight. At that point the forces balance, and she stops accelerating. She keeps falling, but at a steady speed. That's terminal velocity, the constant speed a falling object reaches when drag balances gravity. For a skydiver lying flat, it's around two hundred kilometers per hour. Now, if she tucks into a head-down dive, she presents a smaller area to the air, so drag is lower, and she must fall faster before it matches her weight. Then when the parachute opens, the huge area suddenly increases drag, and she slows to a much gentler terminal velocity. And an ant's terminal velocity is so low that it can survive a fall from almost any height.

at4-16.text: Listen to a talk in a chemistry class.

Okay, let's start with something that seems contradictory. A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen gas can sit in a container for years without reacting, even though the reaction that forms water releases a huge amount of energy. So why doesn't it just happen? Because of something called activation energy, the minimum energy molecules need to start a reaction. Think of pushing a boulder over a hill so it can roll into a valley on the other side. The valley is lower, but first you have to get the boulder up the hill. A spark provides that push, and then the reaction takes off. Now, a catalyst is a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up itself. How? It doesn't push the boulder harder. It provides a different path, a tunnel through the hill, with a lower activation energy. One important point: a catalyst doesn't change where the reaction ends up. The valley is just as deep. It only changes how quickly you get there. A good example is the catalytic converter in a car's exhaust system. It contains metals like platinum. Harmful gases such as carbon monoxide stick to the metal's surface, which weakens their bonds and helps them react to form less harmful products like carbon dioxide. And since the platinum isn't consumed, it keeps working for years.

at4-17.text: Listen to a talk in a materials science class.

Imagine bending a wire, dropping it in hot water, and watching it straighten back into its original shape. With ordinary steel that won't happen, but with a nickel-titanium alloy, it will. These are called shape-memory alloys, and the trick lies in their crystal structure. Now, many solids can arrange their atoms in more than one way, and which arrangement is stable depends on temperature. In nickel-titanium, the high-temperature form is called austenite, a very orderly, symmetrical structure. When it cools, it changes into a form called martensite. And here's the key point. Martensite forms in many tiny regions whose atoms are tilted in different directions, sort of like a crowd of people all leaning different ways. When you bend the cold metal, you're not breaking bonds or making atoms slide past each other, as happens in ordinary metal. Instead, those tilted regions simply reorient to accommodate the new shape. Then, when you heat it, the metal changes back to austenite, and since there's only one way to arrange the atoms in austenite, the material returns to its original shape. That's why it seems to remember. These alloys are used in stents, small mesh tubes inserted into a blood vessel in compact form that then expand at body temperature. There is a limit, though: bend it too far, and the deformation becomes permanent.

at4-18.text: Listen to a talk in a hydrology class.

So, when you turn on a tap in many parts of the world, the water didn't come from a river or a lake. It came from underground, from an aquifer. Now, what exactly is an aquifer? A lot of people picture an underground lake, but that's rarely accurate. An aquifer is a layer of rock or sediment, like sand, gravel, or sandstone, that holds water in the tiny spaces between its grains and lets that water move through it. Think of a sponge rather than a bucket. The top of the saturated zone is called the water table. Now, when you pump water from a well, the water table around the well drops, forming a shape called a cone of depression, like a funnel pointing down toward the well. If many wells are pumping close together, those cones can overlap and lower the water table across a whole region. Then shallow wells can run dry. So how does an aquifer refill? Through recharge, as rain and melting snow seep down through the soil. But here's the problem. Recharge can be very slow. Some deep aquifers hold water that seeped in thousands of years ago, when the climate was wetter. Pump that water out, and it won't come back on any human timescale. Hydrologists sometimes call that groundwater mining, because, like a mineral, it's essentially a resource that's being used up.

at4-19.text: Listen to a talk in a soil science class.

So, why are some soils naturally fertile while others need constant fertilizer? A big part of the answer is something called cation exchange capacity. Many plant nutrients, like potassium, calcium, and magnesium, exist in soil water as cations, which are ions with a positive charge. Now, if those ions just floated freely, every heavy rain would wash them down below the roots, a process called leaching. What holds them in place? Particles with negative charges on their surfaces. Clay particles often carry a negative charge, so they hold onto cations. Decomposed organic matter, called humus, does the same thing, even more strongly. Cation exchange capacity is simply a measure of how many of those positive ions a soil can hold. And here's the exchange part. When a root releases hydrogen ions, they can swap places with the nutrient ions on the particles, freeing the nutrients so the plant can absorb them. It's a bit like a bank account: nutrients are deposited on the particles and withdrawn when roots need them. Now, here's an interesting contrast. Sandy soils have a very low capacity, since sand grains carry little charge. But many old tropical soils are also poor, despite being rich in clay. Millions of years of weathering have left mostly low-capacity clays. So it's not just how much clay a soil has, but what kind.

at4-20.text: Listen to a talk in a forestry class.

Okay, so we usually think of forest fires as pure destruction. But some trees actually depend on fire to reproduce. Take the lodgepole pine of western North America. Many of its cones are what we call serotinous. That means they stay sealed shut, sometimes for years, held closed by a tough resin. Now, the resin melts only at fairly high temperatures, roughly fifty degrees Celsius or more, which normally happens only during a fire. So when a fire sweeps through, the parent trees may die, but the heat opens the cones, and huge numbers of seeds are released onto the freshly burned ground. Why is that such a good place for a seedling? It's cleared away the dense canopy that was shading the ground, so there's lots of sunlight. It's burned off competing plants. And the ash releases nutrients into the soil. So the seeds land in exactly the conditions they need. Here's the interesting part, though. Not every lodgepole pine has serotinous cones. In areas where fires are frequent, a high proportion of trees have them. But where fires are rare, more trees produce ordinary cones that open every year. So the trait seems to match the local fire history. The concern now is that hotter, more frequent fires may burn young stands before they're old enough to produce cones at all.

at4-21.text: Listen to a talk in an agriculture class.

So, nitrogen is one of the nutrients crops need most. It's essential for building proteins and DNA. And here's the irony: the air around us is about seventy-eight percent nitrogen. So why do farmers spend so much money on nitrogen fertilizer? Because plants can't use nitrogen gas directly. The two nitrogen atoms in each molecule are held together by a triple bond, one of the strongest bonds in nature. Breaking it requires either an enormous amount of energy, like the high-temperature, high-pressure process factories use to make fertilizer, or a specialized enzyme. That enzyme is found only in certain bacteria. Converting nitrogen gas into a usable form is called nitrogen fixation. Now, here's where legumes come in, plants like beans, peas, clover, and alfalfa. Their roots form small swellings called nodules, and inside these nodules live nitrogen-fixing bacteria. The plant supplies the bacteria with sugars, and the bacteria supply the plant with usable nitrogen. And there's an interesting detail. The enzyme is damaged by oxygen, so the nodules contain a protein similar to the one in our blood, which binds oxygen and keeps levels low. That's why a healthy nodule, if you cut it open, is often pinkish red. For farmers, the practical lesson is crop rotation. Grow a legume one season, plow its remains back into the soil, and the next crop, say corn, will need less fertilizer.

at4-22.text: Listen to a talk in a mechanical engineering class.

Here's a question that sounds simple: how does a refrigerator make things cold? Most people assume it somehow produces cold. But in engineering terms, there's no such thing as producing cold. A refrigerator moves heat, taking it from inside the box and dumping it into your kitchen. That's why the back or bottom of a fridge feels warm. Now, heat naturally flows from hot to cold, so moving it the other way takes work. The trick is a fluid called a refrigerant, circulating in a closed loop. Let's follow it. First, the liquid refrigerant passes through a narrow valve into the coils inside the fridge. The sudden drop in pressure makes it evaporate, and evaporation absorbs heat. It's the same reason you feel cold stepping out of a swimming pool: the water evaporating from your skin carries heat away. So the refrigerant soaks up heat from the food. Next, a compressor squeezes that vapor, raising its pressure and temperature until it's hotter than the kitchen air. In coils on the outside, it releases that heat and condenses back into a liquid. Then the cycle repeats. And here's a neat point: a heat pump used to warm a house runs the very same cycle, just with the hot side facing indoors. Because it moves heat rather than generating it, it can deliver more heat energy than the electrical energy it uses.

at4-23.text: Listen to a talk in an electrical engineering class.

Today let's look at why our power grids carry alternating current, and why that's starting to change. Here's the basic problem. When electricity flows through a long wire, some energy is lost as heat, and that loss depends on the square of the current. So if you double the current, you lose four times as much energy. The solution is to transmit power at very high voltage, because for the same amount of power, higher voltage means lower current. Now, in the late eighteen hundreds, there was no practical way to change the voltage of direct current. But alternating current could be stepped up and down easily with a transformer, which is basically two coils of wire wrapped around an iron core. The changing current in one coil creates a changing magnetic field, which induces a current in the other. Steady direct current can't produce that changing field. So alternating current won, and the grid was built around it. But alternating current has its own drawbacks. Over very long distances, and especially in undersea cables, a lot of energy is wasted by repeatedly charging and discharging the cable itself. So today, using modern electronic converters, engineers are building high-voltage direct current lines for long-distance links. In a sense, the old rivalry has ended not with a winner but with a division of labor.

at4-24.text: Listen to a talk in an environmental engineering class.

So, how do you clean wastewater without a big treatment plant full of tanks and machinery? One answer is to borrow a design from nature: the constructed wetland. That's an artificial marsh, built specifically to treat water. Here's how it works. Wastewater flows slowly through a shallow basin planted with reeds, cattails, and other marsh plants. And several things happen at once. First, because the water moves so slowly, solid particles settle to the bottom, just as mud settles in a still pond. Second, and most important, bacteria do a lot of the work. They live in huge numbers on the plant roots and stems and in the gravel, and they break down organic waste, using it as food. Now, you might think the plants are the main cleaners. They do absorb some nutrients, like nitrogen and phosphorus, but their bigger role is supporting the microbes. Their roots and stems provide surfaces for bacteria to live on, and some marsh plants even pump oxygen down to their roots, which helps certain bacteria thrive. So the plants are more like the building that houses the workers. Constructed wetlands are cheap to run and need little energy, which makes them popular with small towns. The trade-off is space. They need far more land than a conventional plant, and they work more slowly in cold weather, when bacteria are less active.

at4-25.text: Listen to a talk in a computer science class.

So, here's a problem that seemed impossible for most of history. Suppose you want to send a secret message to someone you've never met, over a channel where anyone can listen in. With traditional encryption, both sides need the same secret key. But how do you share that key in the first place, if everything you send can be overheard? For centuries, the answer was: you can't, so you meet in person or send a trusted courier. In the nineteen seventies, researchers devised public-key cryptography. The idea is that each person has two keys, which are mathematically linked. One is public, for the whole world to see. The other is private, never shared. Anything encrypted with my public key can only be decrypted with my private key. Think of it like a padlock. I can hand out open padlocks to anyone. You snap one shut on a box, and only I can open it. But how can the two keys be linked without one revealing the other? The most famous system relies on a one-way problem. Multiplying two huge prime numbers is easy for a computer. But working backward from the product to find those two primes is extraordinarily hard. Now, here's a concern. That difficulty has never been proven, and large quantum computers could, in principle, factor such numbers quickly.

at4-26.text: Listen to a talk in a mathematics history class.

Okay, so today we're talking about something you've used since you were five: the number zero. It seems so obvious, but it's actually a fairly late invention. Let's separate two ideas. The first is zero as a placeholder. In a place-value system, like ours, the position of a digit tells you its value. So in two hundred five, written two, zero, five, the zero tells you there are no tens, and it keeps the two in the hundreds place. Without it, you couldn't tell two hundred five from twenty-five. The ancient Babylonians had a place-value system, and for a long time they simply left a gap, which was easy to misread. Later they added a special symbol as a placeholder, but they didn't treat it as a number. The second idea is zero as a number in its own right, something you can add, subtract, and multiply with. That step was taken in India. In the seventh century, the mathematician Brahmagupta wrote rules for calculating with zero, like a number minus itself equals zero. Now, he didn't get everything right. Dividing by zero gave him trouble, and honestly, it still gives students trouble today. From India, the system spread through the Arabic-speaking world and eventually into Europe, where, interestingly, it was met with suspicion for quite a while. And by the way, the Maya, completely independently, also developed a zero.

at4-27.text: Listen to a talk in a zoology class.

So, why do zebras have stripes? Biologists have proposed plenty of answers for over a century. Let me walk you through the main ones. The oldest idea is camouflage, but that's hard to defend. On open grassland, a zebra is pretty conspicuous, and studies suggest that lions can't make out the stripes clearly until they're already close enough to detect the zebra by sound or smell anyway. A second idea is motion dazzle: a moving herd of stripes might confuse a predator trying to single out one animal. It's plausible, but experimental support is weak. A third idea is temperature control, that black and white stripes heat up differently and create small air currents that cool the animal. Again, the evidence is mixed. Now, the explanation that's gained the most support recently is the strangest-sounding: biting flies. In Africa, horseflies and tsetse flies spread serious diseases. In one experiment, researchers put striped coats on ordinary horses and filmed the flies. The flies approached just as often, but they failed to land smoothly. They seemed to overshoot or bump into the coat, as if the stripes confused their landing approach. Also, zebras tend to be more strongly striped in regions where biting flies are more active. Of course, stripes could serve more than one purpose. But the fly hypothesis is currently the front-runner.

at4-28.text: Listen to a talk in an entomology class.

Today's topic is one of the strangest life cycles in the animal world. In eastern North America, there are periodical cicadas that spend either thirteen or seventeen years underground as nymphs, feeding on sap from tree roots. Then, in a single spring, millions of them emerge at once, sometimes more than a million per acre. They mate, lay eggs, and die within a few weeks. So, two questions. Why emerge all together, and why such long cycles? The first question has a fairly accepted answer: predator satiation. Birds, squirrels, and other predators feast on the cicadas, but there are so many that the predators simply get full, and most cicadas survive. Now, the second question is more debated. Notice that thirteen and seventeen are both prime numbers. One explanation is that prime cycles help avoid predators with shorter cycles of their own. If a predator's population peaks every two or three years, a seventeen-year cicada will rarely emerge in one of those peak years. Another explanation focuses on hybridization. If a thirteen-year brood and a seventeen-year brood share a region, they emerge together only once every two hundred twenty-one years. Mixing broods could produce offspring with mismatched timing, so prime cycles would keep broods separate. Here's the catch. Neither hypothesis has been directly tested, partly because, well, a single experiment would take up a researcher's entire career.

at4-29.text: Listen to a talk in an ornithology class.

Okay, so most birds put enormous effort into raising their young. But some species have found a way to skip all that work. It's called brood parasitism, when a bird lays its eggs in another species' nest and leaves the host to raise its chicks. The best-known example is the common cuckoo in Europe. Here's how it goes. A female cuckoo watches a host nest, say, of a reed warbler. When the host is away, she swoops in, removes one of the host's eggs, and lays one of her own, all in a matter of seconds. And her egg often closely matches the color and pattern of the host's eggs. Now, the cuckoo chick usually hatches first, and within hours, it does something rather brutal. It pushes the host's eggs, one by one, out of the nest. So the host parents end up raising a single cuckoo chick, which can grow much bigger than they are. Why don't the hosts notice? Well, many do. Some hosts learn to recognize and reject foreign eggs. And that sets off what biologists call an evolutionary arms race. Hosts get better at spotting fake eggs, so cuckoos evolve better mimicry, which pushes hosts to become even more discriminating. Interestingly, though, hosts rarely reject the chick itself, even when it looks nothing like their own.

at4-30.text: Listen to a talk in an oceanography class.

So, if you look at a map of the world's most productive fisheries, you'll notice something odd. Several of the richest ones lie off the western coasts of continents, places like Peru, California, and southwestern Africa. Why there? The answer is a process called upwelling, the rising of cold, deep water to the surface. Now, why does deep water matter? In the open ocean, the sunlit surface layer tends to run out of nutrients, like nitrate and phosphate, because plankton use them up and their remains sink. Meanwhile, those nutrients pile up in the dark water below, where there's no light for plants to use them. So you've got light on top and nutrients below. Upwelling brings the two together. Here's how it works off Peru, for instance. Winds blow along the coast toward the equator. But because of Earth's rotation, the surface water doesn't move straight with the wind. It's deflected, and on these coasts, it's pushed away from shore. And as surface water moves offshore, cold, nutrient-rich water rises from below to replace it. It's a bit like sliding the top sheet off a stack of papers: whatever's underneath is exposed. With nutrients and sunlight together, phytoplankton bloom, and that feeds everything from small fish to seabirds. But when those winds weaken, as they do during El Niño events off Peru, upwelling slows and fisheries can collapse.

at4-31.text: Listen to a talk in a meteorology class.

Let's start by clearing up a popular myth. You may have heard that water drains from a sink clockwise in one hemisphere and counterclockwise in the other. It doesn't, at least not reliably. The direction depends on the shape of the sink and how the water was moving to begin with. But the effect behind that myth is real; it just works on a much larger scale. It's called the Coriolis effect. Because Earth rotates, anything moving freely over long distances appears to curve: to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, and to the left in the Southern. Picture throwing a ball across a spinning merry-go-round. To someone riding it, the ball seems to swerve, though it's really moving straight. Now, apply this to a hurricane. At the center is very low pressure, so air rushes inward from all sides. But in the Northern Hemisphere, each stream of air is deflected to the right, so instead of flowing straight in, the air swirls around the center counterclockwise. In the Southern Hemisphere, the spin is clockwise. The Coriolis effect is zero right at the equator and weak close to it. So hurricanes almost never form within about five degrees of the equator, despite warm water. As for your sink, over such short times and distances, the effect is far too weak to matter.

at4-32.text: Listen to a talk in a paleontology class.

So, how does a living thing become a fossil? Here's the honest answer: almost never. The vast majority of organisms that have ever lived left no trace at all. When an animal dies, scavengers eat it, bacteria decompose it, and weather scatters what's left. For it to become a fossil, it usually has to be buried quickly, by mud on a riverbed, sand in a flood, or ash from a volcano. Burial cuts off oxygen and protects the remains from scavengers. Now, the most common process is called permineralization. Groundwater seeps through the buried bone or wood, and minerals like silica or calcite crystallize in the tiny pores. Over long periods, this makes the remains much harder and heavier, essentially turning them into stone while preserving their shape, sometimes down to the cell structure in petrified wood. So what does this mean for paleontologists? It means the fossil record is biased. Animals with hard parts, like shells, bones, and teeth, are far more likely to be preserved than soft-bodied ones, like jellyfish or worms. And animals that lived in or near water, where sediment builds up, are better represented than ones living on dry hills. It's like trying to understand a city from photos taken only at its harbor. That's why rare sites preserving soft tissues are so valuable.

at4-33.text: Listen to a talk in a genetics class.

Most of you have heard of CRISPR as a gene-editing tool. But it didn't start in a lab. It started as an immune system in bacteria. Bacteria are constantly attacked by viruses called bacteriophages. Starting in the late nineteen eighties, researchers noticed strange patterns in bacterial DNA: short repeated sequences with unique stretches of DNA between them. For years, nobody knew what they were. Then researchers realized that those in-between stretches matched the DNA of viruses. So here's what's happening. When a bacterium survives a viral attack, it cuts out a small piece of the virus's DNA and stores it in this region, like a mug shot in a police file. Later, the bacterium copies those stored pieces into RNA guides. Each guide teams up with an enzyme that cuts DNA, called Cas nine in the best-known system. If the same virus invades again, the guide recognizes the matching sequence, and the enzyme cuts the virus's DNA, disabling it. Now, why does this matter for gene editing? Because the guide can be reprogrammed. Write a guide to match any sequence, and the enzyme will cut there, in a human cell, a plant, anything. Here's a difference, though. In bacteria, the system's purpose is destruction. In gene editing, the cut is just the first step; the cell's own repair machinery makes the actual change.

at4-34.text: Listen to a talk in a neuroscience class.

Okay, so here's something that puzzled doctors for centuries. After someone loses an arm, they often continue to feel it: an itch, a cramp, even pain in a hand that's no longer there. These are called phantom limb sensations, and they're reported by a large majority of amputees. So where do they come from? For a long time, the leading explanation was peripheral. The idea was that the cut nerve endings in the stump become irritated and keep sending signals, and the brain interprets those signals as coming from the missing hand. That certainly contributes in some cases. But it can't be the whole story, because phantom sensations can persist even when those nerves are blocked. So researchers turned to the brain itself. In the cortex, there's a region called the somatosensory cortex that works like a map of the body. Interestingly, the face and the hand sit right next to each other on that map. When the hand stops sending input, neighboring areas, like the face region, seem to gradually take over the hand's territory. And some amputees report that touching their cheek produces a sensation in their missing fingers. This is called cortical remapping. But there's a twist. Some recent studies suggest that the hand's map survives remarkably intact, so remapping alone may not explain phantom pain.

at4-35.text: Listen to a talk in a physiology class.

So imagine you fly from a city at sea level straight to a town high in the Andes, around four thousand meters. You'll probably feel short of breath, maybe get a headache. Why? Well, the air up there still contains about twenty-one percent oxygen, the same proportion as at sea level. What's different is the air pressure. It's much lower, so each breath brings in fewer oxygen molecules, roughly forty percent fewer at that height. Now, the body responds in stages. Within minutes, you start breathing faster and deeper, and your heart rate goes up. Over the next few days, your kidneys detect the lower oxygen level in the blood and release a hormone called erythropoietin, or EPO for short. EPO signals the bone marrow to make more red blood cells, the cells that carry oxygen. That takes weeks to really build up, which is why climbers spend time at intermediate camps before going higher. This is called acclimatization, the gradual adjustment of the body to a new environment. It's also why some endurance athletes train at altitude before competing lower down. Now, here's an interesting contrast. Populations that have lived at high altitude for thousands of years, for example in Tibet, don't simply have more red blood cells. Many have fairly normal levels and adapt in other ways, such as breathing more.

at4-36.text: Listen to a talk in an astronomy class.

So, how do you find a planet around another star when the planet itself is far too dim to see directly, lost in its star's glare? Astronomers mostly rely on two indirect methods, and they tell us different things. The first is the radial velocity method. A planet doesn't simply orbit its star. Both orbit their shared center of mass, so the star wobbles slightly. When the star moves toward us, its light shifts toward the blue; when it moves away, toward the red. By measuring those tiny shifts, we can detect the planet and estimate its mass. The second is the transit method. If a planet's orbit happens to be lined up with our view, it passes in front of its star and blocks a small fraction of the light. A planet the size of Jupiter dims a sun-like star by about one percent; an Earth-sized planet, by less than a hundredth of that. The amount of dimming tells us the planet's size. Now, here's why combining them is so powerful. Radial velocity gives mass, transits give size, and together they give density. And density tells you what the planet is made of, whether it's rocky like Earth or mostly gas. But there's a limitation. Transits only work for the small fraction of systems we happen to see edge-on.

at4-37.text: Listen to a talk in a planetary science class.

Today's question: why does Saturn have rings while our Moon is a solid body? The key concept is the Roche limit, named after the nineteenth-century French astronomer who worked it out. Here's the idea. When a moon orbits a planet, the planet's gravity pulls harder on the moon's near side than on its far side. That difference is called a tidal force, and it tries to stretch the moon apart. Meanwhile, the moon's own gravity is trying to hold it together. Now, the closer the moon is to the planet, the stronger that stretching becomes. And there's a distance, the Roche limit, inside which the stretching wins. A moon held together only by its own gravity, a loose pile of rubble or ice, would be torn apart, and the debris would spread out into a ring. And sure enough, Saturn's main rings lie mostly inside its Roche limit, while its large moons orbit outside it. For the same reason, ring material can't clump together to form a new moon there. Our Moon, by contrast, is far outside Earth's Roche limit. But here's a subtlety. Small solid objects, like a spacecraft, can survive inside the limit, because they're held together by the strength of their material, not just by gravity. And how old are Saturn's rings? Some measurements suggest they're surprisingly young, but that's still debated.

at4-38.text: Listen to a talk in a physics class.

So here's a problem that bothered physicists in the early twentieth century. The Sun shines because, in its core, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium. But to fuse, two nuclei have to get extremely close. And since both are positively charged, they repel each other, more and more strongly as they approach. That repulsion acts like a wall, an energy barrier. Now, the core of the Sun is very hot, around fifteen million degrees, so the nuclei are moving fast. But when physicists calculated it, even at that temperature, almost none of them had enough energy to climb over the wall. By classical physics, the Sun shouldn't be shining. So what's going on? The answer is quantum tunneling. In quantum mechanics, a particle is described by a wave that spreads out a bit, and part of that wave extends through the barrier. So there's a small probability that the particle simply appears on the other side, even without enough energy to go over the top. It's as if a ball rolled at a hill too high for it sometimes turned up on the far side. For large everyday objects, that probability is essentially zero. But for a tiny proton, it's small but real. And with an enormous number of collisions every second, that small probability is enough to power the Sun.

at4-39.text: Listen to a talk in a chemistry class.

Hold up your hands for a second. They're mirror images of each other, but you can't stack one perfectly on top of the other. Chemists call this property chirality, from the Greek word for hand. A chiral molecule is one that can't be superimposed on its mirror image. Usually, it contains a carbon atom bonded to four different groups. The two mirror-image versions are called enantiomers. Now, here's the interesting part. Enantiomers have identical physical properties in most respects: the same melting point, the same boiling point. One measurable difference is that they rotate polarized light in opposite directions. But in the body, they can behave very differently. Why? Because the body's receptors and enzymes are themselves chiral. Think of a glove: a right glove fits only a right hand. So one enantiomer may fit a receptor while its mirror image doesn't. A simple example is carvone. One version smells like spearmint, and the other like caraway seeds. Same atoms, same bonds, different smell. And this has serious consequences for medicine. In some drugs, one enantiomer is effective and the other is useless or even harmful. That's why drug makers now often produce just the useful form. But there's a complication: some molecules convert from one form into the other inside the body, so even a pure dose may not stay pure.

at4-40.text: Listen to a talk in a materials science class.

So, there's a story you may have heard: that old windows in medieval cathedrals are thicker at the bottom because glass is actually a very slow liquid that has flowed downward over the centuries. It's a great story, but it's wrong. Let's see why, and what glass really is. In a crystal, like quartz, atoms are arranged in a regular, repeating pattern. Glass, which is mostly made from the same silica, has no such long-range order. Its atoms are arranged randomly, like a liquid's, but they're locked in place. That's what we call an amorphous solid. How does that happen? When molten silica cools slowly, the atoms have time to find their places in a crystal. But if it cools quickly, it thickens until the atoms are essentially frozen in a disordered arrangement before they can organize. Now, does glass flow at room temperature? Calculations suggest that ordinary glass at room temperature is so viscous that any noticeable sagging would take far longer than the age of the universe. So why are the old windows uneven? Medieval glassmaking simply couldn't produce sheets of uniform thickness, and installers often put the thicker edge at the bottom. And some old panes have the thick edge at the top or the side, which the flowing theory can't explain. So glass is a solid, just not a crystalline one.

at4-41.text: Listen to a talk in a climatology class.

Today we're looking at why the Arctic is warming much faster than the planet as a whole, by some estimates nearly four times faster. Scientists call this Arctic amplification. So what drives it? The best-known factor is the ice-albedo feedback. Albedo is the fraction of sunlight a surface reflects. Snow and sea ice have a high albedo, reflecting most sunlight. Dark open ocean has a low albedo, absorbing most of it. Think of wearing a white shirt versus a black shirt on a sunny day. Now, here's the feedback. As temperatures rise, sea ice melts, exposing dark water. The water absorbs more sunlight and warms, which melts more ice, and so on. It's a loop that reinforces itself. But here's where it gets interesting. Climate models show amplification still happens even when the ice-albedo feedback is switched off. So it can't be the only factor. Another major factor involves how the atmosphere is structured. In the Arctic, especially in winter, the air near the ground is often colder than the air above it. Because of that, warming stays trapped near the surface instead of being mixed upward. And cold surfaces shed extra heat to space less efficiently, so the poles must warm more to get rid of it. So researchers now see amplification as several feedbacks working together, and they still debate which matters most.

at4-42.text: Listen to a talk in a mathematics history class.

For more than two thousand years, one statement in geometry bothered mathematicians more than any other. Around three hundred BCE, Euclid built his geometry on five basic assumptions, or postulates. The first four are simple, like, a straight line can be drawn between any two points. But the fifth, the parallel postulate, is long and awkward. In a common modern form, it says that through a point not on a given line, exactly one line can be drawn parallel to it. Many mathematicians felt it should be provable from the other four. So, for centuries, they tried. Some attempted proof by contradiction: assume the postulate is false, and show that this leads to an absurdity. And here's the irony. They derived strange results, like triangles whose angles add up to less than one hundred eighty degrees, but they never found a true contradiction. In the early eighteen hundreds, the Russian Nikolai Lobachevsky and the Hungarian János Bolyai, working independently, took the bold step of accepting those strange results as a consistent geometry in its own right. Now, this means the parallel postulate can't be proven from the others. There are other perfectly valid geometries. On a sphere, for instance, a triangle's angles add up to more than one hundred eighty degrees. Later, these geometries proved useful for describing space in physics.

at5-01.text: Listen to a talk in an archaeology class.

Okay, so imagine you're digging a trench at an old settlement, and the wall of the trench shows bands of soil in different colors, one on top of another. What can those bands tell you? Quite a lot, actually. The study of these layers is called stratigraphy, and it rests on a simple principle known as the law of superposition. It was first stated in the 1660s by a scientist named Nicolas Steno, who was studying rocks, not ruins. The idea is that in undisturbed deposits, the lower layers were laid down first, so they're older than the layers above them. Now, notice what this gives us. It's relative dating. It tells you that one layer is older than another, but not how old either one is in years. To get closer to that, archaeologists look for objects that can be dated, like a coin. If a coin minted in a certain year turns up in a layer, the layer can't have formed before that year. But here's the catch, and it's the word undisturbed. People dig pits, bury things, and set posts into the ground. Burrowing animals move material around too. So a later object can end up below an earlier one. That's why excavators record every layer so carefully, looking for places where one deposit cuts through another.

at5-02.text: Listen to a talk in an ancient history class.

Today I want to tell you about one of the great code-breaking stories in the study of the ancient world. Around 1900, excavators at Knossos, on the island of Crete, found thousands of clay tablets covered in an unknown script, which came to be called Linear B. Now, the tablets survived for an odd reason. They were never meant to last. They were unbaked clay, used for everyday records, and they were preserved only because the fires that destroyed the palaces baked them hard. So, what language did they record? The excavator, Arthur Evans, was convinced it was a native Cretan language unrelated to Greek, and his authority shaped the field for decades. The breakthrough came in 1952 from Michael Ventris, an architect, not a professional scholar. Building on work by Alice Kober, who had shown that certain words changed their endings, he arranged the signs in a grid of likely sound relationships. When he tested place names from Crete against the grid, the words that emerged were recognizably Greek, an early form of Greek centuries older than Homer. And Ventris himself had expected something else. So what did the tablets say? Mostly inventories: sheep, chariot wheels, jars of oil. No poetry, no history. Which tells us something too: writing here served the palace bookkeepers, not storytellers.

at5-03.text: Listen to a talk in a history of technology class.

So, picture a ship in the middle of the Atlantic in, say, 1700. The navigator can find the ship's latitude, its north-south position, fairly easily by measuring the height of the Sun at noon. But longitude, the east-west position? That was a real problem, and ships were wrecked because of it. Now, here's the key insight. The Earth turns fifteen degrees every hour. So if you know the local time on the ship, from the Sun, and you also know the time back at your home port, the difference tells you how far east or west you've traveled. The catch was keeping home port time at sea. Pendulum clocks couldn't cope with a rolling deck, and changes in temperature made clocks run fast or slow. In 1714, the British government offered a huge prize for a practical solution. Many astronomers believed the answer was in the sky, measuring the Moon's position against the stars, which worked but required long calculations. A self-taught clockmaker named John Harrison took the mechanical route instead. Over several decades, he built a series of timekeepers, and his fourth, which looked like an oversized pocket watch, lost only a few seconds on a voyage to Jamaica. Even so, the officials in charge were slow to reward him, partly because many of them favored the astronomical method.

at5-04.text: Listen to a talk in an anthropology class.

Today we're looking at the potlatch, a ceremony practiced by Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest coast, in what's now British Columbia and the state of Washington. So, what happens at a potlatch? A host family invites guests, sometimes hundreds of them, to mark an important event, like a marriage, a death, or someone taking on a hereditary name. There are speeches, dances, and feasting, and then the host gives away huge quantities of goods: blankets, food, carved objects. In some potlatches, valuable property was even destroyed in public. To many European observers, this looked like pure waste, and the Canadian government actually banned the potlatch from 1885 until 1951. Anthropologists, though, have offered very different readings. One view stresses rivalry: chiefs competed for prestige, and giving away more than a rival could repay was a way of winning status. Another view is economic. Resources along the coast, like salmon runs, varied a lot from place to place and year to year, so the potlatch moved surplus goods to groups that needed them, a kind of insurance. And there's a point the communities themselves emphasize: the guests are witnesses. By accepting gifts, they publicly confirm the host's claim to a name or a right. Notably, the most dramatic destruction seems to date from the 1800s, when trade brought sudden new wealth and epidemics left many titles open to competition.

at5-05.text: Listen to a talk in a linguistics class.

Ever wondered why English spelling seems so disconnected from pronunciation? Why do we write b, i, t, e, but say 'bite'? Part of the answer is a change linguists call the Great Vowel Shift. Between roughly 1400 and 1700, the long vowels of English moved. Most of them came to be pronounced higher in the mouth, and the two highest ones, which had nowhere higher to go, turned into diphthongs, that is, two vowel sounds glided together. So 'bite' was once pronounced much like 'beet,' and 'house' sounded something like 'hoose.' Here's why spelling matters. Printing arrived in England in the 1470s, right in the middle of this shift, and spelling gradually became fixed. So our spelling largely records how words sounded before the shift was complete. That's why letters and sounds don't line up the way they do in Spanish. So what caused the shift? Nobody knows for sure. One explanation points to migration: after the plague of the fourteenth century, many people moved to London, and contact between dialects may have led speakers to adjust their vowels. There's also a debate about the order of events. Did the high vowels change first, leaving gaps that the lower vowels moved up to fill? Or did the lower vowels rise first and push the higher ones out? The evidence fits both, which is why the argument continues.

at5-06.text: Listen to a talk in a literature class.

So far this term, we've mostly read stories where we trust the person telling them. Today, let's talk about what happens when we can't. The critic Wayne Booth introduced the term unreliable narrator in 1961. It describes a narrator whose account of events we come to doubt, because of what they misunderstand, conceal, or distort. Now, how do we know a narrator is unreliable if the narrator is our only source? That's the interesting part. The text gives us clues that the narrator doesn't notice. Take Edgar Allan Poe's story 'The Tell-Tale Heart.' The narrator keeps insisting he's perfectly calm and sane, and the more carefully he explains himself, the less we believe him. His own words work against him. But unreliability isn't always about deception or madness. Some narrators are simply naive. Think of Gulliver in Gulliver's Travels. He describes the strange societies he visits with total sincerity, and he often admires the very things Jonathan Swift wants us to laugh at. Gulliver isn't lying. He just doesn't see what the reader sees. So, why would authors do this? Because it makes the reader an active participant. We're not just receiving a story; we're reading between the lines, comparing what we're told with what we can infer. And that gap is often where the meaning of the work lies.

at5-07.text: Listen to a talk in a theater class.

Today we're heading to Italy in the sixteenth century, to a form of theater called commedia dell'arte. The name roughly means 'theater of the profession,' because these were some of the first professional acting companies in Europe. They traveled from town to town, performing in public squares and at court. So, what made commedia distinctive? First, stock characters. Every company had the same basic types, and audiences recognized them instantly, often by their masks. There was Pantalone, the greedy old merchant; the Doctor, who spouted nonsense in fake Latin; and Arlecchino, or Harlequin, the clever, acrobatic servant. Second, and this surprises people, there was usually no full script. The actors worked from a scenario, a short outline of the plot, often pinned up backstage. They knew who would enter when and what had to happen, but they improvised the dialogue. Now, improvisation doesn't mean they made everything up on the spot. Actors often played the same character for years and built up a stock of speeches and jokes. They also had lazzi, rehearsed comic routines, like an elaborate bit about catching a fly, that could be dropped in whenever a scene needed energy. One more thing: women performed on stage, at a time when female roles in England were still played by boys. And the influence lasted. Playwrights like Molière borrowed its characters freely.

at5-08.text: Listen to a talk in a dance class.

Here's a problem that has troubled dance for centuries. A composer can write down a symphony, and two hundred years later an orchestra can perform it. But how do you preserve a dance? For most of history, choreography survived only in the bodies and memories of dancers, passed from one generation to the next, and a great deal was lost. In 1928, the dance theorist Rudolf Laban published a system for recording movement, now usually called Labanotation. So, how does it work? Picture a vertical staff, read from the bottom up. Columns stand for parts of the body, with the right side of the body on the right and the left side on the left. Then each symbol does three jobs at once. Its shape shows direction, its shading shows level, high, middle, or low, and its length shows how long the movement lasts. Now, you might ask: why bother, when we can simply film a performance? This is a real debate. Supporters of notation point out that a video records one particular performance, including one dancer's habits and mistakes. A score records the choreographer's structure, separate from any single performer. The trouble is that notating a work takes a trained specialist many hours, and relatively few dancers can read a score. So in practice, many companies use both: the score for structure, and video for style.

at5-09.text: Listen to a talk in a music history class.

Imagine you're a young singer in a monastery about a thousand years ago. Your job is to sing hundreds of chants for church services, and you have to learn every one of them by ear, from an older singer. Now, there was some notation at the time. Singers used little marks called neumes, written above the words, which showed whether the melody went up or down. But they didn't show exactly how far. They were reminders for people who already knew the tune. Around the year 1025, a monk named Guido of Arezzo introduced two ideas that changed this. The first was the staff. Guido placed the marks on horizontal lines, so each line or space stood for a definite pitch. He even colored some of the lines, red for one note and yellow for another, so singers could find their place. The second idea was a memory aid. Guido used a hymn in which each line of music began one note higher than the line before. The first syllables of those lines were ut, re, mi, fa, sol, and la. Sound familiar? Later, ut was replaced by do, which is easier to sing, and another syllable was added at the top. Guido claimed that with his methods, training that had taken about ten years could be done in one or two.

at5-10.text: Listen to a talk in a film studies class.

When we think about sound arriving in films in the late 1920s, we usually think of it as pure progress. Silent pictures could finally talk. But many historians argue that, at first, sound made movies worse, at least visually. Why? Think about the equipment. The cameras of the time were noisy, and the microphones would pick up their whirring. So the solution was to put the camera, and its operator, inside a heavy soundproof booth. Crews jokingly called these booths iceboxes, since it was so hot inside. And a camera inside a booth can't move freely. The fluid moving shots that late silent films had developed largely disappeared. Microphones caused problems too. They had limited range, so they were hidden in flower vases or lamps, and actors had to stay close to them. The result was a lot of stiff scenes with people standing around talking. Now, here's where interpretations differ. Some critics at the time argued that sound had damaged cinema permanently, that film's true strength was the image, and that dialogue turned it into recorded theater. Others saw a temporary technical setback. And within a few years, engineers built quieter, insulated camera housings called blimps, and microphones were placed on long booms above the actors. The camera moved again. So which view was right? I'd say the speed of that recovery tells you a lot.

at5-11.text: Listen to a talk in a photography class.

In 1839, two very different photographic processes were announced within months of each other, and comparing them tells us a lot about what photography would become. The first was the daguerreotype, developed in France by Louis Daguerre. The image was formed directly on a polished, silver-coated copper plate, and the detail was astonishing. People examined daguerreotypes with magnifying glasses and found they could read signs across a street. But notice something: each daguerreotype was unique. There was no negative, so the only way to get a second copy was to take a second picture. In England, William Henry Fox Talbot was working on something different. His process, which he later refined and called the calotype, produced a negative on paper. From that one negative, you could print as many positive copies as you liked. The downside? The image had to pass through the fibers of the paper, so it was softer, less precise. So at the time, which seemed better? For portraits and sheer detail, most people preferred the daguerreotype, and it dominated commercial studios for over a decade. But consider what happened next. In the 1850s, photographers began making negatives on glass, which combined fine detail with the ability to make copies. And the daguerreotype faded away. So, in the long run, the principle that mattered most was Talbot's, even though his pictures lost the first round.

at5-12.text: Listen to a talk in an art history class.

Let's start with a question. In many paintings from medieval Europe, the most important figures are the biggest, no matter where they stand in the scene. Why? Because size showed importance, not distance. Then, in early fifteenth-century Florence, something changed. The architect Filippo Brunelleschi carried out a famous demonstration. He painted a small panel showing the city's baptistery and drilled a hole through the center. A viewer stood behind the panel, looked through the hole, and held up a mirror facing the painted side. In the mirror, the painted building lined up with the real one behind it. Brunelleschi had worked out a geometric method for showing depth: linear perspective. Now, how does it work? Lines that are parallel in reality, like the edges of a road or the tiles of a floor, are drawn so that they meet at a single point on the horizon, the vanishing point. And objects shrink at a regular rate as they move away. In 1435, Leon Battista Alberti wrote these rules down in a treatise on painting. He compared the picture to an open window that the viewer looks through. So perspective wasn't just a trick. It changed the idea of what a painting was: no longer a symbolic arrangement, but a view into a world that continues beyond the frame.

at5-13.text: Listen to a talk in a sculpture class.

Okay, stand up for a second, everyone. Just stand naturally, the way you would while waiting for a bus. Now notice: almost none of you are standing with your weight evenly on both feet. You've shifted onto one leg. And when you do that, your hips tilt, and your shoulders tilt the other way to keep you balanced. Okay, you can sit down. That relaxed pose has a name in art history: contrapposto, an Italian term meaning roughly 'counterpose.' Now, early Greek statues of young men, called kouroi, didn't stand like that. They faced straight ahead, arms at their sides, one foot slightly forward, but with the weight shared equally. They look stiff, almost frozen. Then, around 480 BCE, we get a statue known as the Kritios Boy, and something new happens. The weight rests on one leg, the other knee bends, and the body looks as if it could actually move. A few decades later, the sculptor Polykleitos made the pose systematic in his Spear Bearer, balancing tense and relaxed parts of the body against each other. So why does this matter? Because it's the moment sculpture starts to show a living body rather than a symbol of one. And the idea had a long life. When Renaissance sculptors like Michelangelo looked back to ancient art, contrapposto was one of the things they revived.

at5-14.text: Listen to a talk in an architecture class.

So, if you've ever stood inside a Gothic cathedral, you know the feeling: the ceiling seems impossibly high, and the walls seem to be made more of glass than stone. How did medieval builders pull that off? Let's start with the problem. A stone vault, the arched ceiling, is heavy, and it doesn't just push down. It also pushes outward on the walls. Engineers call this sideways force thrust. In earlier Romanesque churches, the answer was simply thick, massive walls with small windows. The walls absorbed the thrust. Gothic builders, starting in twelfth-century France, took a different approach. First, they used ribbed vaults, which gather the weight of the ceiling and direct it to specific points rather than spreading it along the whole wall. Then, at those points, they added flying buttresses. These are arms of stone that leap from the upper walls, over the side aisles, to massive piers standing outside the building. They catch the thrust and carry it down to the ground. Builders even placed heavy stone pinnacles on top of the piers. They look decorative, but their weight actually helps steady the piers. Once the walls no longer carried the load, they could be opened up for huge stained glass windows. Now, the system had limits. At Beauvais, builders pushed for record height, and part of the vault collapsed in 1284.

at5-15.text: Listen to a talk in an urban planning class.

Today we're looking at one of the most ambitious urban projects of the nineteenth century: the rebuilding of Paris. From 1853 to 1870, under the emperor Napoleon the Third, the official in charge of the city, Georges-Eugène Haussmann, demolished large parts of medieval Paris. Narrow, crowded streets were replaced by long, straight boulevards lined with buildings of uniform height and style. Underneath, he built a vast network of sewers and water pipes, and he added parks across the city. So, why do it? The official reasons were health and circulation. Paris had suffered deadly cholera outbreaks, and the old neighborhoods were dark and poorly ventilated. The boulevards brought in light and air, and they connected the new railway stations so traffic could move. But there's another interpretation, and it dates from Haussmann's own time. Paris had a history of uprisings, and in 1830 and 1848, residents had blocked the narrow streets with barricades. Wide, straight boulevards are much harder to barricade, and they let troops move quickly. Some critics argued that this was the real purpose. Now, I'd be careful here. The two explanations aren't mutually exclusive, and the military motive rarely appears in official documents. What's less disputed is the social effect. Rents in the new buildings rose, and many working-class residents were pushed toward the edges of the city.

at5-16.text: Listen to a talk in a design class.

You've heard the phrase 'form follows function.' It's probably the most quoted slogan in modern design. Today I want to complicate it.
