The phrase comes from the American architect Louis Sullivan, in an essay he wrote in 1896 about tall office buildings. His point was that a building's form should express what goes on inside it. For an office tower, that meant a base for shops and entrances, a stack of identical office floors, and a distinct top. Now, here's the irony. Sullivan's own buildings are covered in rich, intricate ornament, swirling leaves and geometric patterns in terracotta. He didn't think function ruled out decoration at all. The slogan was later taken up by twentieth-century modernists who read it much more narrowly: if something isn't necessary for an object to work, remove it. That reading gave us the clean, unornamented look of much modern furniture and architecture, and it was reinforced by the Austrian architect Adolf Loos, whose essay 'Ornament and Crime' attacked decoration as wasteful. So which reading is right? Part of the problem is the word function. Is the function of a chair only to support a body? Or does it also signal comfort, status, or welcome? If you count those as functions, then ornament can be functional too. So the slogan doesn't settle the debate. It just moves it to the definition of one word.

at5-17.text: Listen to a talk in a philosophy class.

In 1688, an Irish scientist named William Molyneux sent a puzzle to the philosopher John Locke. Imagine, he said, a man born blind, who has learned to tell a cube from a sphere by touch. Now suppose he suddenly gains his sight. Without touching them, could he tell by sight alone which is the cube and which is the sphere? So what's at stake? It's a question about where our ideas come from. If the answer is yes, there must be some shared idea of shape that connects touch and vision, perhaps something built into the mind. If the answer is no, the link between what we feel and what we see has to be learned through experience. Locke and Molyneux both answered no, which fit Locke's view that the mind begins as a blank slate. The philosopher Leibniz disagreed. He thought the man could work it out by reasoning, for instance by noticing that a sphere has no corners. For centuries, this remained a thought experiment. But in recent years, researchers have studied people born with treatable blindness who gained sight through surgery. Tested soon afterward, they generally could not match a shape they had touched with the same shape seen. But, and this is key, within days, many of them could. So the answer seems to be no, but the connection is learned remarkably fast.

at5-18.text: Listen to a talk in an ancient philosophy class.

Here's an argument that's about two and a half thousand years old, and it still bothers people. It comes from Zeno of Elea, a Greek philosopher. Achilles, the fastest runner in Greece, races a tortoise, and he gives the tortoise a head start. Now, to catch the tortoise, Achilles must first reach the point where the tortoise started. But by then, the tortoise has moved a little further ahead. So Achilles must reach that new point, and by the time he does, the tortoise has moved again. And so on, forever. There are infinitely many points Achilles must reach, so, Zeno concludes, he can never catch up. Obviously Achilles does catch the tortoise. So why bother? Zeno's aim was to defend his teacher Parmenides, who held that motion and change are illusions. If common sense about motion leads to absurdity, maybe common sense is wrong. Now, the standard modern reply comes from mathematics. An infinite series can have a finite sum. One half plus one quarter plus one eighth, and so on, adds up to exactly one. So infinitely many stages can fit into a finite amount of time. Case closed? Not for everyone. Some philosophers argue that the math tells us how long the race takes, but not how it's possible to actually complete an infinite number of separate steps, one after another. That second question is still debated.

at5-19.text: Listen to a talk in a classical literature class.

If you've read Homer's Iliad or Odyssey, you've probably noticed phrases that repeat over and over. Dawn is always 'rosy-fingered.' Achilles is 'swift-footed,' even when he's sitting still. For a long time, readers treated these as decorative touches, or even as signs of a careless poet. In the 1920s, a young American scholar named Milman Parry offered a different explanation. Homer's poems are composed in a strict meter, the dactylic hexameter. Parry showed that these descriptive phrases, called epithets, form a system: for each major character, there's typically one ready-made phrase to fit each position in the line. In other words, the poet chose the phrase that fit the meter, not the one that best suited the scene. Why would a poet work this way? Parry's answer was that the poems came out of an oral tradition, where singers composed while performing, and formulas made that possible. To test the idea, Parry and his assistant, Albert Lord, went to Yugoslavia in the 1930s and recorded singers who couldn't read or write but could perform epic songs thousands of lines long, built from formulas in exactly this way. Now, this raised a hard question. If Homer was an oral poet, how did we get poems as long and carefully structured as the Iliad? Some scholars think a singer dictated them to a scribe. Others believe writing itself shaped their final form.

at5-20.text: Listen to a talk in a cognitive psychology class.

How many items can you hold in mind at once? In 1956, the psychologist George Miller wrote a famous paper with a playful title about 'the magical number seven, plus or minus two.' He noticed that across many tasks, people could keep about seven items in short-term memory. But Miller's more lasting contribution was a second idea: chunking. A chunk is a meaningful unit of information, and the key is that the limit applies to chunks, not to raw pieces. Here's an example. Try remembering these twelve digits: one, four, nine, two, one, seven, seven, six, one, nine, six, nine. Hard, right? But if you recognize them as three famous years, 1492, 1776, and 1969, it's just three chunks. Same information, much less load. Chunking also helps explain expertise. In classic studies of chess, masters shown a board from a real game for a few seconds could reconstruct it almost perfectly, while beginners recalled only a handful of pieces. But when the pieces were placed randomly, the masters' advantage mostly disappeared. So the masters didn't have better memories in general. They saw familiar patterns as single chunks. Now, about that number seven. Later researchers argued that when people can't rehearse or group items, the true capacity is lower, perhaps around four chunks. So seven may have been an overestimate, but the principle of chunking has held up very well.

at5-21.text: Listen to a talk in a social psychology class.

Imagine someone cuts in front of you in traffic. What's your first thought? Probably something like, 'What a rude driver.' You probably don't think, 'Maybe they're rushing to the hospital.' That tendency has a name: the fundamental attribution error. It's our habit of explaining other people's behavior by their personality while underestimating the power of the situation. One classic demonstration comes from the 1960s. Participants read essays that either supported or opposed a particular political position. Some were told the writer had freely chosen which side to argue. Others were told the writer had been assigned a side, with no choice at all. Now, logically, an assigned essay tells you nothing about the writer's real opinion. Yet participants still judged that the writer believed what they'd written. They knew about the situation, but they didn't adjust enough for it. Why does this happen? One explanation is about attention: the person is vivid and in front of us, while the situation fades into the background. Now, here's the debate. The word fundamental suggests something universal. But cross-cultural research has found that people raised in some East Asian societies tend to pay more attention to context, and in some studies they show the bias less strongly. So some researchers argue it's not really fundamental, but partly shaped by culture. Others reply that the bias appears everywhere; it's just a matter of degree.

at5-22.text: Listen to a talk in a social psychology class.

Have you ever bought something expensive and then found yourself reading lots of good reviews about it, after you'd already bought it? That's a clue to today's topic: cognitive dissonance. The term comes from the psychologist Leon Festinger in the 1950s. Dissonance is the uncomfortable tension we feel when we hold two ideas that don't fit together, or when our actions don't match our beliefs. And because it's uncomfortable, we're motivated to reduce it, often by changing a belief. The classic experiment was published in 1959. Students spent an hour doing extremely boring tasks, like turning wooden pegs a quarter turn, again and again. Then they were asked to tell the next participant that the task was fun and interesting. Some were paid one dollar for telling this lie, and others were paid twenty dollars. Afterward, everyone rated how enjoyable the task really was. So, who do you think rated it higher? Most people guess the twenty-dollar group. But it was the one-dollar group. Why? The twenty-dollar students had a good reason for lying: the money. Little dissonance. The one-dollar students didn't. One dollar isn't much of a reason to lie. So, to make sense of what they'd done, they shifted their belief: maybe the task wasn't so bad after all. That's the opposite of what a simple reward theory would predict. More reward produced less change in attitude.

at5-23.text: Listen to a talk in a developmental psychology class.

If you hide a toy under a blanket in front of a six-month-old baby, the baby usually won't search for it. It's as if the toy has stopped existing. The Swiss psychologist Jean Piaget saw this as evidence that young infants lack object permanence, the understanding that things continue to exist when we can't see them. In his view, it isn't firmly in place until around the end of the first year. Now, notice what Piaget's test requires. To pass it, the baby has to plan an action: reach out, lift the blanket, grab the toy. What if babies understand more than they can show with their hands? Starting in the 1980s, researchers used a different method, called violation of expectation. The idea is simple: babies look longer at events that surprise them. In one well-known study, babies watched a screen rotate back toward a box that should have stopped it. In the impossible version, the screen seemed to pass right through the box. Babies as young as four or five months looked longer at the impossible event, which suggests they expected the hidden box to still be there. But here's the debate. Critics argue that longer looking doesn't necessarily mean surprise based on understanding. Babies might simply be reacting to something new. So the question becomes: how much can we read into a baby's gaze?

at5-24.text: Listen to a talk in a child development class.

Today we're looking at one of the most widely used procedures in developmental psychology. It's called the Strange Situation, and it was designed by Mary Ainsworth in the 1970s to study attachment, the emotional bond between an infant and a caregiver. So, how does it work? A parent and a baby, usually about a year old, come into an unfamiliar room with toys. Over about twenty minutes, a series of short episodes takes place. A stranger enters. The parent leaves the baby with the stranger for a few minutes, then returns. Later the baby is left completely alone, briefly. Now, you might think the key moment is when the parent leaves. But Ainsworth focused on the reunion, what the baby does when the parent comes back. Securely attached babies may cry when the parent leaves, but when the parent returns, they seek comfort, calm down fairly quickly, and go back to playing. Avoidant babies tend to ignore the parent on return, as if they didn't care. And resistant babies seek contact but also push away, staying upset and hard to soothe. Later researchers added a fourth category for behavior that seemed confused or contradictory. One caution, though. In cultures where babies are rarely separated from their mothers, or rarely left with strangers, the same procedure may be far more stressful, so the results have to be interpreted carefully.

at5-25.text: Listen to a talk in a sociology class.

In 1928, the sociologist W. I. Thomas made an observation that's become a basic idea in sociology: if people define situations as real, they are real in their consequences. In other words, what people believe about a situation shapes how they act, whether or not the belief is accurate. Twenty years later, another sociologist, Robert Merton, built on this with a concept he called the self-fulfilling prophecy. That's a false belief that leads to behavior that makes the belief come true. Merton's best-known example was a bank. Imagine a bank that's perfectly healthy. It has enough assets, and it's well managed. But a rumor starts that it's about to fail. What happens? Depositors rush to take out their money, and since no bank keeps all its deposits on hand as cash, the bank really does run out. The prophecy produced the very failure it predicted. Now, Merton stressed that the original belief was false. That's what makes it self-fulfilling, rather than just an accurate prediction. Researchers have since looked for the same pattern in classrooms. A famous study in the 1960s reported that when teachers were told certain students were about to bloom academically, those students later showed greater gains. Later work, though, suggests that teacher expectations do matter, but their effects are usually smaller than that first study claimed.

at5-26.text: Listen to a talk in a sociology class.

When you hear the word bureaucracy, you probably think of long lines, endless forms, and offices where nobody will help you. But for the German sociologist Max Weber, writing in the early twentieth century, bureaucracy was something more interesting. He saw it as the most efficient form of organization humans had devised. So what is a bureaucracy, in Weber's sense? It has a clear hierarchy, with each office reporting to the one above. Tasks are divided among specialists. Decisions follow written rules and are recorded in files. And officials are hired for their qualifications, not because they're someone's relative or friend. Notice that last point. Compared with older systems, where positions were handed out through personal loyalty, bureaucracy was in a sense fairer. Everyone is treated by the same rules, impersonally. That predictability is what made it so powerful. Yet Weber was deeply uneasy about it. As rational rules spread through government, business, and everyday life, he feared that people would become trapped in systems they couldn't escape, valued only for their function. His image for this is usually translated into English as the iron cage. Actually, the German phrase is closer to 'a shell as hard as steel,' which suggests something we come to wear, not just something around us. So Weber's view was neither simply for nor against bureaucracy. Its strengths and dangers came from the same source.

at5-27.text: Listen to a talk in an economics class.

In 1968, the ecologist Garrett Hardin published an essay called 'The Tragedy of the Commons,' and it became one of the most cited arguments in the social sciences. Here's his scenario. Imagine a pasture open to all herders. Each herder thinks: if I add one more cow, I get all the benefit of that cow, but the cost, a little less grass, is shared by everyone. So it's rational for each herder to add another cow, and another. The result, Hardin argued, is that the pasture is overgrazed and ruined. Individual rationality leads to collective disaster. His solutions were essentially two: divide the land into private property, or have the government regulate its use. Now, the political economist Elinor Ostrom challenged this. She studied real communities that had managed shared resources for generations: alpine meadows in Switzerland, forests in Japan, irrigation systems in Spain. These weren't free-for-alls. Users had clear rules about who could use the resource, they made those rules themselves, they monitored one another, and they used gradually increasing penalties for rule breakers. Ostrom won the Nobel Prize in economics in 2009 for this work. So was Hardin wrong? Not exactly. His model describes what happens with truly open access, where anyone can take and nobody coordinates. What Ostrom showed is that real commons are often not like that. The tragedy is possible, but not inevitable.

at5-28.text: Listen to a talk in an economics class.

Okay, here's a puzzle. Suppose one country can produce everything more efficiently than another country. Should it bother to trade with that country at all? It seems like the answer should be no. But in 1817, the economist David Ricardo showed why the answer is actually yes. His example used England and Portugal, and two goods, cloth and wine. In his numbers, Portugal could make both with less labor than England. Economists say Portugal had an absolute advantage in both. But Portugal's advantage was much bigger in wine than in cloth. So, Ricardo argued, Portugal should specialize in wine, England in cloth, and they should trade. Both countries end up with more of both goods. The key concept here is comparative advantage, which is about opportunity cost, what you give up to produce something. Every hour Portuguese workers spent making cloth was an hour not spent making wine, where they were especially productive. Here's an everyday version. Imagine a lawyer who types faster than her assistant. Should she do her own typing? Probably not, because every hour spent typing is an hour not spent practicing law, which earns far more. Now, the model has limits. It assumes workers can easily move from one industry to another. In reality, workers in a shrinking industry may struggle to find new jobs. So the gains are real, but they aren't shared evenly.

at5-29.text: Listen to a talk in an economic history class.

There's an old economic principle usually summarized as 'bad money drives out good.' It's called Gresham's law, after Thomas Gresham, a sixteenth-century English financial agent, although the idea is older. What does it mean? Imagine two coins with the same official value, but one contains more silver than the other. Which one would you spend? The one with less silver, of course. You'd keep the better coin, or even melt it down, because the metal inside is worth more than the coin's face value. If everyone does this, the good coins vanish, and only the bad ones change hands. There's a well-known modern case. In 1965, the United States stopped putting silver in its dimes and quarters. Within a few years, the old silver coins had largely disappeared from everyday use, as people set them aside. Now, here's the important condition, and it's easy to miss. Gresham's law works because the law requires people to accept both coins at the same value. A shopkeeper can't say, 'I'll take your old silver quarter, but not that new one.' When that condition breaks down, the effect can reverse. During periods of very high inflation, sellers often refuse the weak local currency and demand a more stable foreign one. In that case, good money drives out bad. So whether bad money wins depends on the rules, not just on the money.

at5-30.text: Listen to a talk in a management class.

Today's topic is a man whose ideas still shape how work is organized, even if most workers have never heard of him: Frederick Winslow Taylor. In 1911, Taylor published The Principles of Scientific Management. His argument was that most work was done inefficiently, by rule of thumb, and that it could be improved through careful measurement. So, what did that look like? Taylor and his assistants used stopwatches to time each part of a job, broke tasks into their smallest motions, and searched for what he called the one best way to do them. Workers were then trained in that method, and often paid by the piece to encourage output. His most famous example involved workers loading heavy iron bars onto railroad cars. Taylor claimed that with the right method and rest breaks, one worker raised his daily load from about twelve and a half tons to forty-seven. Historians have questioned that story. But the bigger debate is about what the system did to work itself. Taylor separated the planning of work, done by managers, from the doing of it, done by workers. Supporters saw this as a major gain in productivity. Critics argued that it stripped workers of skill and judgment, turning them into parts of a machine. There were strikes against these methods, and even government hearings. Yet look at a modern warehouse. Taylor's influence is everywhere.

at5-31.text: Listen to a talk in a marketing class.

Why do so many prices end in ninety-nine? Two ninety-nine instead of three dollars, nineteen ninety-nine instead of twenty. One cent can't possibly matter, right? Well, research suggests it does. The practice is often called charm pricing, and one explanation for it is the left-digit effect. We read numbers from left to right, and we tend to give the first digit a lot of weight. So when we see two ninety-nine, our first impression is 'two dollars and something,' and that impression sticks, even though the price is almost exactly three dollars. The effect seems strongest when we're making quick decisions, like scanning store shelves. In one field experiment, a clothing catalog offered the same dress at different prices in different versions. Surprisingly, the dress sold more at thirty-nine dollars than at thirty-four. A price ending in nine seemed to signal a bargain. Now, you may have heard a different story about where this practice came from: that odd prices forced cashiers to open the register to make change, which made it harder to pocket the money. It's a nice story, but there's little evidence for it. And here's an exception. Sellers of luxury goods often avoid nines altogether. They use round numbers, because a price ending in nine can make a product look discounted, and that's the last thing an expensive product wants to suggest.

at5-32.text: Listen to a talk in a political science class.

Why do some countries have two dominant political parties while others have five or six? One influential answer comes from the French political scientist Maurice Duverger. In the 1950s, he argued that election rules shape the party system. His most famous claim, now called Duverger's law, says that plurality voting in single-member districts tends to produce two-party systems. Plurality just means the candidate with the most votes wins, even without a majority. Duverger identified two forces. The first is mechanical: in a winner-take-all district, a party that comes third everywhere can win a decent share of the national vote but almost no seats. The second is psychological: voters anticipate this, and rather than waste their vote on a party that can't win, they shift to one of the two front-runners. By contrast, proportional representation, where seats are divided according to vote share, lets smaller parties survive, and it tends to produce many parties. Now, is it really a law? There are well-known exceptions. Some countries with plurality voting have several significant parties. The usual explanation is geography. Duverger's logic works within each district, so a party that's weak nationally but strong in one region can still win seats there, and survive. So most political scientists today treat Duverger's law less as a law than as a strong tendency, one that depends on how votes are distributed.

at5-33.text: Listen to a talk in an education class.

Think about the last time you learned something difficult, maybe a math concept or a new sport. Was there a point where you couldn't quite do it alone, but you could do it with someone guiding you? That in-between space is the heart of today's topic. The Russian psychologist Lev Vygotsky, working in the 1920s and early 1930s, called it the zone of proximal development. It's the gap between what a learner can do independently and what they can do with help from someone more skilled, like a teacher or even a more experienced classmate. Now, why does that matter? Vygotsky argued that teaching is most effective when it's aimed at this zone. Too easy, and the learner doesn't grow. Too hard, and even with help, they can't succeed. Decades later, researchers introduced a related term: scaffolding. Just like the scaffolding around a building under construction, the support is temporary. A teacher might begin by breaking a task into steps, giving hints, or demonstrating. Then, as the learner gains skill, the support is gradually removed. Picture teaching a child to ride a bike. You hold the seat, then you just keep a hand near it, and eventually you let go. Notice how this differs from the view of Jean Piaget, who emphasized children discovering ideas largely on their own. For Vygotsky, learning was fundamentally social.

at5-34.text: Listen to a talk in a media studies class.

Does the news change what we think? For a long time, researchers found surprisingly weak effects. People rarely changed their opinions just because of what they read or watched. But in 1963, a political scientist made an observation that redirected the field. He wrote, roughly, that the press may not be very successful at telling people what to think, but it's remarkably successful at telling them what to think about. That's the core of what we now call agenda-setting. In 1968, two researchers tested the idea in a single town in North Carolina during a presidential election. They asked undecided voters which issues they considered most important, and then measured how much coverage each issue received in the news. The match was striking. The issues that got the most coverage were the issues voters ranked as most important. Now, you should already see the problem. A match like that doesn't tell you which way the influence runs. Maybe the media simply covered what the public already cared about. So later researchers used experiments. They showed people edited newscasts that gave extra attention to one issue, and afterward, those viewers rated that issue as more important than viewers who'd seen other versions. That's much stronger evidence of cause. And the idea has grown since. Researchers now study not just which topics get attention, but which aspects of a topic are emphasized.

at5-35.text: Listen to a talk in a geography class.

Look at the world map on the wall. Greenland looks about as big as Africa, doesn't it? In reality, Africa is about fourteen times larger. So what's going on? This map uses the Mercator projection, created by the Flemish mapmaker Gerardus Mercator in 1569. And to understand it, you need to know what it was designed for. Mercator's goal was navigation. On his map, a line of constant compass direction appears as a straight line. So a sailor could draw a straight line from one port to another, measure the angle, and follow that compass heading. That was enormously useful. But there's a price. You can't flatten a sphere onto paper without distorting something. It's like trying to flatten an orange peel without tearing or stretching it. Mercator's map keeps angles and the shapes of small areas correct, but it stretches areas more and more as you move away from the equator. Near the poles, the stretching becomes extreme, which is why Greenland and Antarctica look enormous. Now, other projections make different trade-offs. Equal-area projections show the sizes of regions correctly, but they distort shapes, so continents can look squashed or stretched. There's no perfect flat map. Every projection is a choice about what to get right. The real problem comes when a map designed for sailors becomes the picture of the world that most people grow up with.

at5-36.text: Listen to a talk in an urban geography class.

Why are towns spaced the way they are? Why does a small village have a bakery but not a specialist hospital? In 1933, the German geographer Walter Christaller proposed an answer, now called central place theory, based on settlements in southern Germany. The idea starts with two concepts. The first is threshold: the minimum number of customers needed to keep a business going. The second is range: the maximum distance people are willing to travel for something. Now, think about bread. People buy it often and won't travel far for it, but it doesn't take many customers to support a bakery. So bakeries appear even in small settlements. A jewelry store or a specialist doctor is the opposite. People need them rarely and will travel farther, but they need many customers. So those appear only in big cities. The result, Christaller argued, is a hierarchy: many small places offering basic goods, fewer towns offering more, and a few cities offering almost everything. He also predicted that market areas would form hexagons. Why hexagons? Because circles would either overlap or leave gaps, while hexagons fit together perfectly. Of course, the theory assumes a flat, uniform plain, with people spread evenly and travel equally easy in all directions. Real landscapes have rivers, mountains, and highways, and people with cars often skip the nearest center. Still, the hierarchy itself remains surprisingly visible.

at5-37.text: Listen to a talk in a history of technology class.

We often credit Johannes Gutenberg with inventing movable type around 1450. But that's not quite right. Movable type was first invented in China, in the 1040s, by a craftsman named Bi Sheng, who made individual characters out of baked clay. And in Korea, printers were using movable metal type by the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. The oldest surviving book printed with metal type is Korean, from 1377, decades before Gutenberg. So here's the question. Why did movable type transform European society so quickly, while in East Asia it remained less dominant? One major factor is the writing system. European languages use alphabets with a few dozen letters. Chinese writing uses thousands of characters. A printer working in Chinese needed an enormous stock of type, and finding and sorting each character was slow. Woodblock printing, where an entire page is carved into a single block, was often simply more practical. The blocks could be stored and reused for new print runs. So it's a mistake to see East Asia as having missed an opportunity. Printers there made a reasonable choice, and woodblock printing produced enormous numbers of books. Gutenberg's real achievement, then, wasn't the idea of movable type. It was a whole system: a mold for casting identical metal letters quickly, an oil-based ink that stuck to metal, and a press adapted from those used to make wine.

at5-38.text: Listen to a talk in a world history class.

The Inca Empire, stretching along the Andes, ran a huge state, with roads, storehouses, and labor obligations, all without writing in the usual sense. So how did they keep records? The answer is the quipu, a set of knotted cords. A quipu has a main cord, with dozens or even hundreds of cords hanging from it. On many quipus, the knots record numbers in a base-ten system. Knots farthest from the main cord represent units, the next cluster up represents tens, then hundreds, and so on. Different types of knots made the system readable; for example, a figure-eight knot marks a one in the units position. This code was worked out in the early twentieth century, and it shows quipus were used for census counts and tribute records. The officials who made and read them were specialists. Now, here's the open question. Spanish chroniclers after the conquest reported that these specialists could recite histories, laws, and family lines from their cords. So did some quipus record language, not just numbers? A significant share of surviving quipus don't seem to fit the numerical system, and features like color, fiber, and knot direction may carry meaning. But no one has deciphered them. One problem is that the chroniclers may have misunderstood what they saw. Another is that the cords may have been memory aids, readable only by their makers.

at5-39.text: Listen to a talk in a history of science class.

In the mid-1800s, most doctors in Europe believed that diseases like cholera spread through miasma, which basically means bad air, foul smells rising from rotting matter. It made sense: disease was common in crowded, smelly neighborhoods. But the London doctor John Snow suspected that cholera spread through contaminated water. In 1854, a severe outbreak struck the Soho district of London, and hundreds of people died within days. Snow went door to door, recording where the victims had lived, and he marked the deaths on a map. They clustered around a single public water pump on Broad Street. Now, some of the most persuasive evidence came from the exceptions. A nearby brewery had almost no cases. Why? The workers were given beer to drink, and the brewery had its own well, so they didn't use the pump. A nearby workhouse, also with its own well, had very few deaths. Meanwhile, a woman who lived miles away had died. It turned out she liked the taste of Broad Street water and had it brought to her house. Snow presented his findings, and local officials removed the handle of the pump. It's a famous story, but one caution: the outbreak was already declining by then, partly because many residents had fled. So removing the handle probably wasn't what ended it. The real importance was the method: careful mapping and close attention to exceptions.

at5-40.text: Listen to a talk in a painting class.

When we talk about Impressionism, we usually talk about artists like Monet and Renoir and their interest in capturing light outdoors. But today I want to look at a humble piece of technology that helped make that possible: the paint tube. Before the 1840s, oil paint was hard to carry around. Painters, or their assistants, ground pigments by hand and mixed them with oil in the studio. If paint was stored at all, it was usually kept in small bags made from pig bladders, tied with string. You'd prick the bladder to squeeze out some paint, but the bags leaked, burst easily, and the paint dried out. Then, in 1841, an American portrait painter named John Goffe Rand patented a collapsible metal tube with a cap. Paint stayed fresh, and it could be carried anywhere. Combined with portable easels and a range of new, bright, ready-made colors, this meant painters could work outdoors, directly in front of the scene, for hours. Renoir is reported to have said that without paint in tubes, there would have been no Impressionism. Now, we shouldn't overstate this. Artists had been making small oil sketches outdoors long before tubes existed. And many Impressionist paintings that look spontaneous were actually reworked or finished in the studio. So the tube didn't create the movement. But it certainly made the Impressionists' way of working far easier.

at5-41.text: Listen to a talk in a music history class.

Today let's talk about an instrument you all know, whose name tells a story. Around 1700, in Florence, an instrument maker named Bartolomeo Cristofori, who worked for the powerful Medici family, built a new kind of keyboard. Now, the dominant keyboard instrument at the time was the harpsichord. When you press a harpsichord key, a small quill plucks the string. And here's the limitation: no matter how hard or softly you press the key, the string is plucked in much the same way, so the volume barely changes. Cristofori's idea was to strike the strings with small hammers instead. The harder you press the key, the faster the hammer moves, and the louder the sound. He also solved a tricky mechanical problem: the hammer had to hit the string and then immediately fall away, so the string could keep vibrating. He called the instrument, roughly translated, a harpsichord with soft and loud, in Italian, piano e forte. And that's where our word piano comes from. Interestingly, the invention didn't catch on right away. It took decades of improvements before the piano became the instrument that composers like Mozart and Beethoven wrote for. There was one older keyboard that could vary its volume, by the way: the clavichord. But it was so quiet that it was mainly used for practice in small rooms, not for public performance.

at5-42.text: Listen to a talk in an anthropology class.

We tend to imagine life before farming as a constant struggle for survival, people working from dawn to dusk just to eat. In the 1960s, the anthropologist Marshall Sahlins challenged that picture with a deliberately provocative phrase: the original affluent society. His argument drew on new studies of foragers, people who live by hunting and gathering, including groups in the Kalahari Desert. Researchers had recorded how much time people actually spent getting food, and the numbers were surprisingly low, often around fifteen to twenty hours a week. So in what sense were they affluent? Sahlins pointed out that there are two ways to satisfy your wants. You can produce a lot, or you can want little. Foragers moved often, so owning many things was a burden, not a benefit. With modest wants and fairly reliable food sources, they had plenty of leisure. Now, the critique. Later anthropologists pointed out that those early figures counted only time spent hunting and gathering. They left out making tools, processing food, collecting firewood, and other household work. Include all of that, and the total comes much closer to a full working week. Studies also found seasonal hunger in some groups. So the strong version of Sahlins's claim hasn't held up. But his deeper point, that affluence depends on what people want, not only on what they have, still challenges ideas of economic progress.

cv1-01.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a librarian.
Hi, I requested a book through interlibrary loan about three weeks ago, and it still hasn't arrived. I need it for a paper that's due next Friday.
Let me look that up. Okay, it's a 1962 study of coastal fishing villages, right? It looks like the lending library flagged it as too fragile to ship.
Oh no. So I can't get it at all?
Not the physical copy, no. But many libraries will scan a chapter or two instead. Do you know which sections you actually need?
Really just chapter four. That's where the author describes how the villages shared their boats.
Then I'll submit a scan request right now. Those usually come back within three or four days, and you'll get a link by email.
That would be perfect. Thanks so much.
Sure. And next time, list the chapters you need when you make a request. It speeds things up.

cv1-02.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an employee at the housing office.

Let me check. Okay, I see it. The problem is that your floor uses an older heating system, and the technicians need a special part. It won't arrive until Thursday.
I know. What I can do is lend you a portable heater from our office today. You'd just need to sign it out and return it once the repair is done.
That'd help a lot. Can I take it now?
Yes. Just fill out this short form, and I'll bring one from the back.

cv1-03.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor.
Professor Navarro, do you have a minute? It's about my proposal on urban heat islands.
Of course. I thought it was a strong proposal. What's on your mind?
Well, most of the research I'm reading focuses on huge tropical cities. Could I study our own town instead? It's much smaller, and nobody seems to have looked at it.
Interesting. The risk, though, is that 'nobody has studied it' can also mean there's no data to work with.
Actually, the county has recorded surface temperatures at a dozen sites since 2015. I found the files last night.
Ah, then you're in better shape than most students who ask me that. Send me a one-page revision by Monday explaining how you'll compare the sites, and I'll approve it.
Great. Should I keep the tropical studies in my literature review?
Definitely. They'll give you a baseline, or help you show how a small town differs.

Not necessarily. How were you doing before you got sick?

Then you might ask your professor for an incomplete instead. You'd finish the remaining work over the break and keep credit for what you've done. If you withdraw, you'd retake the whole course next year.
I didn't know that was possible. Do I just email her?
Talk to her in person if you can, and bring the doctor's note. Then come back, and we'll file the form together.

Unfortunately, no. This machine has its own short training, because the light source can be damaged if it's switched off the wrong way.
Oh. How long does that take?
It's an online module, about thirty minutes, plus a five-question quiz. Once you pass, your name goes on the approved list automatically.
So if I do it over lunch, I could still come in at two?
Exactly. Just write your name on the sign-up sheet by the door so nobody else takes the slot.

Let's take a look. Hmm, the first half is mostly courses you've taken. Why did you put those at the top?
I figured they'd show I know the science.
They do, but the posting emphasizes teaching young visitors. Down here, you mention volunteering at a weekend science club for kids. Tell me about that.
I've done it for two years. I design small experiments, like building rain gauges, and run them for groups of about fifteen children.
That's exactly what they're looking for, and it's buried at the bottom. Move it up, and describe it the way you just did, with numbers.
So the coursework should go lower?
Keep one line listing your most relevant courses. The experience is what will get you an interview.

cv1-09.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a psychology professor.
Professor Lindqvist, I'm worried about my replication project. The original study found that people remembered words better after drawing them, but my results showed no difference.
That's not necessarily a problem. Plenty of published effects don't hold up when someone repeats the study. Tell me about your participants.
There were twenty-four, all from the same evening class. Most had been on campus since morning.
So they might have been tired, and twenty-four is fairly small. Either could hide a real effect, or the effect could be weaker than the original paper claimed.
Should I recruit more people and run it again?
Not before the deadline. Report what you found honestly, and use your discussion section to explain those possible reasons.
Okay. I guess I thought a result like this meant I'd made a mistake.
Not at all. A careful result that shows no effect is still evidence.

The Saturday morning session is full, unfortunately. But there's one on Thursday evening at six with two spots left.
Thursday works. Is there a fee?
Fifteen dollars, and that covers the harness for the class. In the meantime, you can use the bouldering area without the certification. Those walls are short, and there are thick mats underneath.
Oh, nice. So I could try that today?
Sure. Just sign the waiver at the front desk and grab some climbing shoes.

cv1-15.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a tutor at the campus writing center.
Hi, my history professor said my thesis is too broad, but I'm not sure how to fix it.
Let's read it. 'The printing press transformed European society.' Well, she's right. Whole books have been written about that. What did you focus on in your research?
Mostly almanacs. They were cheap little books, and almost every household in rural England seemed to have one.
That's much more specific. What did people use them for?
Lots of things: calendars, weather predictions, advice on when to plant crops.
So what's your argument about them? Remember, a thesis should be something a reader could disagree with.
I guess that almanacs spread practical knowledge to farmers who never would've read longer books.
Now that's a thesis. It's narrow, it's debatable, and your sources can actually support it.

cv2-01.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a bike shop mechanic.
Hi, my bike's been making a clicking noise, and yesterday the chain slipped right off on my way to class. Could you take a look?
Sure. Let me spin the pedals... Yeah, your chain's stretched, and the teeth on the back gears are pretty worn down. That's why it keeps slipping.
Is that expensive to fix? I'm kind of on a student budget.
Replacing both runs about sixty dollars. If you only replace the chain, the new one probably won't grip the old gears, so I'd really recommend doing both.
Okay, that makes sense. How long will it take? I ride to campus every day.
We're a little backed up, so it'd be ready Thursday afternoon. But we lend loaner bikes to repair customers for free. You'd just need to leave your student ID with us.
Oh, perfect. Let's do that, then.

cv2-02.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a staff member at the campus gym.
Hi, I tried to sign up for the Tuesday evening spin class online, but the website says it's full. Is there any way to get in?
That one fills up fast. You can add your name to the waitlist here, though. People cancel all the time, especially around midterms.
How would I know if a spot opens up?
You'd get a text about two hours before class. You just have to reply within thirty minutes, or the spot goes to the next person.
Got it. Are there any other spin classes I could try in the meantime?
There's a Thursday session at seven in the morning. It's early, so it almost never fills.
Seven's tough, but I'll give it a shot. Can you put me on both lists?
Thursday doesn't need a list. Just show up. I'll add you to Tuesday's waitlist now.

cv2-03.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a clerk at the campus bookstore.
Hi, I'd like to return this chemistry textbook. I dropped the course yesterday.
No problem. Do you have your receipt?
Um, I think I threw it away. I bought the book the first week of the semester.
That's okay. If you paid with a card, I can look up the purchase. Otherwise, I can only give you store credit.
I used my debit card. Here it is.
Great, I found it. Since you're returning it within the drop period and it's still in new condition, you'll get a full refund to your card.
What if I'd written in it?
Then we'd treat it as used, and you'd get about half. You're fine, though. These pages look untouched.

cv2-04.text: Listen to a conversation between two roommates.
Marcus, do you have a minute? The electric bill came, and it's way higher than last month.
Almost ninety dollars. I think it's the space heater in your room. You leave it on all night.
Yeah, that's fair. My room's freezing, though. The window doesn't close all the way.
Have you told building maintenance? If they fix the window, you might not need the heater at all.
I didn't even think of that. I'll submit a repair request tonight.
And for this month, how about you cover a bit more of the bill? Say, fifty, and I'll pay forty.
Sounds reasonable. I'll send you the money this weekend.

cv2-05.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a lost-and-found attendant.
Hi, I lost my graphing calculator somewhere in the science building on Monday. Has anyone turned one in?
We get a lot of calculators. Can you describe it?
It's black, with a green sticker on the back. And my initials, K.T., are scratched near the battery cover.
Let me check Monday's bin... Here's one with a green sticker. Do you see your initials?
Yes! That's it. I was about to buy a new one for my exam on Friday.
Lucky timing. I just need you to sign this form and show me your student ID.
Sure. Is there any way to keep this from happening again?
Some students tape their email address inside the cover. Then we can contact them directly.

cv2-06.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a clerk at the campus transit office.
Hi, my bus pass stopped working. The driver's scanner just beeps red every time I tap it.
Let me scan it here... The card's chip is damaged. Did it get bent, maybe?
I don't think so. It's always in my wallet, and it's only two months old.
Hmm, we've had a batch of cards from this fall with faulty chips. Actually, yours is from that batch.
So do I have to pay for a new one? I heard replacements are fifteen dollars.
Normally, yes, but not for defective cards. I'll print you a new one right now, and your remaining balance will transfer over.
That's a relief. Will I need to register it again online?
No, it's linked to your student account automatically.

cv2-07.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and his supervisor at a campus cafe.
Grace, can I ask you something? I'm scheduled for the Saturday morning shift, but my biology lab exam just got moved to that day.
Oh no. Saturday mornings are our busiest time. Have you asked anyone to switch?
I asked Rosa, but she's going out of town. I haven't asked anyone else yet.
Try Ben. He told me last week he wants more hours. If he agrees, he can take your shift, and you could cover his Wednesday evening.
Wednesday works for me. Do I need to fill anything out?
Just update the swap on the shared schedule and message me once he confirms. I need to approve it before Friday.
Okay. I'll text him right after my shift.

cv2-08.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and the advisor of a campus theater club.
Mr. Hart, about the spring production: I'd love to audition for a role, but I also signed up for the lighting crew.
I saw that. The trouble is, lighting is busiest during tech week, which is exactly when actors run full rehearsals. You can't be on stage and in the booth at once.
Right. I was hoping to learn the technical side without giving up acting.

Here's a thought. Audition this spring, and attend a few Saturday workshops with our lighting designer. She runs them before tech week, so there's no overlap. Then next fall, for the smaller studio show, you could design the lights yourself.
Design them myself? I've never done that.
That's why the workshops matter. The studio show uses a much simpler setup, so it's a good place to start.
Okay, that sounds like a better plan.

cv2-09.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a career counselor.
Ms. Okafor, I got an interview with that engineering firm, but they want to meet next Thursday at ten, which is exactly when my statistics midterm is.
Congratulations! Have you contacted them about it yet?
Not yet. I'm worried that if I ask to reschedule, they'll think I'm not serious.
Honestly, recruiters deal with this constantly. What matters is how you ask. Reply quickly, thank them, explain the conflict briefly, and offer two or three specific times that work for you.
Should I mention it's an exam, or just say I'm unavailable?
Mention the exam. It shows you take your commitments seriously, which is exactly what they want in an intern.
Good point. But what if they can't move it?
Then talk to your professor about taking the midterm another day. But I doubt it'll come to that.

cv2-10.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a study-abroad advisor.
Hi, Mr. Silva. I'm finishing my application for a semester in Lisbon, and I have a question about credits. One course I want, urban geography, isn't on the approved list.
That happens a lot. The list only covers courses our students have taken before. It doesn't mean the course won't count.
So how do I get it approved?

You'll need the syllabus, ideally with the reading list and the number of class hours. Send it to the geography department, and they'll decide whether it matches one of our courses or counts as a general elective.
How long does that take? The application's due in three weeks.
Usually about ten days. But you don't have to wait for approval to submit. Just list the course as pending.
Oh, good. I'll email the department today, then.

cv2-11.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a receptionist at the campus health clinic.
Hi, I need a form signed for a hospital volunteer program. They want proof of a tuberculosis test from the past year.
No, I don't think so. Can I get one today?
We can start it today, but it's a two-visit process. The nurse places the test today, and you come back in two or three days so she can read the result. The form can only be signed after that.
Hmm. The program wants everything by Friday, and it's already Tuesday.
Then you're cutting it close, but it works if you come in this afternoon. The nurse has openings at two and three-thirty, and your follow-up would be Thursday or Friday morning.
Let's do two o'clock. Do I need to bring anything?
Just your insurance card and the volunteer form, so the nurse can complete it at your second visit.

cv2-12.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a volunteer coordinator.
Hi, Mr. Brooks. I signed up to tutor in the elementary school reading program, but I just got an email saying I can't start next week.
Right. That's because your background check hasn't cleared yet. It usually takes about two weeks for anyone working directly with children.
Two weeks? I was hoping to log volunteer hours for my education course. I need twenty by the end of the month.
I understand. In the meantime, you could help with our book drive. We're sorting donated books for the school library, and that doesn't require clearance because there's no contact with kids.
Would those hours count for my course?
They should, since it supports the same literacy program. But double-check with your instructor to be safe.
I will. Could I start sorting this weekend?
Absolutely. We're in the community center basement Saturday from nine to noon.

cv2-13.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a technician at the campus IT help desk.
Hi, my laptop won't connect to the campus wireless network anymore. My phone's fine, though.
Did you change your university password recently?
Yeah, on Monday. The system made me update it.
That's almost certainly it. Your phone probably asked for the new password, but laptops often keep trying the old saved one. After a few failed attempts, the network temporarily locks the device out.
Oh. So what should I do?
First, tell your laptop to forget the network. Then wait about fifteen minutes for the lockout to clear before reconnecting with your new password.
Why wait? Can't I just reconnect right away?
If you try during the lockout, it counts as another failed attempt and resets the timer. So grab a coffee and try again afterward.

cv2-14.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and the coordinator of the campus community garden.
Hi, I applied for a plot in the campus garden last month, but I haven't heard anything. Do you know where I stand?
Let me look... You're seventh on the waitlist. Honestly, with only twenty plots, spots don't open up often. Maybe one or two a semester.
That's disappointing. I was hoping to grow vegetables this spring.
Well, have you considered a shared plot? A graduate student, Mei, told me she can't keep up with hers this year and would welcome a partner.
Would I still keep my place on the waitlist?
Yes, sharing doesn't affect your position. And frankly, it's a good way to learn. Mei's been gardening here for three years.
Then I'd definitely like to meet her.
Great. I'll email you both and set something up.

cv2-15.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a technician at the campus print center.
Hi, I'm printing a poster for a research conference this weekend, and the test print looks blurry. On my screen it's perfectly sharp.
Let me see the file... Ah, your photos are low resolution. They look fine on a screen, but when we enlarge them to poster size, every pixel gets stretched.
Oh no. They're photos I took of my lab samples. Can you fix them?
Not really. You can't add detail that isn't there. Do you still have the original images from the camera?
I think so. I probably shrank them when I pasted them into my slides.
That's likely it. Replace them with the originals, export the file again at full quality, and send it over. If it's in by noon tomorrow, we'll have it ready Thursday.
That still gives me a day to spare. Thanks so much.

cv3-01.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a geology professor.
Professor Brandt, could I run my paper topic by you? I'm thinking of writing about how volcanic soils affect farming around the world.
Around the world? In twelve pages?
Well, I know it's big. But there's so much good material, and I didn't want to leave anything out.
That's the trouble, though. If you cover everything, you can only say a sentence or two about each place. Is there a region you've read a lot about?
Actually, yes. Coffee farms on volcanic slopes in Central America. And I found a few studies on rice terraces in Southeast Asia.
Now that could work. Two regions, two very different crops, the same kind of soil. You'd have room to really compare them.
So I'd drop the global part completely?
Mention it in your introduction, as background. Send me a revised outline by Friday.

cv3-02.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a teaching assistant for a chemistry course.
Hi, Aisha. Do you have a second? I got my lab report back, and I lost fifteen points. I'm not sure why.
Sure, let me see. Oh, right. Your results section is fine, but you didn't include any error analysis.
Error analysis? I thought that was only for the final report.
No, it's required for every report this semester. It was in the guidelines. You need to estimate how uncertain your measurements were, like the readings from the balance.
Oh, I must have missed that. Is there anything I can do now?
The professor lets students revise one report per term. If you add the error analysis and turn it in by Monday, you can earn back up to ten points.
Great. I'll work on it this weekend.
Good. And check the example report that's posted online. It shows the format we want.

cv3-03.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an astronomy professor.
Professor Ruiz, I'm sorry I missed the observing session on Tuesday night. I had a swim meet out of town. Is there a make-up session?
I wish there were. The point was to sketch the moon at first quarter, when the crater shadows are longest. That won't happen again for a month, and by then we'll be on to planets.
So I just lose the points?
Not necessarily. The department keeps an archive of telescope images taken at that same phase. You could measure the shadows from a photo and estimate the crater depths the same way.
That sounds like more work than sketching through the telescope.
Probably a bit more, yes. But it's the same skill. Next time, though, tell me before you miss a session.
I will. Where do I find the archive?

cv3-04.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a sociology professor.
Professor Hale, I'm planning my project on why some commuter students don't join campus clubs. I was going to use an online survey.
How many students do you think you'll reach?
Honestly, maybe fifteen. I only know a few commuters, and they'd have to pass it along.
With fifteen responses, a survey won't tell you much. The percentages would jump around too much. But fifteen is plenty for interviews.
Interviews? Wouldn't those take a lot longer?
Each one, yes. But you'd learn the reasons behind their choices, like work schedules or long drives. A survey would just turn those into checkboxes.
That makes sense. Should I write the questions first?
Yes. Draft about six open-ended questions and bring them to my office hours on Thursday.

cv3-05.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a teaching assistant for an economics course.
Hi, Mei. I wanted to ask about question three on the midterm. I drew the supply shift correctly, but I only got half credit.
Let me look. Hmm, your curve moves the right way, but you didn't label the new equilibrium price.
Right, but the question only asked which direction the price would go. I wrote 'price rises' underneath.
I see that. The rubric we used says the label is required for full credit, though.
The question doesn't say anything about labels. I checked.
Okay, you have a point. I didn't write the rubric, so I can't change it on my own. But I'll show your exam to Professor Grant at our meeting tomorrow.
Thanks. I'm not trying to argue about every point. That one just seemed unfair.
No, it's a reasonable question. I'll email you after the meeting.

cv3-06.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a linguistics professor.
Dr. Varga, I'd like to do an independent study next semester. My grandmother's village has its own dialect, and fewer people speak it every year.
That's a wonderful idea. Have you recorded any speakers yet?
Just my grandmother, over the summer. About three hours.

That's a good start. For an independent study, though, the department needs a written proposal. You'd describe what you plan to analyze, maybe the vowel sounds or the vocabulary, and include a reading list.
Two or three pages is fine. The deadline is the end of this month, and I'd be happy to supervise.
Really? Thank you. I'll start on the reading list this week.
Good. I'll send you a few articles on documenting dialects to get you going.

cv3-07.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a biology professor.
Professor Abara, I'm applying to a summer research program at a marine station, and I was hoping you could write me a recommendation letter.
I'd be glad to help. Remind me, you took my genetics lecture last spring?
Yes, I got an A. And this year I've been working in Dr. Petrova's lab, collecting water samples.

Hmm. Well, I can certainly say you did excellent work on exams. But the program will want to know how you handle fieldwork and lab routines. Dr. Petrova has seen that firsthand. I only saw you in a lecture hall of two hundred.
Oh. I just thought a letter from a full professor might carry more weight.
Titles matter less than details. Ask her first. If they need a second letter, I'm happy to write one.
Okay, that makes sense. I'll email her this afternoon.

cv3-08.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and his thesis advisor.
Professor Castillo, I have a problem with my thesis. The city archive is closing for renovations until April, and I was going to use their council records.
Oh, that's bad timing. Which years were you looking at?
The nineteen-twenties, when the city built its first public parks.
Then you might not need the archive at all. The local newspapers covered council meetings in a lot of detail back then, and our library has them on microfilm.
Would those count as primary sources?
Definitely. Newspaper reports from the time are primary sources. You'd just want to note that a reporter was summarizing, not quoting the official record.
That's a relief. I'll go to the library tomorrow and start with nineteen twenty-two.

cv3-09.text: Listen to a conversation between two students.
Grace, can I ask you something? Are you still going to the Wednesday study group for organic chemistry?
Honestly, I've been thinking about quitting. Last week we spent the first hour talking about a concert.
Same here. I went home and hadn't solved a single problem. But I don't want to study alone either.
What if we started our own? Just the two of us, maybe one more person. We'd each do the practice set beforehand and only meet to go over the ones we got stuck on.
I like that. Should we tell the others, though? I don't want them to feel like we're abandoning them.
We can just say we need a slower pace for the reaction mechanisms. That's true, anyway.

cv3-10.text: Listen to a conversation between two students working on a group project.
Diego, did you see Lucas's email? He says he can't edit our documentary at home anymore.
Why not? I thought he had the editing software.
He did, but it was a free trial, and it ran out. The full version is really expensive.
Hmm. The media lab in the arts building has that same program on every computer. Students in our course can use it for free.
Right, but the lab's always packed the week before projects are due.
You can reserve a station online, though. If we book a three-hour block on Saturday morning, all three of us could work on it together.
That might actually be better. Lucas has been doing all the editing alone, and he's kind of overwhelmed.
Then I'll make the reservation tonight and let him know.

cv3-11.text: Listen to a conversation between two students.
Sam, you're a psych major too, right? I can only fit one more course next term, and I'm torn between statistics and the social psychology seminar.
I took stats with Professor Kowalski last year. Brutal. Weekly problem sets, and she grades every one.
That's what I've heard. The seminar sounds like a lot more fun.
It is. But didn't you say you want to work in Dr. Amari's lab next year?
Yeah, I'm applying in the spring.
Well, everyone in that lab runs their own data analysis. When I applied, the first thing they asked was which stats course I'd taken. And the seminar's offered every term anyway.
Hmm. So I could take the seminar later. Okay. Kowalski it is, then. Wish me luck.

cv3-12.text: Listen to a conversation between two students.
Bianca, you work at the natural history museum on campus, don't you? I saw they're hiring tour guides.
Yeah, I've been giving tours for a year. You should apply. The pay's decent, and the hours are flexible.
Do I need to know a lot about fossils already? I'm an English major.
Not at all. Half the guides are from the humanities. There's a two-week training where you learn the main exhibits, and you shadow a guide before leading a tour yourself.
It is. But it's the first two weeks of the semester, every weekday afternoon. So you'd need to keep those afternoons free.
I have a seminar on Tuesday afternoons, though.
Then email the coordinator before you apply. Sometimes they let people do a Saturday session instead.

cv3-13.text: Listen to a conversation between two members of a campus chess club.
Felix, bad news about the chess tournament. Someone else booked the student center ballroom for the same Saturday.
What? We reserved it in September.
Apparently our booking was never confirmed. The events office says the other group finished their paperwork first.
Great. We already have forty players signed up. Could we use classrooms instead?
I asked. The math building has three rooms free, but they're on different floors.
That's a nightmare for running the pairings. We'd be running up and down the stairs between rounds.
Or we move it a week later. The ballroom's free then.
Hmm. A few players might drop out, but honestly, I'd rather lose a few people than run a messy tournament. Let's email everyone tonight.

cv3-14.text: Listen to a conversation between two students.
Chloe, have you decided about next year? You were choosing between a single room in Brookside Hall and the apartment with Maya.
Still deciding. The single is so convenient. It's right next to the science buildings.
That's the thing. The apartment's about two hundred dollars cheaper a month, even with utilities. And I'd have a kitchen, so I could stop paying for the meal plan.
About twenty minutes by bus. I've got early labs on Mondays and Wednesdays, though.
The bus starts at six, so you'd be fine. And with what you'd save, you'd hardly have to work weekends.
True. Okay, I'll tell Maya tonight that I'm in.

cv3-15.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and his research supervisor.
Dr. Achebe, I have some bad news about the camera traps at the creek site. The batteries in four of them died, so we lost almost two weeks of footage.
Two weeks. During the cold snap?
Exactly then. I'm really sorry. I can go out tomorrow and replace them, and maybe extend the study two more weeks to make up for it.
Replace the batteries, yes. But extending won't give us the same data. Animals behave differently once it warms up.
So the gap just stays there?
It stays, and we report it. Honestly, the failure is useful. The next team needs to know these units can't handle freezing nights.
I guess I was expecting you to be more upset.
Equipment fails. What matters is that you told me right away. Write up what happened in the field log tonight.

cv3-16.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and her research supervisor.
Dr. Whitfield, I wanted to update you on the memory study. We've only had nine participants in three weeks, and we need forty.
Hmm, that's slow. When are the sessions scheduled?
Weekday mornings, nine to noon. That's when the lab room is free.
That might be the problem. A lot of students have classes then, and the ones who don't are probably asleep.
I hadn't thought of that. But the room's booked in the afternoons.
What about evenings? It's open after six. I'd also post the study on the participant website, where students sign up for course credit.
Okay. I'll add evening sessions starting next week and get the posting up today.
Good. Let me know how the numbers look by Friday.

cv3-17.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an art history professor.
Professor Duarte, for my final paper I'd like to write about the mural in the old train station downtown. The one that was restored last year.
Good choice. Have you been to see it since the restoration?
Not yet. I've mostly been working from photos online. Some of them are really clear.
Photos are fine for the composition. But you know the restorers found an earlier painting underneath, right? Parts of it were left visible on purpose.
Wait, really? None of the photos I've seen show that.
Most were taken before the work was finished. That's why I'd go in person. And the restoration team is still in town. They might be willing to talk to you.
That would change my whole argument. I was going to say the colors were all the artist's originals.
Then you'd better see them first.

cv3-18.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a teaching assistant for a physics course.
Hi, Carmen. I missed the pendulum lab on Monday because I had the flu. Is there any way I can make it up?
Sorry to hear that. Are you feeling better now?
Good. Well, another section does the same lab on Thursday at two. You could join them for that week.
Thursday at two? I have a history class until two fifteen.
Hmm. The lab runs until four thirty, and the pendulum experiment only takes about an hour. If you get there by two thirty, you'll have plenty of time.
Great. Do I need to tell the other TA?
I'll email him today so he expects you. Just bring your lab notebook and your safety glasses.

cv3-19.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a philosophy professor.
Professor Osei, you wrote on my draft that it has 'no argument yet.' I'm a little confused. I spent pages on both positions about free will.
And you explained both very clearly. That's actually the problem. By the end, I still don't know what you think.
I guess I didn't want to pick the wrong side.
In philosophy, there isn't really a wrong side. There's only a weak defense of a side. Which position did you find more convincing while you were reading?
Honestly, the second one. The examples about choices made under pressure really stuck with me.
Then start there. Keep your summary of the first view, but treat it as the objection you have to answer.
So the paper doesn't get longer. It just takes a direction.
Exactly. Bring me a new introduction next week.

cv3-20.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a teaching assistant for a computer science course.
Hi, Raj. I couldn't submit my programming assignment last night. The submission site kept giving me an error.
Yeah, the server went down around ten. You weren't the only one. We got about thirty emails.
Oh, good. I mean, not good, but does that mean it'll count as late?
No. The professor extended the deadline to midnight tonight for everyone. She posted an announcement this morning.
I haven't checked the course page today. So should I just submit it again tonight?
Yes, through the site, the normal way. And if you saved your code before ten, you might mention the time in a comment, just in case.
I finished around nine thirty, so I'll do that. Thanks.

cv3-21.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and his research supervisor.
Dr. Leclerc, I've finished six interviews at the farmers' market, but three of the vendors didn't want to be recorded. I took handwritten notes for those.
That's fine, and you were right to respect that. Did you note it on their consent forms?
Consent forms? They agreed to the interview, so I just didn't think about it.
The plan we filed with the review board says every interview would be recorded. If we're switching methods for some people, the board needs to know.
Does that mean I can't use those three interviews?
You probably can. It's usually a quick amendment. But until it's approved, keep those notes separate, and leave them out of your analysis.
Okay. Should I write the amendment?
Draft it, and I'll sign it. Then we'll see.

cv3-22.text: Listen to a conversation between two members of a hiking club.
Lucy, I tried to reserve a van for the hiking club trip, but there's a problem. The campus rental office only allows drivers who are twenty-one or older.
Yeah. And so is everyone else on the planning committee. I already asked.
What about Dominic? He's a grad student, and he comes on almost every hike.
That could work. Do you think he'd want to drive two hours each way, though?
If we cover his lunch and let him pick the trail, I bet he would. He's always complaining that we choose easy ones.
Ha. Okay. Can you ask him? You know him better than I do.
Sure. I'll text him right now.

cv3-23.text: Listen to a conversation between two students.
Andre, can I ask you about being an RA? I'm thinking of applying for next year. Free housing sounds amazing.
It is nice. But you know you're on call two nights a week, right? Plus every few weekends.
Staying in the building, answering the door when someone's locked out at two in the morning, that kind of thing. Last semester I couldn't go home for my sister's birthday.
Hmm. I've got my internship in the spring, too. That's already fifteen hours a week.
Some RAs manage it. You'd just have to be really organized.
Organized isn't exactly my strong point. Maybe I'll wait until senior year, when my schedule's lighter.
That's not a bad idea. They hire seniors all the time.

cv3-24.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a nutrition professor.
Professor Adeyemi, I'd like to write my term paper on whether school lunch programs improve children's nutrition. Is that okay?
It's a good question. What evidence were you planning to use?
Mostly news articles. There've been a lot of stories about schools changing their menus.
News stories are useful for background, but they won't tell you much about nutrition itself. You'll need real data, like what children actually ate.
Where would I find something like that?
There's a national health survey done every two years. It asks families about children's diets, and the data's free online. Our health sciences librarian can show you how to search it.
Oh, that'd be great. I'll make an appointment with her.
Good. And narrow it to one age group. Elementary students would be a good start.

cv3-25.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an engineering professor.
Professor Nakamura, our team's truss bridge failed the load test yesterday. It broke at about sixty percent of the target weight.
I heard. Do you know where it failed?
At one of the joints near the middle. We think the glue didn't cure long enough. We were hoping to rebuild it and test again before the report's due.
You could. But the rubric doesn't reward a successful bridge so much as good analysis. A clear explanation of why it failed, with photos and calculations, often makes the stronger report.
So we'd just write about the failure?
Write about it honestly, and then say what you'd change. That's what engineers actually do.
That's a relief, honestly. Rebuilding in a week would've been a nightmare.
Just don't blame the glue without evidence. Look at the broken joint carefully first.

cv3-26.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a teaching assistant for a Spanish course.
Hugo, I have a scheduling problem. My oral exam is on the twelfth, but I'm presenting a poster at a student research conference that day.
Congratulations on the poster. Is the conference out of town?
Yes. I leave the morning of the eleventh and come back on the thirteenth.
Okay. The exams run all week, from the eighth through the twelfth. Could you take it earlier? I still have a slot on the ninth at ten.
The ninth works. Is it the same format? Ten minutes of conversation and a short reading?
Exactly the same. I'll switch your slot in the schedule today and send you a confirmation.
Thank you so much. I was worried I'd have to choose between them.

cv3-27.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and his research supervisor.
Dr. Sorensen, the alarm on the minus-eighty freezer went off over the weekend. When I came in this morning, it was only at minus twenty.
Oh no. Which shelves were our samples on?
The coral tissue was on top, and the seawater filters were on the bottom. I'm afraid it's all ruined. That's three months of collecting.

Not necessarily. The filters are for counting algae cells, and those hold up fine at minus twenty for a few days. The coral is another story. We're measuring proteins, and those break down quickly once they warm.
So we'd have to collect the coral again?
Probably. But the reef trip in May could cover that. Move the filters to the backup freezer now, and label the coral as damaged. Don't throw it out yet.
Okay. I'll do that right away.

cv3-28.text: Listen to a conversation between two students.
Ruby, you took Intro to Geology last year, right? I need one more science course, and I'm choosing between that and astronomy for non-majors.
I did. It was great. We went out to look at rock layers in the canyon a few times.
That sounds fun. When were the trips?
Saturdays, all day. There were four of them, and they counted for a big part of the grade.
Oh. I work at the bakery every Saturday morning, and I can't really switch.
Then astronomy's probably safer. My roommate took it. Everything's during the week, and there are a couple of evening viewing nights, but they're optional.
Optional is good. I'll sign up for astronomy, then.

cv3-29.text: Listen to a conversation between two students.
Isla, congrats! I heard the library offered you more hours at the circulation desk.
Yeah, they did. Twenty a week instead of twelve. I haven't said yes yet, though.
Why not? You were saying last month that rent was tight.
It still is. But the extra shifts are Tuesday and Thursday afternoons, and that's when I volunteer in Dr. Fenwick's lab.
Couldn't you volunteer some other time?
Not really. That's when they run the experiments. And Dr. Fenwick hinted she might have a paid position opening up this summer.
Ah. So you'd be giving up a sure thing now for something that might be better later.
Something I actually want to do. I think I'll tell the library twelve is enough for now.

cv3-30.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a statistics professor.
