Professor Holt, I'm interested in doing an independent study on sports statistics. Specifically, whether playing at home really helps basketball teams win.
That's a classic question. Which statistics courses have you taken so far?
Just the intro course, last fall.
Then you haven't done regression yet. To answer your question properly, you'd need to account for things like team strength and travel distance. That takes regression.
Not yet. Take Regression Methods in the spring, and we could do the independent study next fall. In the meantime, you could start collecting game results from past seasons.
Okay. That actually gives me time to build a really good data set.

cv3-31.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a literature professor.
Professor Whitaker, I know this is short notice, but I'm applying to a master's program in comparative literature, and the deadline is Monday. Would you be able to write me a letter?
I know. One of my other recommenders had to back out yesterday.
Hmm. I'd like to help. You did some of the best work in my translation seminar. But a rushed letter doesn't do anyone any favors.
I understand. If it's too much, I can ask someone else.

Let's try this. Send me your statement of purpose and your paper on the Portuguese poets tonight. If I can write something I'm proud of by Sunday, I'll submit it. If not, I'll tell you Saturday, so you have time for a backup.
That's more than fair. Thank you.

cv3-32.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a teaching assistant for an environmental science course.
Hi, Sana. I'm in your Friday lab section. I just realized the river sampling trip is the same day as my brother's graduation, two states away.
Ah. That trip's hard to reschedule, since we need the bus and the permits.
I figured. Is there anything I can do instead?
Yes. Students in the other sections collect the same measurements, water temperature, oxygen levels, and so on. You can use their data from the same sites.
And write the report from that?
Right. Same questions as everyone else. But you'd also add a short paragraph on what you couldn't observe directly, like the weather that day.
Sounds fair. How do I get the data?
I'll put it in a shared folder this afternoon and email you the link.

cv3-33.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and her thesis advisor.
Dr. Moreau, I've hit a wall with my thesis. I wanted to compare bike lane use in Ashford and Millbrook, but Millbrook never counted cyclists.
They counted cars at intersections, but never bikes. I've emailed three different offices.
Then a two-city comparison is out, I'm afraid. But think about Ashford on its own. Didn't some neighborhoods get protected lanes while others only got painted lines?
Yes, the east side got the protected ones a few years ago.
And Ashford counts cyclists everywhere. So you could compare neighborhoods within one city. Same weather, same traffic rules. Honestly, that's a cleaner design than comparing two cities.
Huh. I spent a month on Millbrook, though.
Use it in your introduction. It shows why cities need to collect this kind of data.

cv3-34.text: Listen to a conversation between two lab partners.
Mina, about our lab report on the spring experiment. I can't meet this weekend. My cousin's visiting.
Hmm. The report's due Tuesday, and we haven't even graphed the data.
What if we split it? You take the graphs, since you're better with the software, and I'll write the methods and the conclusion.
That could work. But the conclusion depends on the graphs. You can't write it until you see the slope.
Right. Okay, how about this. I'll do the methods on Saturday. You send me the graphs by Sunday night, and I'll finish the conclusion Monday morning.
Fine. Let's keep everything in a shared document so we can see each other's changes.
Good idea. I'll set it up tonight.

cv3-35.text: Listen to a conversation between two members of a photography club.
Aiden, the student activities council approved our budget for the spring exhibition, but only half of what we asked for.
Half? That barely covers printing. We were going to show forty photos.
I know. But I've been thinking. What if we showed fewer, but printed them really large? Like fifteen big prints instead of forty small ones.
Fifteen? Then we'd have to tell most of the members their work isn't in.
Not if each member picks their single best photo. We only have about fifteen active members anyway.
Huh. Everyone getting exactly one piece. Honestly, that might look better than a crowded wall. Professional galleries never cram things together.
That's what I was thinking. I'll bring it up at Thursday's meeting.

cv3-36.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an architecture professor.
Professor Farrow, I'm sorry I missed the model review yesterday. My train was stuck for two hours, and the model was with me the whole time.
That's frustrating. The review is a big part of the studio grade, though. Is the model finished?
Yes, it is. I have it right here, actually.
Okay. Here's what we'll do. Take photos of it from four angles, including a top view, and upload them by tonight. Then you'll present it at the start of next week's session.
In front of the whole studio?
Yes, just like everyone did yesterday. Five minutes, and then the class can ask questions.
That's fine. Should I bring the model too, or just the photos?
Bring both. The photos are for my records.

cv3-37.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a communications professor.
Professor Reyes, I got my midterm grades, and my participation score is a C. But I've been to every single class.
You have, and I've noticed. But participation here means contributing to discussion, and I don't think I've heard you speak more than once or twice.
I know. It's just that by the time I've figured out what I want to say, the discussion's already moved on.
That's more common than you'd think. Did you know the online forum counts toward participation too? Thoughtful posts after class count the same as comments in class.
Really? I thought the forum was optional.
Posting is optional, but it's one way to participate. You could also look at the questions I post the night before and come with one point prepared.
I could try that. Having something ready would definitely help.

cv3-38.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and his research supervisor.
Dr. Iyer, I'm flying home for winter break on the eighteenth, but the drought experiment in the greenhouse runs through the end of the month.
Right, the plants still need their measured watering every other day. Have you asked anyone to cover for you?
I asked Wen, but she's leaving too. I'm not sure who's staying.
Tobias is here over break. He's done watering for another project, so he knows the system.
Oh, great. Should I write out the schedule for him? Each group gets a different amount.
Yes, please. Make a table with the dates and amounts for each group, and tape a copy to the greenhouse door. Then walk him through it before you leave.
Okay. I'll message him today and set up a time.

cv3-39.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a mathematics professor.
Professor Kaur, I'm thinking of switching from your real analysis course to applied math. The proofs just aren't clicking for me.
I'm sorry to hear that. What makes you feel that way?
I spend hours on every problem set, and I'm never sure my proofs are right.
Hmm. Can I tell you something? Feeling unsure is normal in this course. Your last two problem sets were among the better ones in the class.
Really? I lost a few points on each.
So did everyone. The difference is that your mistakes were small. Some students are missing the main idea entirely.
Huh. I guess I've been comparing my proofs to the ones in the textbook.
The textbook's had ten years of editing. Give it until the midterm. If you still want to switch then, I'll sign the form.

cv3-40.text: Listen to a conversation between two roommates.
Nathan, I have to tell you something. I got the internship in the city, so I'll be gone from January to May.
That's amazing, congratulations! But wait, what about the apartment? Our lease runs until July.
I know. I'm not going to leave you paying my half. I was thinking I could find someone to sublet my room.
I checked. It does, as long as the landlord approves the person and they sign a short agreement.
Okay. Could we post on the graduate housing board? A lot of visiting researchers arrive in January.
Good idea. I'll write the post tonight, and you can look at it before I put it up.
Sure. Just make sure whoever it is doesn't mind my cat.

cv3-41.text: Listen to a conversation between two students working on a class project.
Jasper, I know this is late, but I'm having second thoughts about our business plan. The meal-kit idea for students.
We present in a week, Ama.
I know. But I was looking at our survey again. Most students said they'd pay about five dollars a meal. Our kits cost eight just to make.
Not really. Unless we sold to faculty and staff instead. They worry less about price, and they're busy.
That's actually not a whole new idea. Same product, different customers. We'd only have to redo the market section and the pricing.
Okay. But we can't run a new survey in a week, so we'll have to be upfront that the faculty market is an assumption.

cv3-42.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a journalism professor.
Professor Gallo, I'm writing my feature on the campus parking shortage, and someone on the parking staff gave me great quotes. But now he says he doesn't want his name used.
Did he ask for that before or after the interview?
After. He's worried his supervisor won't like it.
Well, our class follows a standard rule. Anonymous sources are allowed only if the information is important and you can't get it any other way.
He told me how many permits are sold compared to the number of spaces. That isn't public anywhere.
Then you might be able to use it. But you'll need to explain in the article why he isn't named, and I'll need to know who he is, privately.
Okay. I'll ask him if he's comfortable with that.

cv3-43.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and his research supervisor.
Dr. Halloran, the regional neuroscience conference is accepting student posters until the fifteenth. I'd love to submit our sleep and learning project.
I'm glad you're excited. But we've only run eight of our thirty participants. I'd hate for you to present something that changes completely.
I know it's early. But the conference has a category specifically for work in progress. They actually want preliminary results.
Really? I didn't realize that. Then the question is what you'd claim. With eight people, you can't say the effect is real.
I wouldn't. I'd focus on the method, the way we track sleep at home, and present the early numbers as a pilot.
That's a much more defensible poster. All right. Draft the abstract, and keep the language careful. Send it to me by the tenth.
Will do. I'll start on it tonight.

cv3-44.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an education professor.
Professor Dlamini, I'm worried about my observation hours. I need twenty by the end of the month, and I have twelve. But my elementary school just closed because of a broken water pipe.
Oh, I heard about that. When are they reopening?
The Monday after next. That only leaves me about a week.
Eight hours in a week is doable if you go every morning. But as a backup, the middle school on Fairview Road takes observers too.
Would hours at a different school still count?
They would, as long as it's the same grade level. Hmm, actually, middle school isn't. So stay with your elementary school, and I'll ask for a short extension just in case.
Thank you. That takes a lot of pressure off.

cv3-45.text: Listen to a conversation between two students.
Ivy, I made flashcards for chapters one through six for the economics final. Want to split them for our study session tonight?
One through six? Wait, didn't Professor Lund say the final only covers material after the midterm?
Did she? I thought it was cumulative.
She said it in class last week. Hang on, let me check the syllabus. Yeah, here it is. The final covers chapters seven through twelve.
Oh, great. So I spent three evenings on chapters we don't even need.
Not completely wasted. Chapter seven builds on five and six, so those cards could still help with the basics.
I guess. But that means we have nothing ready for eight through twelve.
Then let's skip the flashcards tonight and just work through the practice problems for those chapters together.

cv4-01.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a clerk at the registrar's office.
Hi, I ordered an official transcript about ten days ago for a summer research program, but they just emailed me saying it never arrived.
Let me check your order. Okay, it shows the transcript was printed and mailed on the fourth.
Mailed? I thought it would go electronically. Their deadline is Friday.
Well, on the order form, you chose paper delivery. That's probably why it's taking so long. Does the program accept electronic transcripts?
Yes, actually. That's what they prefer.
Then the simplest thing is to place a new order and choose the electronic option. It usually arrives within a few hours. There's a small fee, but I can waive it, since the first one never got there.
That'd be great. Can I do it here?
Sure. Use the computer by the window, and I'll approve it as soon as you submit.

cv4-02.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a clerk at the campus parking office.
Hi, I found a warning on my windshield this morning, but I have a student parking permit. It's hanging right on the mirror.
Let me see. Okay, the permit's valid, but the license plate on our record doesn't match the car that was parked in Lot C.
Oh. I sold my old car last month and got a new one. I didn't know I had to tell anyone.
Yeah, the permit's tied to your plate number, not just the tag. Our cameras scan plates, so the system thought your car didn't have a permit.
So do I need to buy a new permit?
No, you can just update the plate in your parking account online. It takes a couple of minutes. And since this was only a warning, there's no fine.
Great. I'll do it as soon as I get home.
Do it before tomorrow morning, though. The next one would be an actual ticket.

cv4-03.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an employee at the campus mailroom.
Hi, I got a text saying my package was delivered to locker twelve, but the code doesn't open it. I've tried three times.
Let me look up your name. Kenji Watanabe? Okay, I see what happened. The package turned out to be too big for the lockers, so we kept it back here.
But the text gave me a locker number.
Yeah, the system sends that automatically, before we actually sort things. It's confusing, I know. We've asked for it to be fixed.
So can I just take it now?
Sure, I just need to see your student ID. It's a pretty big box, though. Did you walk here?
Kind of. We have a cart you can borrow, as long as you bring it back by five.

cv4-04.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an advisor at the international student office.
Hi, Mr. Hendricks. I got an internship offer from an engineering firm downtown, and they want me to start June first. I just need you to sign something, right?
Congratulations! It's a bit more than a signature, though. Off-campus work needs authorization. The paperwork goes through our office, and then there's an outside review.
How long does that usually take?
Honestly, it varies. I've seen it come back in three weeks, and I've seen it take two months. And you can't start until it's approved. Not even unpaid training.
Two months? That would push me into August. Hmm. They did mention that some interns start in July.
Then that's a conversation worth having with them now, rather than in May. Employers tend to be flexible when they hear about it early.
Okay. I'll email the recruiter this afternoon. And I'll bring you the offer letter tomorrow.

cv4-05.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a coordinator at the disability services office.
Hi. Um, I'm not sure I'm in the right place. I broke my wrist skiing last weekend, and I've got two midterms coming up. I can't really write.
You're in the right place. A lot of students assume we only work with long-term conditions, but temporary injuries count too.
Oh. I was just going to email my professors and ask if I could type my answers.

You could, but each professor might handle it differently. If you register with us, even temporarily, we send one letter to all of them, and the arrangements are guaranteed. Extra time, a laptop, or someone to write for you.
That does sound easier. What do I need?
A note from the doctor who treated you, saying how long you'll be in the cast.
I've got a follow-up appointment on Thursday. I'll ask for one then.

cv4-06.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a staff member at the campus art museum.
Hi, I'm looking for a painting called Harbor at Dusk. My art history assignment is to describe it in person, but it's not in the gallery the map shows.
Ah, yes. That one was taken down last week. It's being cleaned in our conservation lab.
Oh no. My paper's due in ten days. When will it be back?
Not until next month, unfortunately. But here's something you might like. The lab has a big glass window, and on Saturday mornings it's open to visitors. You can watch the conservators working on it.
So I could still see the actual painting?
Exactly. And honestly, you'd notice details nobody sees when it's hanging on the wall. You might want to check with your professor that it counts, though.

cv4-07.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an assistant at the language lab.
Hi. I recorded my Spanish speaking assignment here yesterday, but my professor says the file she got was empty.
Hmm. Which booth were you in, and where did you save it?
Booth six, I think. I just saved it to the desktop and then uploaded it from there.
Ah, that might be it. If you upload while the recording program is still open, sometimes the file isn't finished saving yet. So it sends a blank copy.
And the original's still on the desktop?
Unfortunately, no. These computers erase everything overnight. You'll have to record it again.
Ugh. Okay. Is there a booth free now?
Booth two is open. Just close the program before you upload this time, and play the file back once to be sure.

cv4-08.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an attendant at the art studio supply room.
Hi, I need four more bags of the red clay. I'm building a big piece for my final project.
I can only give you one this week. Our delivery got delayed, so it's one bag per student until it comes.
One? That'll barely cover the base.
Have you looked at the reclaim bins? That's all the scraps people throw back, mixed with water and dried out again. It's free, and you can take as much as you want.
I thought that stuff was kind of lumpy. I don't want my piece cracking in the kiln.
It can be, if you don't wedge it well. But half the seniors use nothing else. If you mix it with your fresh bag, you'll barely notice.
Hmm. Okay, give me the one bag, and I'll fire a small test tile with the mix first.

cv4-09.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an attendant at the music practice room desk.
Hi, I'm trying to book one of the rooms with a grand piano, but the system keeps saying I'm not eligible.
No, I'm in biology. But I'm auditioning for the music minor in two weeks, and the audition's on a grand piano. The uprights feel totally different.
Yeah, the grand rooms are reserved for majors during the day. But after nine at night, anything that's empty is open to everyone. You'd just sign in here.
After nine? I have an early lab most mornings, so that's tough.
Then talk to the piano faculty. If someone there sends us a short email saying you're auditioning, we can give you a temporary pass until the audition.
Oh, that's perfect. My audition's being organized by Professor Hale. I'll ask her today.

cv4-10.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a staff member at the campus makerspace.
Hi, I'd like to use the laser cutter. I want to make a wooden sign for my sister's birthday on Friday.
Sure. Have you done the safety training? The next session's Saturday morning, and we can't make exceptions. Those machines can start fires if they're set up wrong.
Saturday's too late. Could you maybe run it for me? I already have the design file.
Sorry, staff can't do personal projects. What's the design, though? Just lettering?
Yeah, her name and a little star.
Then try the vinyl cutter. You'd cut the letters out as a sticker and press them onto painted wood. That one only needs a fifteen-minute video, and you can watch it right over there.
Oh, that could actually look nice. Okay, where's the video?

cv4-11.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and the editor of the student newspaper.
Hi, I'm Grace. I emailed you last week about an opinion piece on the library closing at ten. Did you get a chance to read it?
I did. It's well written. The thing is, we ran almost the same argument in March, and it got a lot of responses.

Not necessarily. Another opinion piece won't add much. But nobody's actually found out how many people are in the library at nine thirty. If you could get those numbers, maybe from the front desk's entry counts, that's a news story.
So you'd want facts instead of my argument.
Facts that make the argument for you, really. Readers trust numbers more than they trust columnists.
Okay. I'll ask the library for their counts this week.

cv4-12.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and the director of his residence hall.
Hi, Ms. Nakamura. I wanted to ask about the bike rule. Is there any way I could get permission to keep my bike in my room?
Ah. Would this be the blue road bike that's been leaning against the wall outside room two-oh-eight?
Uh, yeah. Sorry. It's just, the racks outside are uncovered, and it's been raining for a week. The chain's already rusting.
I understand. But hallways need to stay clear for fire safety, and rooms aren't really an option either. Have you seen the storage room in the basement?
It was, in September. But a lot of people took their bikes home over break and didn't bring them back. I can activate your key card for it today.
Oh, that'd be great. I'll move it down tonight.

cv4-13.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an officer at the campus police lost ID desk.
Hi, I lost my student ID sometime yesterday. I already reported it online, but I can't get into my dorm or the dining hall without it.
Let's check the box first. People turn in a lot of cards here. What's your last name?
Moreno. Here we go. Someone found it outside the science building this morning.
Oh, thank goodness! So I can just use it again?

Not quite. Since you reported it lost online, the system shut it off so nobody else could use it. You'll need to go to the ID card office to turn it back on. It's free, since you're not getting a new card.
Ground floor of the student center. They're open until four.

cv4-14.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a scheduler at the tutoring center.
Hi, I'd like to set up weekly appointments with Mia, the organic chemistry tutor. A friend said she's really good.
She is, and that's the problem. Her schedule's full through the end of the semester.
Oh. Is there anyone else for organic chem?
Two other tutors, but they're mostly booked too. Have you thought about a group session? Mia actually runs one on Tuesday evenings. Up to six students, same material.
A group, hmm. I was hoping for one-on-one. I've got a lot of questions.
Understandable. I can put you on her waitlist as well. Students cancel more often than you'd think, especially after midterms.
Okay, let's do both. Sign me up for Tuesday, and put me on the list.

cv4-15.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a clerk at the outdoor equipment rental center.
Hi, I want to rent a four-person tent for this weekend. A few friends and I are going camping at the lake.
Let me check. Hmm, all our four-person tents are reserved through Sunday. It's a popular weekend because of the holiday.
Oh no. We already booked the campsite.
Well, I do have two-person tents left. You could take two of those. They're lighter to carry, actually.

Two small ones cost the same as one big one, twenty-four dollars a night. The only difference is the deposit. It's twenty dollars for each tent, and you get it back when you return them clean and dry.
That's fine. I'll take two. Can I pick them up Friday morning?

cv4-16.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and the manager of the campus farm.
Hi, I'm with the cooking club. We're holding a fundraising dinner next month, and we'd love to use vegetables from the farm. Could we buy some from you?
I wish I could say yes. But everything we grow is already promised to dining services. That's how the farm pays for itself.
Even a few boxes? We'd pay whatever they pay.

It's in the contract, unfortunately. Now, here's a thought. Saturday mornings are harvest days. Volunteers who stay the full shift each take home a share of whatever's left after the dining hall order.
Depends on the week. In October, honestly, more squash than anyone knows what to do with.
Well, there are twelve of us in the club. If most of us come for a couple of Saturdays...
Then I'd say your menu's going to have a lot of squash in it.

cv4-17.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a clerk at the campus event ticket office.
Hi, I bought two tickets online for the comedy show, but I just noticed they're for Thursday. I meant to get Saturday. I have a lab Thursday night.
Okay, we can exchange them. There's a two-dollar fee per ticket for exchanges, though.
That's fine. Are there still seats on Saturday?
Let me look. The main floor's sold out, but there are a few in the balcony. They're actually a little cheaper, so the difference would cover the fee.
Oh, nice. Can we sit together up there?
Yes, I have two together in the front row of the balcony. Honestly, those are some of the best seats for this kind of show. You can see the whole stage.
Okay. I'll just need the card you paid with.

cv4-18.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a coordinator at the scholarship office.
Hi, Ms. Vasquez. My application for the Whitfield Scholarship is due Friday, but one of my recommendation letters still isn't uploaded.
Let's take a look. Yes, I see. Doctor Patel's letter is missing. Have you reminded her?
Twice. She's doing fieldwork in the mountains this month, and I don't think she has much internet. She said she'd send it, though.
Well, the good news is the committee accepts letters up to a week after the deadline. So submit everything else on time.
Still, if she can't get a signal for another week... Is there anyone else who knows your work well?
My lab supervisor, maybe. I hadn't really thought about him.
It might be worth asking him. We'd use whichever letter arrives first.

cv4-19.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a receptionist at the counseling center.
Hi, I saw a flyer for a workshop on managing study time during exams. Is this where I sign up?
It is. Let me check. Oh, I'm sorry. Thursday's session filled up yesterday.
Oh. Exams start in three weeks, so I was hoping to get in soon.

There's a second session two weeks from Thursday, which is still before exams. And in the meantime, there's a short online version on our website. It covers the basics, like breaking big tasks into smaller ones.
Is the second session the same as the first one?
Yes, same leader, same material. A lot of students do the online part first and then come with questions.
Okay, put me down for the second one, then.
Sure. Can I get your name and student email?

cv4-20.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an attendant at the campus laundry service.
Hi, I picked up my wash-and-fold order yesterday, but when I opened the bag at home, these weren't my clothes.
Oh no, I'm so sorry. Can I see the tag on the bag?
Here. It says Larson. My name's Arjun Mehta.
Okay, so the bags got switched. Do you have your claim slip?
Yeah, here it is. Number four-oh-two.
Let me check the back. Here we go, four-oh-two, still on the shelf. Someone must've grabbed the wrong bag earlier, and we gave you what was left.
So the other person hasn't come in?
Not yet. I'll keep this bag for them. And since this was our mistake, your next order is free. I'll write it on your slip.

cv4-21.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a worker at the student union information desk.
Hi, I'd like to put up some flyers for my chess club's tournament. Can I just pin them on the boards by the entrance?
Almost. Everything on those boards needs an approval stamp from this desk first. Otherwise, the cleaning staff take it down at night.
Oh, okay. Can you stamp them now? I have twenty.
Sure. But we only allow five per event, so that one group doesn't cover the whole board.
Five? Hmm. Then what do I do with the rest?
You could try the residence halls, though they have their own rules. Or, honestly, the digital screens might reach more people. You just submit an image online, and it runs for a week.
Oh, I didn't know about those. I'll do both, then. Five here, and the screens.

cv4-22.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an officer at the alumni office.
Hi. I'm hoping to talk to some graduates who work in marine conservation. Could you give me a list of names and emails?
I can't share personal contact details, I'm afraid. Alumni give us that information with the understanding that it stays with us.
Oh. I didn't think about that. I just wanted to ask a few people how they got started.

Which is exactly what a lot of them like to talk about. Here's what we can do. If you write a short message, a paragraph about who you are and what you'd like to know, I'll forward it to alumni in that field. Whoever's interested replies to you directly.
So they choose whether to contact me.
Right. And in my experience, people respond better that way than to a message from a stranger.
That makes sense. I'll draft something tonight and send it over.

cv4-23.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a bank teller.
Hi, I deposited a check here on Monday, but when I looked at my account this morning, the money still wasn't there. My rent's due Friday.
Let me take a look. Okay, I see the deposit. It's on hold until Thursday.
Your account was opened less than a month ago. For new accounts, larger checks are held for three business days while we confirm them with the other bank.
So it'll definitely be there by Thursday?
It should be available Thursday morning. And if that's cutting it too close, I can release two hundred dollars of it right now.
That would actually help. My landlord takes online payments, so Thursday should be fine for the rest.
Okay. I'll release the two hundred now.

cv4-24.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an apartment leasing agent.
Hi, I'm interested in a one-bedroom for next fall. But I'd only need it from September to May. Do you offer nine-month leases?
Our standard is twelve months, unfortunately. A lot of students sublet over the summer, though. We allow it, as long as we approve the person.
I'd rather not deal with finding someone. I'm going home for the summer, and I'd be managing it from far away.
Fair enough. Hmm, actually, wait. I've got a tenant who's relocating for work in August. She wants someone to take over the rest of her lease. It runs through the end of next May.
Oh. So basically exactly what I need?
Pretty much. It's a one-bedroom on the third floor, same rent as the others. You'd just need to apply like any new tenant.
Could I see it this week?
Let me call her. Thursday afternoon might work.

cv4-25.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a pharmacist.
Hi, I've been taking these allergy tablets for about a week. They help with the sneezing, but I'm practically falling asleep in my morning classes.
Let me see the box. Ah, yes. This one causes drowsiness in a lot of people. When do you usually take it?
One option is to take it at bedtime instead. It lasts twenty-four hours, so you'd still be covered the next day, and you'd sleep through the drowsy part.
Would that be enough, though? My sneezing's worst in the morning.
It should be. But if not, there's another kind that's labeled non-drowsy. It's on the shelf behind you, same price. Just don't take both on the same day.
I'll try taking this one at night first, since I still have most of the box.

cv4-26.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a ticket agent at a train station.
Hi, I was supposed to be on the three fifteen to Riverton, but my bus got stuck in traffic and I missed it by about five minutes. Can I use my ticket on the next one?
Let me see it. Hmm, this is an advance ticket, so it's only good for that specific train.
So I have to buy a whole new ticket?
Not necessarily. You can change it to a later train for a fee. It's fifteen dollars, plus any difference in price.
Is there a difference for the next train?
The four forty is a busier one, so it's a bit more. The six ten costs the same as your original ticket, so you'd only pay the fee.
I'd really rather not wait until six. My sister's picking me up at the station.
Then the four forty it is. That'll be twenty-two dollars total.

cv4-27.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a clerk at a phone store.
Hi, I dropped my phone yesterday, and the screen cracked. How much would it cost to fix?
For this model, a new screen is about a hundred and twenty dollars. Can I check your account first, though?
Okay, you've got the protection plan on this phone. That covers one screen repair a year, at no cost.
Really? I forgot I even had that. Can you fix it today?
Not quite yet. You have to file a claim online first. Once it's approved, usually within a day, bring it back, and we'll replace the screen in about an hour.
Okay. I'll file it tonight, then.
Great. And take a photo of the crack for the claim. They usually ask for one.

cv4-28.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a librarian at a public library in town.
Hi, I'd like to get a library card. I'm a student at the university, and I just moved here this fall.
Welcome! I just need a photo ID and something that shows your local address, like a bill or a lease.
Hmm. I live in a dorm, so I don't really get bills. Will my student ID work?
The ID's fine for the photo, but it doesn't show where you live. Do you have anything from the university housing office? A room assignment letter, maybe?
There was an email over the summer with my room number and the building's address. I could find it on my phone.
That works. Pull it up, and I'll get your card started. It'll be ready in about five minutes.
Great, thanks. That's easier than I expected.

cv4-29.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and her landlord.
Hi, Mr. Whitaker. I wanted to ask you something about the apartment. Would it be okay if I painted my bedroom? The white walls feel a little cold.
Hmm. You know, the last person who asked me that painted the living room a very dark purple. It took three coats to cover when she moved out.
Oh, I wasn't thinking of anything like that. More of a pale green. Really light.
Well... a pale color I could live with. Tell you what. Buy a sample, put a small patch on the wall, and text me a photo. If I like it, go ahead.
That's fair. And I'll pay for the paint, of course.
You'd better. And if it doesn't look good in the end, you'll repaint it white before you leave.
Deal. I'll pick up a sample this weekend.

cv4-30.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and his internship supervisor.
Hi, Ms. Reyes. Do you have a minute? I just got my final exam schedule, and two of my exams are on the Tuesday and Wednesday of the week of the fifteenth.
That's the week of the Harmon presentation, isn't it?
Yes. That's why I wanted to bring it up early. I know I was supposed to help get the slides ready.

I appreciate the warning. Honestly, the slides are mostly data charts, and you're faster at those than anyone here. What if you built them the week before, and someone else handled the last-minute changes?
I could do that. I'd have to stay a little later that Thursday and Friday.
We'll count those as your hours for the following week. Then just take Tuesday and Wednesday off.
That works. Thanks for being so flexible.

cv4-31.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an employee at the registrar's office.
Hi. I need to drop a course, but the online system won't let me. It says the deadline has passed.
Yes, the drop deadline was last Friday. What's the course?
Intro to Astronomy. I just found out it doesn't count toward my major, so it's basically a waste of my time.
I see. After the deadline, you'd have to petition the dean, and to be honest, petitions are usually approved for medical or family reasons. A course not counting toward your major rarely qualifies.
Not entirely. You can still switch it to pass-fail until the end of this week. Then the grade won't affect your average.
Oh. Well, I'm actually doing fine in it, so passing should be easy. I'll do that.

cv4-32.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an employee at the international student office.
Hi, I'm trying to open a bank account, and the bank wants a letter proving I'm a full-time student here. Can you write one for me?
We can, but our letters take about three business days. How soon do you need it?
Well, my scholarship payment can't go through until I have an account, so as soon as possible.
In that case, you might not need us at all. The registrar's website has an enrollment letter you can print yourself. It's official, with the university seal and everything.
Really? Will the bank accept it?
Most banks around here do. If yours doesn't, come back, and we'll put a rush on ours.
Okay. I'll print it at the library and go straight to the bank.

cv4-33.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a clerk who handles parking appeals.
Hi, I got a ticket on Tuesday for parking in the visitor lot. But my usual lot was closed for construction, so I didn't have much choice.
Let me see. Hmm. The closure email that went out last week told permit holders to use Lot F during the work.
I know. I went to Lot F first. It was completely full. I drove around it twice.
Did you happen to have any way to show that?
Actually, yes. I was annoyed, so I took a picture and sent it to my roommate. It has the time on it.
Well, then, that changes things. Attach that photo to an appeal. That's exactly the kind of thing the review board looks for.
So I don't have to pay right now?
Not while the appeal's open. You've got ten days to file it.

cv4-34.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and the supervisor of the campus mailroom.
Hi, I'm leaving for a summer research program in Chile next week. Can you forward my mail there while I'm gone?
I'm afraid we can only forward within the country. International forwarding gets expensive, and things get lost.
Hmm. The thing is, I'm expecting a replacement bank card. Mine expires in July.
Well, even if we could forward it, banks usually mark those envelopes do not forward. It'd just get sent back to them.
Your best bet is to ask the bank to send it early, before you leave, or mail it straight to you down there. Then for everything else, you can have it forwarded to a friend or relative here.
My cousin lives in town. I'll set it up with her, and I'll call the bank this afternoon.

cv4-35.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a staff member at the campus makerspace.
Excuse me, this sewing machine keeps jamming. The thread bunches up underneath every few stitches.
Let me take a look. What are you making?
A tote bag out of old jeans. It's for my costume design class.
Ah, there's your problem. Denim's really thick, and this machine has a regular needle in it. That's made for thin cotton, like T-shirts and sheets.
So I need a different machine?
Just a different needle. We keep heavy-duty ones in the drawer under the counter. I'll switch it for you, and I'll show you how, so you can do it yourself next time.
Thanks. Should I change the thread too?
Thicker thread would be better for a bag, yes. Take a spool of the gray one from the wall. It's free for members.

cv4-36.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and the photo editor of the student newspaper.
Hi, Ms. Castellanos? I just saw the photo assignments for this weekend. I'm on the basketball game Saturday night, but my brother's getting married that day.
Oh, congratulations to him! Well, you can't miss that. Let me look at who's free.
I'm really sorry for the short notice. The schedule only went up this morning.
Don't worry. Okay, Lina's covering the debate tournament on Sunday, but she told me she'd rather shoot sports. Could you take the debate instead?
Sunday's fine. I'll be back by noon.
It starts at two, in the student center. It's mostly people at podiums, so bring your long lens. The lighting in there is pretty dim.
Got it. Thanks for working it out.

cv4-37.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a teller at his bank.
Hi, my debit card got declined three times this weekend. I was visiting a friend in another state, and it just stopped working. I'm worried someone stole my number.
Let's see. Hmm. Actually, it looks like our system blocked it on purpose. Three purchases far from where you normally shop, all in one day. It looked unusual.
Not that I can see. These charges were all yours, right? A gas station, a restaurant, a bookstore?
Then I'll unblock it now. Are you traveling again any time soon?
Actually, I'm going to a conference overseas next month.
Then before you go, open the app and add your travel dates. It takes a minute, and it'll save you from another weekend like this one.

cv4-38.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a clerk at a phone store.
Hi, I'm studying abroad in Spain for four months starting in January. I want to add an international plan so my phone works there.
We can do that. But honestly, for four months, it'd cost you around three hundred dollars. Most people in your situation just get a local SIM card when they arrive.
But wouldn't I lose my number? My bank sends codes to it when I log in.
Not if you put your line on hold. For five dollars a month, we keep your number reserved. And you can still get texts over Wi-Fi with the right settings.
Five a month, versus three hundred. Hmm. Can my phone even take a different SIM?
Let me check. Yes, it's paid off, so I can unlock it for you right now.
Okay, then let's do that instead.

cv4-39.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and an apartment leasing agent.
Hi, I'm here for the two o'clock tour. I'm interested in the studio apartment you posted online, the one with the big windows.
Oh, I'm so sorry. That one was rented this morning. I meant to update the listing and call you, but things got busy.
Oh. That's disappointing. I took two buses to get here.
I understand. Let me make it worth the trip. We have another studio opening up next month. It's a bit bigger, with a small balcony, but it's fifty dollars more per month.
Hmm. Which floor is it on?
The fourth, so it's quieter than the other one would've been. It's empty right now, so we can go up and see it.

cv4-40.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and the education coordinator at the campus museum.
Hi, Ms. Whitlock. I got the email saying I was accepted as a student tour guide, which is great. But the training's on Wednesday afternoons, and I have a lab then all semester.
Ah. That's a problem, because the training isn't optional. Guides have to learn the whole collection before they lead groups.
Is it offered at any other time?
Only once a year, sadly. But let me think. Our gallery attendants don't need the training. They sit in the rooms, answer questions, keep an eye on things.
For this year. And honestly, attendants who spend a year in the galleries tend to make the best guides later. They already know what visitors ask about.
That's true. I guess I'd be learning the collection anyway.
Exactly. Then next fall, you'd do the training.

cv4-41.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and the manager of the music practice rooms.
Hi. I just finished practicing in room fourteen, and one of the keys on the piano stopped working. The low E. It just sort of stays down. I promise I wasn't banging on it or anything.
Don't worry, you're not in trouble. That key's been sticking for weeks. You're the third person to mention it.
Oh, good. I mean, not good, but... you know what I mean.
I do. The technician only comes once a month, and she's not due until the twentieth. I'll call and see whether she can come sooner.
The thing is, I booked fourteen every afternoon this week. My recital piece uses that E a lot.
Then let me move you to room nine. The piano there was just tuned. Same time slots?

cv4-42.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a clerk at the campus outdoor equipment rental.
Hi, I'm returning the kayak I rented Saturday. Um, before you check it, I should tell you there's a dent near the front. We hit a rock pretty hard.
Thanks for being upfront. Let me pull up your checkout form. Front, left side, about the size of a coin?
Then you're fine. It's already on here. Whoever rented it before you must have done it. We marked it during inspection.
Seriously? I spent the whole drive back calculating how much I'd owe you.
That's why we write everything down. But for future reference, you're supposed to walk around the boat with us before you leave. You'd have seen the dent and saved yourself a stressful drive.
Fair enough. I think I just signed and ran out to the car.
Most people do. Here's your deposit back.

cv4-43.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a staff member at the disability services office.
Hi, I'm registered for note-taking support, and I'm supposed to get notes for my biology lecture. But nothing's been uploaded for almost two weeks.
Let me check who's assigned to that class. Hmm. It looks like your note-taker dropped the course. I'm sorry, we should have caught that.
Oh. I have a quiz next Monday, so I'm kind of behind.
Understood. I'll email your professor today to ask for a new volunteer from the class. Usually someone signs up within a few days.
And what about the two weeks I've missed?
Your accommodation letter also allows you to record lectures, so I'd start doing that for now. And I'll ask the professor whether she can share her slides from the past two weeks.
Okay. I'll bring my recorder tomorrow.

cv4-44.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and the coordinator of the language lab.
Hi, I signed up for the conversation partner program last month, hoping to practice Japanese. I haven't heard anything back.
Let me see. Yes, you're on the list. The problem is, we only have four Japanese exchange students this year, and they're all paired already.
Oh. So that's it until next year?
Not necessarily. There's a Japanese conversation table every Thursday at lunch. Several exchange students come, and so do a few teachers.
I've heard about that. I'm just... I'm only in second-year Japanese. Everyone there probably talks really fast.
Some do. But plenty of people at your level go, and the first few times, most of them mainly listen. Nobody minds.
Well, I guess listening's better than nothing. Maybe I'll go this Thursday and see what it's like.

cv4-45.text: Listen to a conversation between a student and a librarian at the public library.
Hi, I got an email saying our Tuesday room reservation was cancelled for the rest of the month. I run a study group, and we meet in Room B.
Let me check. Ah, yes. The system cancels standing reservations after two no-shows. It looks like nobody checked in on the third or the tenth.
Oh. We met online those two weeks because of the snow. I guess I never cancelled the room.
That happens. Unfortunately, once it's released, other groups can book it, and someone's already taken Room B for the next two Tuesdays.
Room D is free. It's smaller and doesn't have a screen, but it fits six.
There are five of us, and we mostly use the whiteboard anyway. We'll take it. And I'll cancel properly next time.

iv-01-1.text: Thanks for joining us today. To start, could you tell me where you usually study and what a typical study session looks like for you?

iv-01-2.text: Think about a time when you had to prepare for a really important exam. How did you get ready, and how did it turn out?

iv-01-3.text: Some students like to study in groups, while others prefer to work alone. Which do you prefer, and why do you think it works better for you?

iv-01-4.text: Many universities now offer courses on how to study effectively. Do you think schools should require all first-year students to take a course like that? Why or why not?

iv-02-1.text: Let's begin with your daily routine. How do you normally get to campus or work, and roughly how long does the trip take you?

iv-02-2.text: Can you describe a time when your usual way of getting around wasn't available, maybe because of weather or a breakdown? How did you handle it?

iv-02-3.text: Some people argue that cities should make public transportation completely free. Would you support that idea? Please explain your reasons and any concerns you might have.

iv-02-4.text: As more people work from home part of the week, commuting patterns are changing. How do you think this shift might affect the way cities plan roads, buses, and train lines in the future?

iv-03-1.text: First, I'd like to know which devices you use most often during a normal day, and what you mainly use each one for.

iv-03-2.text: Tell me about a piece of technology, like an app or a tool, that made some part of your life easier. What changed after you started using it?

iv-03-3.text: Some teachers ask students to put away their phones and laptops during class. Do you think that's a good policy? Why or why not?

iv-03-4.text: Many young children now grow up using tablets and smartphones. In your opinion, what are the biggest benefits and risks of children using technology so early?

iv-04-1.text: To get us started, could you walk me through what you ate yesterday, and whether that was a fairly typical day for you?

iv-04-2.text: Have you ever tried to change your eating habits in a significant way, for example by cooking more or cutting back on something? What motivated you, and did it last?

iv-04-3.text: Some schools have removed sugary drinks and snacks from their cafeterias. Do you think that's an effective way to encourage healthier eating, or is it better to let students choose for themselves?

iv-04-4.text: Food choices are shaped by price, convenience, culture, and advertising. Which of these factors do you think has the greatest influence on what people eat today, and what, if anything, should be done about it?

iv-05-1.text: Let's start simple. What kinds of physical activity do you do in a normal week, and how often do you do them?

iv-05-2.text: Can you tell me about a sport or activity you really enjoyed at some point in your life? What did you like about it?

iv-05-3.text: Some people prefer exercising at a gym, while others would rather exercise outdoors. Which do you prefer, and what are your reasons?

iv-05-4.text: Many adults say they're too busy to exercise regularly. What do you think employers or schools could do to help people stay more active?

iv-06-1.text: Thanks for taking the time to talk with me. Apart from assigned course material, what do you usually read, and how much time do you spend reading each week?

iv-06-2.text: Is there a book or article that changed the way you think about something? Tell me what it was and how it affected you.

iv-06-3.text: Some readers insist that printed books offer a deeper reading experience than screens do. Do you agree with them? Please support your view with reasons or examples from your own experience.

iv-06-4.text: Studies suggest that people are reading fewer long texts and more short posts and headlines. What long-term effects do you think this trend could have on education and public discussion?

iv-07-1.text: First, what kind of music do you usually listen to, and at what times of the day do you listen to it most?

iv-07-2.text: Tell me about a memorable experience you've had with music, such as a concert, a performance, or learning to play an instrument.

iv-07-3.text: Some students say they study better when listening to music, but others find it distracting. What's your opinion, and why?

iv-07-4.text: Some schools have cut music classes to save money. Do you think music education should be a required part of school? Please explain your reasons.

iv-08-1.text: To begin, have you ever done any kind of volunteer work? If so, what did you do, and how did you first get involved?

iv-08-2.text: Describe a time when helping others turned out to be more challenging or more rewarding than you expected. What did you learn from that experience?

iv-08-3.text: Some high schools require students to complete a certain number of volunteer hours before they can graduate. Do you think required service still counts as real volunteering? Why or why not?

iv-08-4.text: Many communities depend heavily on volunteers to run libraries, shelters, and local events. Is it fair for society to rely on unpaid work this way, or should governments take on more of that responsibility?

iv-09-1.text: Let's start with your schedule. What time do you usually go to bed and wake up during the week, and is it different on weekends?

iv-09-2.text: Can you describe a time when you didn't get enough sleep for several days? How did it affect your studies or your mood?

iv-09-3.text: Some people take short naps during the day to stay alert. Do you think napping is a good habit for students? Why or why not?

iv-09-4.text: Some researchers suggest that high schools should start classes later in the morning so teenagers can sleep more. Do you think this is a good idea? Explain your answer.

iv-10-1.text: First, which social media platforms do you use, and roughly how much time would you say you spend on them on a typical day?

iv-10-2.text: Think of a time when something you saw on social media influenced a decision you made, like a purchase, a trip, or an opinion. What happened?

iv-10-3.text: Some people take long breaks from social media to improve their well-being. Do you think stepping away completely is more effective than simply cutting back? Explain your reasoning.

iv-10-4.text: Social media has made it much easier for false information to spread quickly. Who do you think should be mainly responsible for limiting this problem: the platforms, governments, or individual users? Why?

iv-11-1.text: To begin, have you ever taken a class online? If so, what was the subject, and how was the class organized?

iv-11-2.text: Tell me about a challenge you faced while learning online, and explain what you did to deal with it.

iv-11-3.text: Do you think students learn better in a regular classroom or in an online course? Please give specific reasons for your answer.

iv-11-4.text: Many universities now offer entire degree programs online. In your opinion, how might this change higher education over the next ten or twenty years?

iv-12-1.text: Let's start with where you live. Could you describe your neighborhood and tell me what you like or dislike about living there?

iv-12-2.text: Have you ever moved from one place to another, for example from a small town to a city? What was the hardest part of adjusting, and what surprised you?

iv-12-3.text: Some people believe that large cities offer a better quality of life than small towns because of the opportunities they provide. Do you agree? Explain your position with specific reasons.

iv-12-4.text: As cities grow, housing often becomes too expensive for many residents. What approaches do you think city governments could take to keep neighborhoods affordable without discouraging new development?

iv-13-1.text: First, could you tell me about the last trip you took? Where did you go, and who did you travel with?

iv-13-2.text: Describe something unexpected that happened to you while traveling. How did you handle the situation?

iv-13-3.text: Some travelers like to plan every detail before a trip, while others prefer to be spontaneous. Which style do you prefer, and why?

iv-13-4.text: Tourism brings money to many places, but it can also cause crowding and pollution. Do you think popular destinations should limit the number of visitors? Why or why not?

iv-14-1.text: Thank you for applying. To start, could you tell me about your current field of study and which country or university you're hoping to attend?

iv-14-2.text: Living abroad often means adapting to unfamiliar situations. Describe a time when you had to adjust to a new environment, and explain what helped you succeed.

iv-14-3.text: Some people argue that a semester abroad is valuable mainly for personal growth rather than academic learning. Do you agree with that view? Please explain your reasoning.

iv-14-4.text: International student exchange programs are often expensive to run. Why do you think universities and governments should, or should not, continue to invest in them?

iv-15-1.text: Thanks for your application. Can you tell me a little about yourself and explain what made you interested in this summer research program?

iv-15-2.text: Describe a class project or assignment that you were especially proud of. What was your role, and what did you learn from it?

iv-15-3.text: In research, experiments often fail before they succeed. How do you usually react when something doesn't go as planned? Please give an example.

iv-15-4.text: Do you think every undergraduate student should have the chance to take part in research, even if they don't plan to become scientists? Why or why not?

iv-16-1.text: Let's begin with your background. What groups or activities are you currently involved in on or off campus, and what responsibilities do you have in them?

iv-16-2.text: Tell me about a situation in which you had to resolve a disagreement within a team. What steps did you take, and what was the outcome?

iv-16-3.text: Some people believe that good leaders are born with natural talent, while others think leadership can be taught. Which view do you find more convincing, and why?

iv-16-4.text: Many organizations say they want leaders who represent a wide range of backgrounds and perspectives. Why might diverse leadership matter, and what challenges could it create for a group?

iv-17-1.text: To begin, could you tell me why you applied for this sustainability fellowship and what you hope to gain from it?

iv-17-2.text: Describe something you've done, at home or at school, to reduce waste or save energy. How did you get started?

iv-17-3.text: If you could change one thing on our campus to make it more environmentally friendly, what would it be? Explain why you chose that idea.

iv-17-4.text: Some people think individual actions, like recycling, make little difference compared to large government policies. Do you agree or disagree? Explain your view.

iv-18-1.text: Thanks for coming in today. Could you tell me about your class schedule this term and how many hours a week you'd realistically be able to work?

iv-18-2.text: Library assistants often help visitors who are confused or frustrated. Tell me about a time you helped someone solve a problem, and explain how you approached it.

iv-18-3.text: Suppose a group of students keeps talking loudly in a quiet study area even after a polite reminder. How would you handle it, and why would you choose that approach?

iv-18-4.text: With so much information available online, some people question whether university libraries are still necessary. What role do you think libraries should play on campuses in the future?

iv-19-1.text: Let's start with the basics. What's your major, and what's your favorite place on campus to spend time?

iv-19-2.text: Tell me about a time when you spoke in front of a group of people. How did you prepare, and how did it go?

iv-19-3.text: If a visiting family asked you about a weakness of our university, how would you answer them honestly? Explain your approach.

iv-19-4.text: Do you think campus visits are still important when students can take virtual tours online? Why or why not?

iv-20-1.text: To begin, could you tell me what kinds of writing you do most often, both for your classes and outside of school?

iv-20-2.text: Think about a piece of feedback on your own writing that was especially helpful. What made it useful, and how did you apply it?

iv-20-3.text: Imagine a student asks you to simply fix all the grammar mistakes in their essay. Would you do it? Explain how you would handle the session and why.

iv-20-4.text: Some instructors worry that automated writing tools may prevent students from developing their own writing skills. How do you think universities should respond to these tools in their writing programs?

iv-21-1.text: Thanks for applying. Could you tell me why you're interested in working in the dining hall and whether you've had a job before?

iv-21-2.text: Describe a time when you had to work quickly under pressure. What did you do to stay organized?

iv-21-3.text: Which do you think is more important when working with customers: speed or friendliness? Please explain your answer.

iv-21-4.text: Many students work part-time while studying. Do you think having a job helps or hurts a student's academic performance? Explain your opinion.

iv-22-1.text: Let's start with your experience. What kinds of technical problems have you solved before, either for yourself or for friends and family?

iv-22-2.text: Tell me about a time you had to explain something complicated to someone without much technical knowledge. How did you make sure they understood?

iv-22-3.text: When a frustrated user is in a hurry, would you rather fix the problem for them quickly or teach them how to fix it themselves? Explain the reasoning behind your choice.

iv-22-4.text: Universities collect a great deal of personal data about their students. How should institutions balance the convenience of digital services with the need to protect student privacy?

iv-23-1.text: Hi, thanks for your interest in the debate club. Can you tell me a bit about yourself and why you'd like to join?

iv-23-2.text: Tell me about a time you changed someone's mind about something, or someone changed yours. What happened?

iv-23-3.text: In a debate, you're sometimes asked to argue for a side you personally disagree with. Do you think that's a useful skill? Why or why not?

iv-23-4.text: Some people feel that public discussions today have become less respectful. What do you think people could do to have more productive conversations about difficult topics?

iv-24-1.text: To start, how long have you been taking photos, and what subjects or styles do you find yourself drawn to most?

iv-24-2.text: Describe a photograph you've taken that you're particularly proud of. What was happening when you took it, and why does it matter to you?

iv-24-3.text: Our club debates whether editing photos heavily makes them less authentic. Where do you stand on that question? Please explain your reasoning with an example if you can.

iv-24-4.text: Since nearly everyone now carries a camera in their phone, millions of images are shared every day. Has this made photography more meaningful as an art form, or less? Why?

iv-25-1.text: Thanks for applying. Could you tell me what kinds of outdoor activities you've done before and how often you get outside?

iv-25-2.text: Describe the most memorable time you've spent in nature. What made that experience stand out for you?

iv-25-3.text: On group trips, safety rules sometimes limit what people can do. Do you think strict rules make outdoor trips better or worse? Explain why.

iv-25-4.text: Some popular parks have become very crowded in recent years. What do you think should be done to protect natural areas while still allowing people to enjoy them?

iv-26-1.text: Let's start with your interests. Which sections of a newspaper do you usually read first, and what kinds of stories would you most like to write for us?

iv-26-2.text: Tell me about a time you had to meet a tight deadline on a writing project. How did you manage your time, and what would you do differently now?

iv-26-3.text: Student journalists sometimes have to report critically on their own university. Do you think a campus newspaper should be fully independent from the school's administration? Why or why not?

iv-26-4.text: Many local newspapers have closed in recent years as readers move online. What do you think communities lose when local journalism disappears, and how might that gap be filled?

lr-01-2.text: You can grab a map right here.

lr-01-3.text: The penguins are fed every morning at ten o'clock.

lr-01-4.text: The reptile house is kept warm for the snakes and lizards.

lr-01-5.text: This is where keepers prepare the food, so please stay behind the yellow line.

lr-01-6.text: Volunteers get a small discount at the gift shop, so remember to show your badge.

lr-01-7.text: If a visitor feels sick or gets hurt, bring them to the first aid booth right away.

lr-02-2.text: The locker rooms are down this hallway.

lr-02-3.text: Treadmills and bikes can be used for thirty minutes.

lr-02-4.text: Always wipe down the benches after you finish your workout.

lr-02-5.text: Yoga and spin classes are held in this studio throughout the week.

lr-02-6.text: You need to complete a short safety session before you can use the climbing wall.

lr-02-7.text: Towels, jump ropes, and resistance bands can be borrowed here, but they must be returned before closing time.

lr-03-2.text: These machines let you borrow books yourself.

lr-03-3.text: Recently published titles are displayed on this shelf.

lr-03-4.text: Please keep your voice down on the quiet study floor.

lr-03-5.text: Course reserve materials can only be borrowed for two hours at a time.

lr-03-6.text: You can send documents to these printers from any computer connected to the library network.

lr-03-7.text: When the library is closed, you can drop your books into this slot beside the main door.

lr-04-2.text: Your student ID photo is taken here.

lr-04-3.text: This quad is the center of campus life.

lr-04-4.text: Most of your first-year classes will meet in this building.

lr-04-5.text: Make an appointment with your academic advisor before you register for classes.

lr-04-6.text: Career services can help you write a resume and find a part-time job on campus.

lr-04-7.text: The campus shuttle stops here every fifteen minutes and will take you to the dorms and the downtown area.

lr-05-2.text: Coats and bags can be left here.

lr-05-3.text: This dinosaur skeleton is our most popular exhibit.

lr-05-4.text: In the space exhibit, you can step inside a model rocket.

lr-05-5.text: Children can try simple experiments in this lab with help from our staff.

lr-05-6.text: Short films about the ocean and outer space are shown in the theater every hour.

lr-05-7.text: If you get hungry, the cafeteria on the lower level serves sandwiches, soup, and snacks until four o'clock.

lr-06-1.text: Let's start at the visitor center.

lr-06-2.text: The roses bloom from late spring to fall.

lr-06-3.text: You may touch and smell the herbs here.

lr-06-4.text: The tropical greenhouse is warm and humid all year round.

lr-06-5.text: Turtles and frogs live in this pond, so please don't feed them.

lr-06-6.text: At the seed library, members can borrow seeds and return new ones after harvest.

lr-06-7.text: Before you leave, be sure to visit the garden shop, which sells plants grown right here in our greenhouses.

lr-07-2.text: The salad bar is refilled throughout the day.

lr-07-3.text: Burgers and grilled sandwiches are made to order here.

lr-07-4.text: This station serves meals that are free of nuts, gluten, and dairy.

lr-07-5.text: Machines for water, juice, and iced tea are located along this back wall.

lr-07-6.text: When you finish eating, please place your tray and dishes on this moving belt.

lr-07-7.text: If you want to add more meals to your plan, visit the office next to the exit.

lr-08-1.text: Welcome to the campus art gallery.

lr-08-2.text: Please don't touch any of the paintings.

lr-08-3.text: These portraits were painted over two hundred years ago.

lr-08-4.text: The sculptures in this courtyard were made by local artists.

lr-08-5.text: Photography is allowed in this wing as long as you turn off your flash.

lr-08-6.text: Students can watch printmakers at work in this studio on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons.

lr-08-7.text: The special exhibition changes every season, and this one features landscapes from artists around the world.

lr-09-2.text: Ask at this desk if you get lost.

lr-09-3.text: The lounge is a great place to relax between classes.

lr-09-4.text: The food court has six restaurants and stays open until midnight.

lr-09-5.text: Most student clubs have offices on this floor, and their doors are usually open.

lr-09-6.text: You can rent pool tables and board games in the game room with your student ID.

lr-09-7.text: Large events like concerts and dances are held in the ballroom, which can hold about five hundred people.

lr-10-1.text: Never enter the lab without permission.

lr-10-2.text: Put on your safety goggles before every experiment.

lr-10-3.text: Any chemicals with strong smells must be used under the hood.

lr-10-4.text: If chemicals splash in your eyes, rinse them here for fifteen minutes.

lr-10-5.text: Pull this handle if your clothes catch fire or get covered in chemicals.

lr-10-6.text: The fire extinguisher is beside the door, and every student must learn how to use it.

lr-10-7.text: Never pour chemicals down the sink; instead, place them in the labeled waste containers along the back wall.

lr-11-2.text: Please use the elevators for heavy boxes.

lr-11-3.text: Each room comes with two beds and two desks.

lr-11-4.text: The washers and dryers in the basement accept your student card.

lr-11-5.text: There's a shared kitchen on every floor, but please clean up after yourself.

lr-11-6.text: The study lounge is open all night, so it's a good spot to prepare for exams.

lr-11-7.text: Please flatten your empty boxes and leave them in the recycling area behind the building by tonight.

lr-12-1.text: Each station holds about twenty bikes.

lr-12-2.text: Unlock a bike by entering your membership code.

lr-12-3.text: Before riding off, check that both brakes respond smoothly.

lr-12-4.text: You can raise or lower the seat by flipping this lever underneath.

lr-12-5.text: Riders are expected to stay in the marked bike lanes whenever they're available downtown.

lr-12-6.text: Should you notice a flat tire or loose chain, report it before taking the bike.

lr-12-7.text: Make sure the bike clicks firmly into the dock, or you may continue to be charged for the ride.

lr-13-1.text: Our aquarium houses hundreds of species.

lr-13-2.text: This coral reef tank mimics tropical ocean conditions.

lr-13-3.text: Use two fingers when gently touching the sea stars.

lr-13-4.text: The jellyfish drift in circular tanks designed to keep them from getting injured.

lr-13-5.text: Walking through this tunnel, you'll see sharks gliding just inches above your head.

lr-13-6.text: Through this window, visitors can observe biologists analyzing water samples collected from the bay.

lr-13-7.text: Injured sea turtles are brought to this center, where they're cared for until they're healthy enough to be released.

lr-14-1.text: Please check in at reception first.

lr-14-2.text: Bring your insurance card to every appointment.

lr-14-3.text: Prescriptions can usually be picked up within an hour.

lr-14-4.text: A nurse will take your temperature and blood pressure before the doctor arrives.

lr-14-5.text: Flu shots are offered free of charge to all enrolled students throughout the fall.

lr-14-6.text: Counselors are available for confidential appointments if you're feeling stressed or overwhelmed by coursework.

lr-14-7.text: If you need advice when the center is closed, call the after-hours line printed on your student ID.

lr-15-1.text: This is the main control room.

lr-15-2.text: Engineers adjust every track on this mixing console.

lr-15-3.text: Singers record in the booth to minimize background noise.

lr-15-4.text: Each microphone must be signed out and handled with extreme care.

lr-15-5.text: Guitars and keyboards are stored here, although drums stay set up in the live room.

lr-15-6.text: Always close this heavy door completely, because even a small gap can let outside sound leak in.

lr-15-7.text: Students may reserve the studio for up to three hours per week, provided they've completed the introductory training course.

lr-16-1.text: Everyone signs in at this kiosk.

lr-16-2.text: Soldering irons must be switched off after use.

lr-16-3.text: The laser cutter is never left running unattended.

lr-16-4.text: These sewing machines are ideal for costumes, bags, and other fabric projects.

lr-16-5.text: Closed-toe shoes and protective eyewear are required whenever you're working in the woodshop.

lr-16-6.text: Every tool has an outlined spot on this wall, so it's easy to notice what's missing.

lr-16-7.text: Unfinished projects can be stored on these shelves for two weeks, but they must be clearly labeled with your name.

lr-17-1.text: Our tour begins in the rotunda.

lr-17-2.text: These stone tools are thousands of years old.

lr-17-3.text: Early maps reveal how people imagined distant lands.

lr-17-4.text: Light levels here are kept low to protect fragile fabrics from fading.

lr-17-5.text: In the conservation lab, specialists repair damaged artifacts using carefully tested techniques.

lr-17-6.text: Researchers wishing to examine original letters in the archive must request them in advance.

lr-17-7.text: We'll finish on the rooftop terrace, which offers a remarkable view of the oldest neighborhood in the city.

lr-18-1.text: The market opens at seven sharp.

lr-18-2.text: Most of these vegetables were harvested yesterday.

lr-18-3.text: Ask the cheese vendors before sampling anything on their tables.

lr-18-4.text: The bakery tent usually sells out of bread well before noon.

lr-18-5.text: Local chefs demonstrate seasonal recipes here, and visitors are welcome to taste the results.

lr-18-6.text: Shoppers can exchange their benefit cards for tokens, which are accepted at nearly every stall.

lr-18-7.text: At closing, help vendors collect food scraps so they can be composted rather than sent to a landfill.

lr-19-2.text: Our largest meteorite weighs nearly two hundred pounds.

lr-19-3.text: This model shows the planets' relative sizes and distances.

lr-19-4.text: Inside the dome theater, the projector recreates the night sky in remarkable detail.

lr-19-5.text: Once the lights dim, please put away your phones, since screens disrupt the view.

lr-19-6.text: This wall map identifies the constellations that are visible from our latitude during each season.

lr-19-7.text: On clear evenings, the observatory upstairs opens to the public, and volunteers help visitors locate planets through the telescope.

lr-20-1.text: Textbooks are organized by course number.

lr-20-2.text: Used copies are considerably cheaper than new ones.

lr-20-3.text: Renting a textbook can save you over half the cost.

lr-20-4.text: Notebooks, calculators, and lab coats are stocked in this aisle.

lr-20-5.text: At semester's end, we buy back books that remain in good condition.

lr-20-6.text: Before purchasing anything, double-check your syllabus, because professors sometimes switch editions at the last minute.

lr-20-7.text: Feel free to browse in the reading nook, but please return any books you've finished looking at to the cart.

lr-21-1.text: Follow the signs to ground transportation.

lr-21-2.text: University shuttles depart from this marked zone.

lr-21-3.text: Show your acceptance letter to receive a free ticket.

lr-21-4.text: Large suitcases should be placed in the compartment beneath the bus.

lr-21-5.text: Please board only when the driver confirms that your name appears on the passenger list.

lr-21-6.text: If the shuttle is delayed, you can wait on these benches, which are sheltered from the weather.

lr-21-7.text: The shuttle makes three campus stops, so check this map to find the one nearest your dorm.

lr-22-1.text: The lap pool reopens after maintenance.

lr-22-2.text: Please run counterclockwise on the indoor track.

lr-22-3.text: Courts can be reserved online up to three days ahead.

lr-22-4.text: Kayaks and tents can be rented here for weekend camping trips.

lr-22-5.text: Staff members in the gear shop can recommend equipment suited to your experience level.

lr-22-6.text: Squash rackets are provided, but you'll need to bring non-marking shoes to protect the floor.

lr-22-7.text: Guided hiking trips are posted on this board, and spaces often fill up within hours of being announced.
